full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed J: Both the Rules Nisi are predicated on similar facts find the application of the Companies Profit (Workers Participation) Act, 1968 ("the Act of 1968") as repealed by the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 ("the Act of 2006") and are, therefore, taken up for joint consideration and disposed of by this common judgment.

2. In Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why they shall not be directed to pay the Petitioners' share of the profits earned by Unilever Bangladesh Ltd (the Respondent No. 4 Company) which has accumulated in the Workers Participation Fund and welfare Fund of the Respondent No. 4 Company January, 2007 and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. As regards Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007, the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why they shall not be directed to pay the Petitioners their share of the profits earned by the Proforma Respondent No, 4 Company in the year 2006 which has accumulated in the Workers Participation Fund of Unilever Bangladesh Limited (Proforma Respondent No. 4) and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

PURVIEW OF THE LAW

3. These Writ Petitions, by their very nature require the purview of both the Act of 1968 and the Act of 2006 as provide the legal basis for the disposal of the same. This introduction to the law, as extensively submitted on by the learned Advocate for the Petitioners in both the Writ Petitions Mr Abdur Razzaq, begins first with the definition of a worker as found in the Act of 1968 and its metamorphosis in the Act of 2006. A simply structured definition of a worker is to be found in section of 2(f) of the Act of 1968 thus:

"2(f) "Worker" in relation to a company means an employee of the company whose basic monthly wages does not exceed Taka nine thousand and who has been in the employment of the Company for a period of not less than six months."

Section 233(1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006 brings about a change in that definition by introducing, an exclusionary standard leaving out those performing administrative, management and supervisory roles from its purview. That section reads thus:

“২৩৩। (১) (জ) কোন কোম্পানীর “শ্রমিক” বলিতে ঐ ব্যক্তিকে বুঝাইবে যিনি পদ-মর্যাদা নির্বিশেষে উক্ত কোম্পানীতে অন্যুন ছয়মাস যাবত চাকুরীতে নিযুক্ত রহিয়াছেন; তবে নিম্নোক্ত কোন ব্যক্তি এই আইনের আওতায় শ্রমিক সংজ্ঞার অন্তর্ভূক্ত হইবে না-

১। ব্যবস্থাপনা কিংবা প্রশাসনিক দায়িত্ব নিযুক্ত ব্যক্তি,

২। তদারকি কর্তৃত্বে নিযুক্ত ব্যক্তি যিনি পদাধিকারবলে বা তাহার উপর অর্পিত ক্ষমতাবলে ব্যবস্থাপনা বা প্রশাসনিক ধরণের কাজ করিয়া থাকেন।

4. Going beyond the definition of 'worker', the two Acts however follow a common pattern of setting out the manner of establishment and management of a Workers Participation Fund and Welfare Fund thereby delineating the spheres of function and statutory duties of three entities i.e., the Government, the employer Company and the Board of Trustees ("BOT"). Reproduced herein below are such of the provisions of the Act of 1968 followed by the corresponding provisions of the Act of 2006 appearing in the Bangla Text.

"3. Establishment of (Participation Fund and welfare Fund—Every company to -which the scheme applies shall-

(a) Establish a Workers Participation Fund and a Worker Welfare Fund in accordance with the scheme within one month of the date on which the scheme becomes applicable to it; and

(b) pay every year to the participation fund and welfare find, not later than nine months from the dose of the year, five percent of its net profits during such year, the proportion of the payment to the participation Fund and the Welfare Fund being 90 :

4. Management of the Participation Fund and Welfare Fund– (1) As soon as may be, after the establishment of the Participation Fund and a Welfare Fund, there shall be constituted a Board of Trustees consisting of the following, namely:

(a) two persons Dominated by the collective bargaining agent as defined in clause (v) of section 2 of the industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 (XXIII of 1969), and if there be no collective bargaining agent in the company, two persons elected by the workers of the company from amongst themselves and

(b) two persons nominated by the management of the company of whom at least one shall be a person from the accounts branch of the company.

(2) The persons holding office as Trustees shall elect for one year a person to be the Chairman of the Board alternately from amongst the Trustees [nominated or elected] under clause (a) of sub-section,(1) and those nominated under clause (b) of that sub-section, the first Chairman being from amongst, the latter.

(5) The Board shall manage and administer the Participation Fund and the welfare Fund in accordance with the provisions of this Act, the scheme and any rules made in this behalf.

(6) The. Board shall, in the exercise of its powers and performance of its functions under this Act, be subject to such, directions by the Government as may, from time to time, give.

(7) the Government if it is of opinion that a Trustee or a Board has been persistently failing in the performance of his or its functions or has generally been acting in a manner inconsistent with the objects and interests of the Participation Fund and the Welfare Fund may, after giving such Trustee or, as the case may be, the .Board, an opportunity of showing cause against it by order.

(a) remove such Trustee from his office or direct that the Board shall stand superseded for such period as may be specified in the order, and

(b) direct that, pending the election or nomination of a person in place of the Trustees removed from office or, as the case may be, the reconstitution of the Board, the powers and functions of the Trustees so removed or the Board shall exercised and performed by a person specified in the order.

5. Penalty—(1) Where any company fails to comply with the provisions of section 3, the Government may, by order in writing, require it to comply with those provisions within such time as may be specified in the order.

6. Power to call for information.—The Government may, at any time, call upon a company or a Board to furnish it with such information or documents, including the records of the proceedings of the company or the Board, as may be relevant or useful for the purposes of, or necessary, for ensuring proper compliance with, the provisions of this Act, the rules and the scheme.

7. Settlement of disputes, etc.—(1) Any differences arising between the Board and the company relating to the administration of the scheme shall be reported to the Government whose decision thereon shall be final.

9. Powers to make rules.—The Government may make rules to carry out the purposes of this Act."

5. As contemplated in section 4(5), find relevant to our purpose, are provisions as to the powers of the Government in the context of the 'Scheme' spelt out in the Schedule to the Act of 1968 ("the Schedule") Paragraph 14 of which specifically provides thus:

"14. Special provisions for industries working seasonally.- Notwithstanding any-thing contained in this Act or this Scheme, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make special provisions for the participation of the workers in the profits of companies engaged in industrial undertakings which operate only for a part of the year."

6. Paragraph 14 of the Scheme is cited here chiefly as an indicator of the extent of control and authority the Government is intended to wield in the overall workings of the Participation and Welfare Fund.

7. Similar to the provisions of the section 3 of the Act of 1968 are those of section 234 of the Act of 2006 which reads thus:

“২৩৪। অংশগ্রহণ তহবিল ও কল্যান তহবিল স্থাপন।–(১) এই অধ্যায় প্রযোজ্য হয় এরুপ প্রত্যেক কোম্পানী-

(ক) এই অধ্যায় প্রযোজ্য হইবার তারিখ হইতে এক মাসের মধ্যে এই অধ্যায়ের বিধান মোতাবেক একটি শ্রমিক অংশগ্রহণ তহবিল ও একটি কল্যান তহবিল স্থাপন করিবে; এবং

(খ) প্রত্যেক বৎসর উহা শেষ হইবার অন্যুন নয় মাসের মধ্যে উক্ত বৎসরের নীট মুনাফার পাঁচ শতাংশ অংশগ্রহন তহবিল ও কল্যাণ তহবিলে ৮০ঃ২০ অনুপাতে প্রদান করিবে।

(২) উপ-ধারা (১)(খ)এর অধীন উক্ত তহবিলদ্বয় প্রদত্ত অর্থ যে বৎসরের জন্য  প্রদান করা হইবে সে বৎসর শেষ হইবার অব্যবহিত পরের বৎসরের পহেলা তারিখে উহা তহবিলদ্বয়ে বরাদ্দ হইয়াছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে।

8. Section 235 of the Act of 2006 is equivalent to section 4 of the Act of 1968 and reads thus:

“২৩৫। তহবিলদ্বয়ের ব্যবস্থাপনা-(১) অংশগ্রহন তহবিল ও কল্যান তহবিল স্থাপিত হইবার পর যথাশীঘ্র সম্ভব নিম্নরুপ সদস্য সমন্বয়ে একটি ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড গঠিত হইবে,যথা-

(ক)কোম্পানীর যৌথ দরকষাকষি প্রতিনিধি কর্তৃক মনোনীত দুইজন সদস্য এবং এইরুপ কো্ন প্রতিনিধি না থাকিলে কোম্পানীর শ্রমিকগন কর্তৃক তাহাদের নিজেদের মধ্য হইতে নির্বাচিত দুইজন সদস্য ; এবং

(খ) কোম্পানীর ব্যবস্থাপনা কর্তৃক মনোনীত দুইজন সদস্য যাহাদের মধ্যে অন্তত একজন হইবেন কোম্পানীর হিসার শাখা হইতে মনোনীত ব্যক্তি।

(২) ট্রাস্টি বোর্ডের সদস্যগণ পালাক্রমে উপ-ধারা (১) (ক)ও(১)(খ) এর অধীন সদস্যগণের মধ্যে হইতে প্রত্যেক বৎসরের উহার একজন চেয়ারম্যান নির্বাচিত করিবেন তবে প্রথম চেয়ারম্যান উপ-ধারা (১)(খ) এর অধীন সদস্যগণের মধ্যে হইতে হইবে।

(৩) এই অধ্যায় এবং এতদউদ্দেশ্য প্রণীত বিধির বিধান অনুযায়ী ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড তহবিলদ্বয়ের ব্যবস্থাপনা ও পরিচালনা করিবে।

(৪) ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড উহার ক্ষমতা প্রয়োগ ও দায়িত্ব পালনের ব্যপারে সরকার কর্তৃক সময় সময় প্রদত্ত নির্দেশের অধীন থাকিবে।

(৫) সরকার যদি এই মত পোষণ করে যে ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড বা উহার কোন সদস্য দায়িত্ব পালনে পুনঃপুনঃ ব্যর্থ হইতেছে অথবা সাধারণত তহবিলদ্বয়ের লক্ষ্য ও স্বার্থের সহিত অসংগতিপূর্ণভাবে কাজকর্ম করিতেছে তাহা হইলে সরকার বোর্ড বা সদস্যটিকে কারণ দর্শাইবার সুযোগ দান করিয়া আদেশ দ্বারা-

(ক) উহাতে নির্দিষ্ট মেয়াদের জন্য বোর্ড বাতিল করিতে পারিবে অথবা সদস্যটিকে তাহার পদ হইতে অপসারন করিতে পারিবে; এবং

(খ) ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড পুর্নগঠিত না হওয়া পযর্ন্ত বা উক্ত সদস্যের পদে নূতন সদস্য মনোনীত বা নির্বাচিত না হওয়া পর্যন্ত বোর্ডের বা ইক্ত সদস্যের ক্ষমতা ও দায়িত্ব আদেশ উল্লিথিত ব্যক্তি কর্তৃক প্রয়োগ ও পালনের জন্য নির্দেশ দিতে পারিবে।

(৬) উপ-ধারা (৫) এর অধীন ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড বাতিল হইবার পর উহার সদস্যগণ তাহাদের পদে আর বহাল থাকিবেন না এবং এই অধ্যায়ে বা কোন বিধিতে ট্রাস্টি বোর্ডের উল্লেখ থাকিলে উহা উক্ত উপ-ধারার অধীন প্রদত্ত আদেশে উল্লিথিত ব্যক্তিকে বুঝাইবে।

(৭) বাতিলের মেয়াদ শেষ হইবার পূর্বেই এই অধ্যায়ের বিধান অনুযায়ী ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড পুনগঠিত হইবে যাহাতে উহা্ উক্ত মেয়াদ শেষ হইবার পর উহার কার্যভার গ্রহন করিতে পারে”।

9. Section 236 of the Act of 2006 as is equivalent to section 5 of the Act of 1968 reads thus:

“২৩৬। দন্ড –(১) সে ক্ষেত্রে কোন কোম্পানী ধারা ২৩৪ এর বিধানগুলি মানিতে ব্যর্থ হয় সেক্ষেত্রে সরকার আদেশ দ্বারা উক্ত আদেশে উল্লিখিত সময়ের মধ্যে উক্ত বিধানগুলি মানিবার জন্য নির্দেশ দিতে পারিবে”।

10. Section 237 of the Act of 2006 as is equivalent to section 6 of the Act of 1968 reads thus:

“২৩৭। তথ্য তলবের ক্ষমতা-এই অধ্যায় অথবা সংশ্লিষ্ট কোন বিধির যথাযথ প্রয়োগ নিশ্চিত করার লক্ষ্যে এবং ইহার প্রয়োজনে সরকার যে কোন সময়ে কোন কোম্পানি বা ট্রাস্টি বোর্ডর নিকট হইতে তথ্য দলিল-দস্তাবেজ অথো কার্যধারার নতি পত্র তলব করিতে পারিবে।

11. Section 238 of the Act of 2006 as is equivalent section 7 of the Act of 1968 reads

thus:

“২৩৮। বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তি, ইত্যাদি-(১) তহবিলদ্বয়ের প্রশাসন সংক্রান্ত কোন বিষয়ে ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড এবং কোম্পানীর মধ্যে কোন মতবিরোধ দেখা দিলে বিষয়টি সরকারের নিকট পেশ করিতে হইবে এবং ইহার উহার সরকারের সিদ্ধান্ত চুড়ান্ত হইবে।

(২)তহবিলদ্বয় হইতে প্রাপ্ত সুযোগ-সুবিধা সম্পর্কে ট্রাস্টি বোর্ড অখবা কোম্পানীর বিরুদ্ধে কোন শ্রমিকের কোন অভিযোগ থাকিলে উহা দশম অধ্যায়ে বর্ণিত মজুরী হইতে কর্তন সম্পর্কে বিরোধ নিস্পত্তির পন্থা অনুযায়ী নিস্পত্তি করিতে হইবে।

12. Section 250 of the Act of 2006 follows on the lines of Paragraph 14 of the Schedule of the Act of 1968 and reads thus:

“২৫০। মৌসুমী কাজে নিযুক্ত শিল্পের ক্ষেত্রে বিশেষ বিধান এই অধ্যায়ে যাহা কিছু থাকুক না কেন  যে সকল কোম্পানী সমস্ত বৎসরের পরিবর্তে উহার কোন অংশে উহাদের কাজ চালায়ে সে সকল কোম্পানীর মুনাফায় শ্রমিকগণের অংশ গ্রহণের জন্য সরকার সরকারী গেজেটে প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা বিধান করিতে পারিবে।

FACTS GERMANE

13. The above provisions of law come into play in the facts as arise commonly in both these Writ Petitions. This Court notes further at the outset that facts common to both these Writ Petitions have been argued upon by the learned Advocate for the Petitioners Mr Razzaq and Mr Imran Siddiq by treating Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 to be the lead Petition in that regard. The Respondent No. 2 BOT (or "Board" as and where necessary) has been established by section 4 of the Act of 1968 which provides that there shall be a Board comprising of two per-sons nominated by the collective Bargaining Agent ("CBA") of the Respondent No. 4 Company, Unilever Bangladesh Limited, a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act 1913 and two persons nominated by the Company's management. The 130T performs its functions under the direct control and supervision of the Government of Bangladesh under the Act of 1968. Section 4(6) of the Act of 1968 provides that the BOT shall in the exercise of its powers and performance of its functions be subject to such directions as the Government may from time to time issue. By section 4(7) of the Act of 1968, the Government has been empowered to dissolve the BOT and /or remove a Trustee from office and appoint any other person to perform the functions of the Board. Furthermore, Paragraph 14 of the Schedule provides that the Government may by Gazette notification make special provisions for the participation of workers in the profits of companies engaged in industrial undertakings which operate for only part of the year. Paragraph 15 of the Schedule empowers the Government, at the request of a company engaged in more than one industrial undertaking in different locations, to permit the splitting up of the Participation Fund and Welfare Fund. Furthermore, Paragraph 16 of the Schedule provides that the BOT may with the approval of the Government enter into agreements with the Investment Corporation of Bangladesh or Sonali Bank, entrusting the management of the Workers Participation and Welfare Fund to the said Corporation or Bank. Thus, it is apparent from the aforesaid provisions of the Act of 1968 and the Schedule thereto that the BOT of the Company operates under the complete control and supervision of the Government of Bangladesh.

13A. Furthermore, the affairs of the Respondent No. 4 Company, insofar as it relates to the administration of the Workers Participation and Welfare Fund, are conducted under the direct control and supervision of the Government of Bangladesh, which owns more than 39% of shares in the Company. By section, 5(2) of the Act of 1968, the Government has been empowered to impose a penalty upon the Respondent No. 4 Company if the said Company fails to establish a Workers Participation and Welfare Fund in accordance with section 3 of the said Act. Section 6 of the said Act empowers the Government to call upon the Company or the BOT to furnish it with such information and /or documents as may be necessary for the purpose of determining compliance with the provisions of the Act. By section 7(1) of the Act of 1968; any difference between the Board and the Company relating to the administration of the Scheme is to be reported to the Government, whose decision thereon shall be final.

14. In view of the nature and extent of control of the Government of Bangladesh in relation to the administration of the Workers Participation and Welfare Fund, it is stated that the Company and the BOT are merely acting as subordinate functionaries of the Government in administering the said Funds under the provisions of the Act of 1968. The Company or the Board has no discretion in the administration of the said Funds but are required by the provisions of the Act of 1968 to act in strict compliance with the directions issued by the Government of Bangladesh from time to time in this regard.

15. In categorically introducing the Petitioners as workers it is asserted in the Applications that the Petitioners have no authority to appoint or dismiss any employee of the Company. They have no authority to sign/execute any documents or operate any transaction on behalf of the Company.

16. It is specifically stated that the Petitioners have never been entrusted with any managerial or administrative functions during their tenure of service in the Company. The Petitioners have, at no point in time, been entrusted with any supervisory role in the management of the affairs of the Company. Furthermore, there is no evidence, documentary or otherwise, to show that the Petitioners duties and responsibilities altered after their promotion.

17. Section 3 of the Act of 1968 provides that every company to which the Scheme applies shall establish a Workers Participation Fund and a Workers Welfare Fund within one month of the date on which the Scheme became applicable to it. The scope of the Scheme has been defined in the Schedule to the Act of 1968 to include companies engaged in industrial undertakings having a hundred or more workers in one shift or having a paid-up capital of Taka 50 lakh or fixed assets of Taka 100 Lakh.

18. In 1968, the Company established a Workers Participation Fund in accordance with section 3 of the Act of 1968. It is stated that the existence of the Workers Participation and Welfare Fund continues, despite the repeal of the Act of 1968, by virtue of a savings clause contained in section 353(2)(ka) of the Labour Act 2006 i.e., the Act of 2006.

19. Pursuant to the establishment of such Workers Participation and Welfare Fund, the Company deposited 5% of its net profits in the Participation and Welfare Fund each year in the proportion of 90:10 in accordance with section-3(b) of the Act of 1968. By section 234 of the Act of 2006, the proportion to be deposited in the said funds has been changed from 90:10 to 80:20.

20. Once the profits are deposited by the Company in the Workers Participation Fund and Welfare Fund, they are distributed by the BOT in accordance with Paragraph 5 of the Schedule of the Act of 1968, which provides that two-thirds of the said Funds shall be distributed in cash among all workers.

21. It is stated that prior to the coming into force of the Act of 2006, the two original Petitioners in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 209 fulfilled the criteria to be classified as 'workers' within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Act of 1968. Both these Petitioners were in employment of the Company for more than six months and were receiving a monthly salary of less than Taka 9,000. As such, the Petitioners, being 'workers', were receiving their share of the Workers Participation and Welfare Fund in accordance with the provisions of the Act of 1968. A further categorization of the Petitioners in both the Writ Petitions is necessitated, submits the learned Advocate for the Petitioner Mr lmran Siddiq by reference, to section 336 of the Act of 2006 which reads thus:

“৩৩৬। কতিপয় ক্ষেত্রে চাকুরীর বর্তমান শর্তাবলী সংরক্ষণ ।-এই আইন অথবা কোন বিধি, প্রবিধান বা স্কীমের কোন কিছুই এই আইন প্রবর্তন হওয়ার সময় উহার দ্বারা রহিত কোন আইনের অধীন অথবা কোন রোয়েদাদ চুক্তি নিস্পত্তি বা প্রচলিত প্রথার অধীন কোন শ্রমিকের ভোগকৃত অধিকার বা সুযোগ-সৃবিধা তিনি যতদিন উক্ত প্রবর্তনের তারিখে যে মালিকের অধীন কর্মরত ছিলেন সে মালিকের অধীন চাকুরীরত থাকিবেন ততদিন পর্যন্ত ব্যাহত বা ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত করিবেন, যদি তাহার উক্ত অধিকার এবং সুযোগ সুবিধা এই আইন, বিধি প্রবিধান বা স্কীমের অধীন প্রদত্ত অধিকার ও সুযোগ সুবিধা হইতে অধিকতর অনুকূল হয়।

22. Mr Siddiq therefore takes care to point out that in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 the following Petitioners had fulfilled the definition of 'worker' under section 2(f) of the Act of 1968 and continue in their employment of the Company under the Act of 2006 and, therefore, can take advantage of section 336 of the 2006 Act, i.e., the Petitioner Nos. 1-12, 14, 19-22, 24, 26-28, 30, 32-36, 40, 43-45, 46,51, 53, 55, 56, 59, 61, 66-68, 71-75, 78, 94-97, 99, 101-104. This Court is also informed that the following Petitioners, having not fulfilled the definition of 'worker' under the Act of 1968 and/or having been employed under the Act of 2006, cannot take advantage of section 336 of the Act of 2006. These are Petitioner Nos. 13, 15-18, 23, 25, 29, 31; 37-39, 41/42, 47, 48, 49, 50, 52, 54, 57, 58, 60, 62-65, 69, 70, 76-77, 79-93, 98, 100. It is also submitted further by reference to the Petitioners' Affidavit-in-Reply filed dated 26-5-210 that the Petitioner Nos. 79-90 have been inadvertently added as Petitioners and since they have already filed cases before the Labour Court, therefore, Petitioner Nos, 79-90 may be excluded from the ambit of any Order of this Court. With regard to Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007, Mr Siddiq submits that all Petitioners i.e., Petitioner Nos. 1-46 fulfilled the definition of 'workers' under the Act of 1968 and continued their employment under the Act of 2006 and, therefore, can take advantage of section 336. As such, any Petitioners who had participated in the profits of the Company in their capacity as 'workers' in accordance with the Act of 1968, had acquired a vested right to participate in the Company's profits, which has not been taken away by an express provision of law. Such vested right of these Applicants under the Act of 1968 to participate in the Company's profits" has in fact been expressly preserved by section 336 of the Act of 2006."

23. On 11-10-2006, the Act of 2006 came into force, repealing the Act of 1968. Under the Act of 2006, the definition of 'worker' has been altered such that an employee may be classified as a "worker' if he/she has been in service of a company for a minimum period of six months irrespective of his/her designation and pay-scale, however, he/she may not be so classified if he/she is employed in a managerial or administrative position.

24. All the Petitioners above in varying degrees have been deprived of payments from the Funds, till date. This, for example, is attributed in the case of Petitioner Nos, 1 and 2 in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 to their promo-ions on varied dates completely failing to appreciate, however, that they were performing exactly the same functions after being promoted as were being performed by them in their earlier positions. In this the BOT also completely failed to appreciate the purport of section 233(f)(Ja) of the Act of 2006 according to which an employee, irrespective of his designation and pay, scale, would continue to classified as a 'worker', provided he is not employed in any managerial or administrative position.

25. Furthermore, it is asserted that the Petitioners, being 'workers' under the Act of 1968 and having participated in the Company's profits since their appointment, have acquired a vested right to participate in the profits of the Company, notwithstanding the repeal of the Act of 1968. Such vested right of the Petitioners is submitted to have been protected under section 336 of the Act of 2006. Section 336 of the Act of 2006 provides that a 'worker' who had been enjoying benefits under any scheme framed under an Act which has been repealed by the Act of 2006, would continue to enjoy such benefits, if such benefits are better than those provided under the Act of 2006. As such, by section 336 of the Act of 2006, the Petitioners are submitted to be entitled to participate in the profits of the Company, as availed by them earlier under the provisions of the Act of 1968. Thus, for example, if is stated that the benefits availed of by the Petitioners under the Workers Participation and Welfare fund Scheme set out in the Act of 1968 are much better than those available to the Petitioners under the Act of 2006. In 2007, the annual earnings of the Petitioner No. 1 in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009, including the amount he received from the Workers Participation and Welfare Fund under the Act of 1968, amounted to approximately Taka 4,26,000. In 2008, the said Petitioner is stated to have been unlawfully deprived of the Company's profits from the said Fund and earned a total amount of Taka 3,00,000 which was significantly lower than his earnings in the previous year. Furthermore, the Petitioner No. 2 in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 calculates that his total earnings in the year 2009 will be substantially less than his earnings in 2008, which included a share of the profits earned by the Company that accumulated under the Company's Workers Participation and Welfare Fund Scheme set up under the Act of 1968.

26. This Court is informed that on 13-5-2009, a Division Bench of this Court disposed of a Writ Petition (which was filed by one-Md. Jalaluddin, an employee of Meghna Petroleum Ltd. claiming a share of the said company's Workers Participation and Welfare Fund), making the Rule absolute and holding that the new legislation (i.e., the Act of 2006) cannot take away the financial benefit of a worker which was being enjoyed by him earlier (i.e., under the Act of 1968). The said Bench, it is noted, also directed the authorities to pay the Writ Petitioner his share of the company's Workers Participation and Welfare Funds.

MAINTAINABILITY

27. Two specific submissions are made by reference to these Applications. First, that the Respondent No. 2 BOT failed to appreciate the purport of section 336 of the Act of 2006 which protects and preserves the vested right of the Petitioners accrued under the Act of 1968 to receive a share of the Company's profits accumulating each year in the Workers Participation and Welfare Funds of the Company and as such the Respondents should be directed by this Court to pay the Petitioners a share of the Company's profits from the such Funds of the Company. Second, the Petitioners having been classified and treated as 'workers' by the Company under both the Act of 1968 and the Act of 2006, the subsequent refusal of the Company to allow the Petitioners to participate in the profits of the Company is arbitrary and suffers from complete non-application of mind and, as such, the Respondents should be direct-ed by this Court to pay the Petitioners their dues from the said Funds of the Company.

28. It has been asserted at the outset by and on behalf of the Respondent No. 2 BOT that no Writ lies against the BOT given that it is not a 'person' within the meaning of Article 102(5) of the Constitution. In other words, the BOT declares itself as not being a statutory public authority performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority. That assertion stands to be tested against the Schemes of both the Act of 1968 and that of 2006 by examining the nature and extent of control of the Government over the functions of the BOT. The learned Advocates for the Petitioners Mr Abdur Razzak and Mr Imran A. Siddiq have impressed upon this Court that the rationale of the functions of the BOT and the reason for its establishment under both the 1968 and 2006 statutory regimes is to ensure that workers remain free from exploitation by employers as in fact reflected in the Preamble and Article 14 of the Constitution as enjoins upon the State a duty to ensure such freedom from exploitation. It is asserted that both the 1968 and 2006 legislations operate as beneficial legislations in that light. It is noted that sections 4(6); 4(7), 6, 7 and Paragraph 14, 15 and 16 of the Schedule of the Act of 1968 and the corresponding or similar provisions in sections 235(3)(4) (5), 236, 237, 238, 239, 248, 250-252 of the Act of 2006 do indeed contemplate that the BOT operates under a considerable control and supervision of the Government.

29. It is submitted that the BOT in fact acts as an instrumentality or agent of the Government in administering the Welfare and Participation Funds and that in fact the BOT has not any discretion reserved to itself in the administration of the Funds and is required to act in strict compliance with the directions issued by the Government from time to time. The learned Advocates for the Petitioners in substantiation of this line of argument have introduced strands of reasoning that help in testing the extent to which the BOT may indeed be found to be a, functionary of and administratively dominated by and under the control of the Government. These strands aim at establishing either that the BOT acts as (a) subordinate functionary or (b) is under the effective Government Control, or indeed the nature of its function partakes of both such characteristics. The specific provisions of the two legislations of 1968 and of 2006 as referred above establish overwhelmingly the fact that the BOT is not only a body the activities or the principal activities of which are authorised by the relevant legislations but that fundamentally these successive enactments have had the intended cumulative effect of both creating and sustaining it.

30. Functioning with such statutory credentials it is also noted that the BOT has been intended to operate with a specific purpose in view. It is agreed by all parties across the board that the purpose of the two successive legislations is indeed to protect the rights of workers and to ensure their share in the Company's profits, thereby, removing the spectre of any form of exploitation of these workers by their employers. That, Messrs Razzaq and Siddiq strenuously argue, brings the activities of the BOT into the public realm thereby, justifying a designation of the BOT not only as a statutory authority but significantly as a statutory public authority. This Court is reminded here that the BOT in administering the Funds in accordance with the Government's directives in fact facilitates the discharge of a fundamental responsibility of the State to ensure the protection of all workers from all exploitation under Article 14 of the Constitution. The two legislative enactments in that context ensure, the mechanism in accordance with which the State can effectively discharge its responsibility as above through the agency of the BOT reserving nevertheless to itself substantial authority of oversight, control, imposing penalties and to act as an arbiter of differences that otherwise hinder a proper administration of the Funds as contemplated in the legislations. That takes us to the provisions in Article 152 of the Constitution that defines 'State' as including, inter alia, statutory public authorities. That provision read with Article 102(5) of the Constitution under which the term 'person' is extended to include a statutory public authority clearly, in this Court's opinion, substantiates the argument on behalf of the Petitioners that Article 102(2)(a)(i) does indeed contemplate a Writ of Mandamus to issue against any entity as the BOT performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic. Extensive arguments have been made by the learned Advocates for the Petitioners by reference to decisions in Arif Sultan vs DESA reported in 60 DLR 431, Mofizul Huq vs Mofizur Rahman reported in 49 DLR (AD) 38, MH Chowdhury vs GM Titas Gas reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 61, New Dacca Industries vs Quamrul Huda reported in 31 DLR (AD) 234, Zakir Hossain Munshi vs Bangladesh reported in 55 DLR 130, Farzana vs Securities and Exchange Commission reported in 54 DLR 66, Abdus Sabur vs REB reported in 10 BLC 502, Zahir Akhter vs Bangladesh Biman reported in 61 DLR 446, Conforce Limited vs Titas Gas Transmission report-ed in 42 DLR 33 and Shafiqur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 8 BLC 521.

31. In this Court's view, the Appellate Division's Judgment in the Mofizul Huq Case serves as an appropriate staring point for determining the public nature of the functions of the BOT. In that case, the Appellate Division took due note of the provisions of section 3(28) of the General Clauses Act that identifies a 'Local Authority' as inter alia a "body or authority constituted or established by this Government under any law". The ratio decidendi of that judgment applied to the BOT serves to establish that the 130T is indeed a 'local authority' within the definition in the General Clauses Act as it owes its existence to the Acts of 1968 and 2006. In other words, indisputably the BOT is a creature of statute which has no identity distinct from that granted it by the two Acts of 1968 and 2006, as held in Vaish Degree College vs Lakshmi Narain reported in AIR 1976 (SC) 888:

"...the position seems to be that the institution concerned must once its very existence to a statute which would be the fountainhead of its points. The question in such cases to be asked is, if there is no statute would the institution have any legal existence. If the answer is in the negatives, then undoubtedly it is a statutory body".

32. It is deduced by this Court from the above that the BOT is so deeply rooted into both the Act of 1968 and the Act of 2006 that it has no separate existence of its own without any reference to either of those statutes. It is of the nature of a statutory body the umbilical cord of which cannot be and was never intended to be severed from its parent statutes.

33. Secondly, perusal of these judicial precedents leads this Court to hold that there is indeed no hard and fast rule in determining the extent to which a creature of a statute like the BOT may or may not have an autonomy of existence distinct from a regulatory entity like the Government. The answer would be dependent m each case on the dynamics of such relationship and the workings of the statutory body within the particular statutory scheme.

34. This Court holds that the tests here, as prescribed in the Arif Sultan Case, would be

(1) the existence of deep and extensive control of the Government, and

(2) the true rationale in setting up the BOT as well as the Funds.

In applying the two tests above, it is this Court's conclusion that the purpose of the Acts of 1968 and 2006 has indeed been to establish the BOT as an instrument or agency of the Government over which the Government was always/intended to have a deep and pervasive control. The BOT, thereby, acquiring the complexion of the instrumentality of the Government is found by this Court to be indeed amenable to Writ jurisdiction.

35. It is noted furthermore that taking a cue from the Arif Sultan Case, this Court in the Zahir Akhter Case deduced that when the Government has a supervisory as opposed to a mere regulatory role over another statutory body, a case of instrumentality or agency of the Government as above is well established. In that Case it was also held that judicial precedents have established that when an authority exercises the power of the Government as its instrumentality in any manner, that makes the authority a public body, amenable to the jurisdiction of judicial review of the superior Court (61 DLR 446 at para 65, page 461).

36. The public nature of the functions of the BOT is found further to be predicated on the very scheme of the Acts of 1968 and 2006. The purpose of both the Acts is to protect the rights of the workers i.e., to ensure in the present instance that they get a fair share of the Company's profits and to prevent exploitation of the workers by their employers. The BOT by administering the Welfare and Participation Funds in accordance with the directions of the Government is ensuring that workers are protected from exploitation by their employers. To that extent, the BOT by implementing the provisions presently of the Act of 2006 is intended to facilitate fulfillment of the fundamental responsibility of the State to emancipate workers from all forms of exploitation. In that regard, this Court takes due note of the Preamble of the Constitution which states that it shall be the fundamental aim of the State to realize through the democratic process a socialist state free from exploitation i.e., a society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice, political, economic and social, will be secured for all citizens. Indeed, in keeping with the demands of a socialist state, the framers of the Constitution enacted Articles 10 and 14 of the Constitution, Article 10 provides that a socialist economic system shall be established with a view to ensuring the attainment of a just and egalitarian society, free from exploitation of man by man (e.g, of workers by employers). Article 14 of the Constitution makes it a fundamental responsibility of the State to protect peasants and workers from all forms of exploitation. Given further that Articles 10 and 14 are fundamental principles of State policy, according to Article 8(2) such fundamental principles of State policy are fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh and shall be applied by the State in the making of laws (i.e., the Acts of 1968 and 2006) and shall form the basis of the work of the State i.e., the duties and responsibilities vested by statute in the BOT (which being a statutory public authority, is a component of the State) to implement the provisions presently of the Act of 2006. This Court holds in this regard that the BOT, being a statutory public authority, is a component of the State. And in view of the socialist character of the State, the functions of the BOT in protecting workers from exploitation by implementing the provisions of the Act of 2006 are in fact public governmental functions and closely related to those required to be performed by the State in its sovereign capacity.

37. Furthermore, according to the Judgment in Khondker Delwar Hossain, Secretary, BNP. Party (in CP, No. 1044/09), Munshi Ahsan Kabir and others (in CP No. 1045/09) vs Bangladesh Italian Marble Works Ltd., Dhaka and others (in-both the cases) (Bangladesh Constitution (Fifth Amendments) reported VI(B) ADC (2010) 1, the socialist character of the State is a basic feature of the Constitution. As such, the functions intended to be performed by the BOT in implementing the provisions presently of the Act of 2006, being such as to strengthen the basic structures or structural pillars of the Constitution, the functions of the BOT are clearly not only of public importance but also are of the same nature as those required to be performed by the State in its sovereign capacity.

38. In view of the fact that the BOT is for all practical purposes, being run by the Government and is also instrumental to the fulfillment of the fundamental responsibility of the State, it is clear to this Court that the illegalities of the BOT in administering the funds of the Workers Participation and Welfare Funds are amenable, therefore, to the Writ jurisdiction.

39. Furthermore the petitioners rely on the judgment of the High Court Division in the Meghna Petroleum Case and the Padma Oil Case and submit that the High Court Division has held the Writ Petition against Meghna Petroleum Ltd. (which is similar to the instant case) to be maintainable. It is noted that in this regard the Petitioners rely on-Chapter VII of the High Court Rules and the decisions in particular in Chittagong Port Authority vs Sad/wan Bima reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 373 and Pubali Bank vs Chairman, 'Labour Court reported in 44 DLR (AD) 40.

40. It is evident, therefore, that the higher judiciary of this land has time and time again endorsed the tests of "subordinate functionary" and "governmental control" to equip various statutory authorities with the status of statutory public authorities whose functions are indeed amenable to Writ jurisdiction. It is indeed ascertainable from a few of these cases additionally that statutory authorities who operate, in particular, in the commercial sector or operate with a profit motive remain all the same amenable to intervention through Writ Applications provided that such nature of the work does not sufficiently detract from the overwhelmingly beneficial or altruistic aspect of their functions. Indeed in one case in particular, i.e., the Arif Sultan Case, there is an implicit endorsement of the fact that the profit motive will not necessarily detract from any authority being amenable to Writ Jurisdiction provided sufficient Governmental control over that authority can be established. Of the test or guidelines devised in that case to determine whether an entity is an "instrumentally or an agency" of the Government or indeed "a local authority" those of the existence of an extensive and pervasive control of the Government -and of the true rationale in the setting up of that particular authority are found by this Court to be particularly relevant in the present facts and circumstances.

41. It is this Court's finding, therefore, that the two successive legislations of 1968 and 2006 not only constitute the fountainhead of power granted the BOT, and without which legislative sanctions the BOT would not exist, but also significantly envisage such powers to be exercised for and on behalf of the Government and under its express and continuous supervision. That being the finding of this Court, it is consequentially also found on this preliminary issue of maintainability that the BOT's activities, as appear in the facts and circumstances, are indeed amenable to Writ Jurisdiction as impressed upon this Court by the Petitioners. That leads this Court now to deal with the more substantive issues that arises in these Writ Applications considered in the context of the specific provisions of the law as already referred to above.

SUBSTANTIVE ISSUES

42. In this regard, two avenues of inquiry have had to be undertaken by this Court in the context of the extant provisions of the Act of 2006 in particular. The first relates to the legislative and judicial standards determining whether the petitioners before this Court are indeed 'workers' or not. The second being the entity in which the statutory authority is primarily reposed to decide on such status as 'workers'. These avenues of inquiry do not in fact run parallel to each other but appear some-what intertwined to this Court given this Court's opinion that unlike a definition of a 'worker' provided in section 2(f) of the Act of 1968, that under section 233(1) (Ja) of the Act of 2006 appears to repose in one authority or the other the responsibility to decide upon the status of a 'worker'. But the assignment of such responsibility is implicit in section 233(1) (Ja). That means that this provision of the law is itself silent in identifying such authority. In other words, section 233(1)(Ja) proceeds to assign such responsibility to an unidentified authority. The matter gets murkier given that this section is also notably vague or silent as to the objective standards that must be taken into consideration by such unidentified authority to necessarily give any meaning to the test introduced therein by drawing a clear line Demarcation between who may and may not be entitled to the beneficial application of the Funds in their favour. However, clear indicators of the intent in the Act of 2006 to ascertain the identity of the authority which may have the primary responsibility to assign the status of a 'worker' or not upon any individual are to be found in the other fairly extensive provisions of that law pertaining to the management and oversight of the Funds in general and in that context, unlike in section 233(1)(Ja), clearly delineating the extent and spheres of the power and authority of the BOT, the Company and the Government in the due and proper administration of the Funds.

43. It is here that arguments have been made on behalf of the BOT that the power in section 235(3) in particular of the Act of 2006 to manage and administer the Funds is to be deemed to be inclusive of determining who is a 'worker' to qualify for the beneficial application of the Funds. In other words, the BOT will have this Court believe that the power of Fund-management and administration under section 235(3) is an all encompassing and an all-empowering power recognized in favour of the BOT. But upon a reading, for example, of sections 240, 242, 243 and 252 of the Act of 2006, it is, however, clear to this Court that such notion of an all-empowering authority gets whittled down somewhat by very specific provisions otherwise laying down the boundaries within which the BOT must operate with regard to, for instance, investing on behalf of the Funds, the utilization and overall management of the Funds, etc. It is noted further that in so specifically setting out the specific functions of the BOT, significantly no authority is expressly reserved by the terms of the Act of 2006 in the BOT to determine on the powers and duties of the Petitioners, that is, whether these are supervisory, managerial or administrative in nature. It has been submitted on behalf of the Petitioners that such authority in fact, upon a true construction of section 233(1)(J4), must be read as lying with the Company itself in preference to the BOT. It is here that Messrs Razzak and Siddiq have satisfactorily argued that the notion of an all-encompassing power and discretion in this regard vesting in the BOT as pro-pounded by Counsel for the BOT, Mr Kamal-ul Alam remains notably further qualified by Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the Company under which the power to appoint, fix and determine the power and duties of employees resides solely with the Board of Directors of the Company. Indeed, Article 114, in ideal circumstances, would be the provision by dint of which any company could and should assert itself in this regard to the exclusion wholly of any other authority perniciously arrogating to itself any similar authority to make such determination on the status of workers.

44. It is painfully evident, however, in the facts and circumstances that the situation prevailing within the Company is far removed from such an ideal situation. The Company, since 2006, appears to have abdicated its responsibility to play an assertive role in this regard as reflected in its failure to provide specific, comprehensive and due information as to the status of workers to the BOT. Equally alarming is the case of the Company failing to ensure strict compliance with section 235 of the Act of 2006, sub-section (2) of which mandates, a yearly rotation in the post of Chairman of BOT in a manner that a representative of the Company and of the CBA must alternatively be elected to occupy that post. It is found that the Company has thus directly contributed to the BCT's assumption of apparently extra-statutory responsibility and authority by turning a blind eye to the express violation of Article 235(2) for over twelve years now. Evidently, the Company has opted for such a dent in its authority in administering the Fund much earlier than the coming into force of the Act of 2006. That scenario of express, sustained and tolerated violation of the provisions of both the Acts of 1968 of 2006 is further exacerbated by the Government itself not attaching due significance to its role of oversight and ensuring accountability of the administration of the Funds. In this regard, this Court's attention has been drawn, in particular, to the specific responsibilities to be undertaken by the Government under sections 4, 5 and 6 of the Act of 1968 and corresponding provisions of the-Act of 2006 found in sections 235, 236 and 237. Of these provisions, section 237 of the Act of 2006 corresponding to section 6 of the Act of 1968 is germane given that it grants the Government absolute authority to summon information at any time to examine due compliance with other provisions of the Act and the rule in the administration of the Fund. That power appears, however, never to have been invoked thus far by the Government not with standing the festering disputes that have plagued the Company for so many years and have compelled numerous of its employees to seek recourse to this Court's jurisdiction leading to resultant judicial interventions. Cleanly, the Company has not deemed it necessary to treat, for whatever reason such loss of its control over the BOT, evident in it being denied the post of Chairmanship in alternate years, to itself refer the matter to the Government by invocation of the provisions of section 238(1) of the Act of 2006 that gives the Government the final authority to resolve disputes as may arise with regard to the administration of the Funds. A laissez-aller culture has, thereby, been allowed to develop within the Company equipping, and illegally so the BOT so with authority in a manner and to the extent that was clearly never within the contemplation of the two legislations concerned so to grant. It was clearly further-more not within the legislative intent that the Company should be complicit in contributing to the accretion to the BOT of such authority purely as an apparent trade off between the Company's management and the CBA for considerations that have not been fully explained before this Court but only hinted at, but the reasons for which this Court can clearly guess at. It is crystal clear, however, that adverse impact upon the rights and interests of the Petitioners as a result of such trade off to otherwise ensure a peaceful environment within the company has been considerable.

45. Furthermore, the Government turning a blind eye to this unholy alliance between the Company and the CBA has also led to the operation of entire segments of the Act of 1968 and, thereafter, the Act of 2006 to be held in abeyance. In that context this Court views the merit in this Application to lie in the fact of prodding both the Company and the Government to resuscitate such of those provisions of the law and restore the essential statutory balance between their roles and in their dealings with the BOT.

46. The Company appears, in particular, in these proceedings to be happily sitting on the fence, as it were, in responding to the claims of the Petitioners. Unhappily, however, that has led the Company to be prone to equivocation in adopting a stance vis-a-vis the Petitioners' Case, While for example, therefore, in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 the Company has sought to establish that the Petitioners do not indeed perform managerial and administrative functions as substantiated by a chart ("Job Description Chart") produced and brought on record as Annexure 'X2', to the Company's Affidavit-in-Opposition describing the nature of the work performed by the Petitioners, it appears nevertheless to be more forthcoming in disputing such status to be accorded to the Petitioners in Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007, "That latter stance is evident from submissions made by the learned Advocate for the Company in Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007 Mr AJ Mohammad All by arguing that the definition in section 233(1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006 is so very exclusionary of the status and the claimed entitlement of the Petitioners as workers that their applications before this Court are devoid of all merit and substance. That line of argument has necessarily required this Court to embark on the exercise of determining the tests of managerial, administrative and supervisory functions under which any employee may be disqualified from the beneficial application of the legislations concerned. That exercise has been undertaken solely to put all three actors concerned i.e., the Company, the BOT and the Government, on notice of the objective judicially endorsed standards that are already in place and which must be referred to prior to determining who is a 'worker' or not. That exercise is also necessitated further by the fact that the Act of 2006, as earlier noted, remains silent in prescribing those standards. Undoubtedly such a statutory lacuna, has led to arbitrary exercises of discretion, and that too by an unauthorized entity being the BOT, to exclude the Petitioners from the beneficial application of the Funds.

47. This Court notes that notwithstanding that the Company at least took a stand, albeit a feeble one, in producing a job description of the Petitioners and stating on record "that the said employees, regardless of the name of their respective designation, discharge their duties and responsibility in accordance with the instructions from their superior and the said employees do not have any authority to deviate from the instruction, the process, policy and guidance laid down by their superior "and also that "the said employees do not have the authority to hire or fire other employee" it has notably fallen short of stating on record that such employees necessarily, therefore, under the law qualify to be treated as 'workers'. Such reluctance on the part of the Company has been taken by this Court as an indication that the Company would prefer rather that this Court take on itself the responsibility to draw that conclusion. It is noted with some interest that the statement above of the Company is in fact replete with references to objective standards which cumulatively operate to determine the status of the 'worker' who does not discharge managerial, supervisory or administrative functions. In this regard, the learned Advocate for the Petitioner, Mr Imran Siddiq, has referred to a range of cases adjudged in this jurisdiction and otherwise, thereby, identifying certain of those judicially recognized objective standards. Given that the Company has not stated that the Petitioners do not perform managerial or administrative functions, its statement above, read in light of these decisions, in this Court's view, nevertheless clearly establishes that the Petitioners are indeed not performing any managerial or administrative functions. Those tests and decisions are enumerated herein below:

(a) Since the Petitioners have no power to hire or fire their functions are "neither managerial nor supervisory in nature in the sense in which those terms are understood in industrial law" (Ved Prakash Gupta vs Delton Cable India (P) Ltd. reported in 1984 2 SCC 569 at para 12);

(b) the Petitioners have no authority to appoint any employee or take any disciplinary action at their own initiative and, therefore, do not perform managerial or administrative functions (SK Verma vs Mahesh Chandra reported in 1983 4 SCC, 214 alone Mcleodead & Co vs Sixth Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal reported in AIR 1958 Cal. 273);

(c) there is nothing on record to show that the Petitioners can remotely discharge any policy-making responsibility on behalf of the Company (Omar Sons Ltd. vs Chairman 1st Labour Court reported in 28 DLR 1976, 178). In the Omar sons Case the Court additionally cautioned against being misled by someone's designation to the exclusion of a probe into the nature of the function actually performed for here the "criterion is not the designation but the function"; and

(d) no discernible degree of discretionary power appears to have been reserved to any of the Petitioners in the discharge of their duties (Hussain Mithu Mhasvadkar vs Bombay Iron and Steel reported in '2001 7 SCC 394). As in the Omar Sons Case, so in the Hussain Mithu Case the "true and proper" test "is the predominant nature of the services" i.e., a consideration of the nature of the duties and the powers conferred upon as well as the functions assigned to an undivided.

48. In Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 the' Petitioners to a great extent have relied on the Job Description Chart in Annexure- 'X2' generated by the Company to assert that there is in fact no dispute between the Company and the Petitioners to the effect that the latter are not indeed performing managerial or administrative work and that, accordingly, they are indeed 'workers' within the meaning of section 233 (1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006. The Petitioners relying on Annexure-'X(2)' submit that it is evident from the said document that the petitioners do not have the power to appoint or dismiss other employees nor do they have the power to make policy decisions on behalf of the Company, and that as such, they do not perform any managerial or administrative functions.

49. The BOT has however, submitted that Annexure-'X(2)' merely sets out the Petitioners' Job Description and that this refers only to the nature of the work done by them and not the model or manner in which they discharge their responsibilities. Accordingly, the BOT submits that the Job Description Chart cannot be used as a basis for determining the manner in which the Petitioners perform their functions.

<u>50. The Petitioners dispute such contention of the BOT by arguing that the prima facie test for the determination of the relationship between master and servant lies in the existence of the right in the master to supervise and control the work done by the servant not only in the matter of directing what work the servant will do, but also the manner in which he shall do his work. Thus, in determining to job description of an employee, an employer decides not only the work that will be done by him but also the manner in which he shall do his work. As such, the Petitioners contend that it would be incorrect to argue that the job description of the Petitioners, as contained in Annexure-X(2)', does not refer to the mode of discharge of responsibilities of the Petitioners. The Petitioners' contention in this regard is further supported by the Job Description Chart in Annexure-'X(2)', which refers to exercise of supervisory powers by certain of the Petitioners in the discharge of their responsibilities, i.e., the manner or mode, of discharge of their functions (for example the job description of the Petitioner No. 92 includes supervising overall manufacturing operations, encompassing production quality, safety, capacity utilization, people management, conflict management, capacity management and asset care). Here the Petitioners clarify that a mere exercise of supervisory powers, however, does not by itself mean that an employee ceases to be a 'worker' within the meaning of section 233(1) (Ja) of the Act of 2006. According to section 233 (1)(Ja)(1) and (2) of the Act of 2006, the primary determinant of an employee's status as a 'worker' is whether he/she is performing managerial and administrative, functions. Section 233(1) (Ja)(2) refers to persons employed in a supervisory capacity who are performing managerial and administrative functions, such category of persons having been excluded from the definition of workers. Thus a person may be exercising supervisory powers, but if he/she is not engaged in managerial or administrative responsibilities, he cannot be termed a 'worker'. In this regard, the Petitioners rely on the Judgment of the High Court Division in Mujibur Rahman vs Chairman Labour Court reported in 31 DLR 301, wherein interpreting section 2(v) of the Act of 1968 (which is similar to section 233(1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006), the High Court Division held that a person does not cease to be a 'worker' only because of being employed in a supervisory capacity. It has to be further established that such person exercises functions as are mainly of a managerial and administrative nature.</u>

51. Thus the job description of each of the Petitioners (which refers to the nature of their work and the mode of discharge of their functions), as contained in Annexure- 'X(2)' may be resorted to in determining whether the Petitioners perform functions which may be described as managerial or administrative in nature. In this case, the Petitioners reiterate that their job descriptions clearly show that they have no power to appoint or dismiss other employees and/or make policy decisions on behalf of the Company and, as such, they do not perform managerial and administrative functions and thus qualify as 'workers' under section 233(1) (Ja) of the Act of 2006.

<u>52. Barring the somewhat contradictory stance, as above noted, adopted by the Company itself on this point in Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007, the opposition to recognizing the Petitioners as 'workers' understandingly comes from the Respondent No. 2, BOT in both the cases. That opposition was placed before the Court by the learned Advocate for the BOT, Mr Kamal-ul-Alam who submitted that the Job Description Chart merely sets out the Petitioners' job description and that this refers only to the nature of the work done by them and not the mode or manner in which they discharge their responsibility. Predicated on this stance, Mr. Alam has submitted that the Annexure 'X-2 Job Description Chart can, there-fore, not be used as the basis for determining the manner in which the Petitioners perform their functions. The learned Advocate for the Petitioners Mr Siddiq in response to this contention of the BOT has referred to the judgment of the Indian Supreme Court in DC Works. Ltd vs State of Saurashtra reported in AIR 1957(SC) 264 wherein it has been held that the prima facie test for the determination of the relationship between an employer and employee is that of the authority concentrated in the former to supervise and control work done by the latter not only in the matter of directing what kind of work the employee will engage in but also the manner in which this shall be discharged. Mr Siddiq submits that the job description in Annexure-, 'X2', therefore, reflects not only the work done by any given Petitioner but is also declaratory of the manner he or she does it. In this regard, he does the examples of certain of the Petitioners ostensibly exercising supervisory powers in the discharge of their responsibilities, thereby, bringing to the fore the manner or mode of discharge of their function. The mere reference to exercise of supervisory power, however, Mr Siddiq cautions, must not readily lead one to deduce that such powers of them-selves cause an employee to cease to be treated as a worker with the meaning of section 233(1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006. This Court finds in that line of argument an appeal to this Court to necessarily draw a line between a general description of the mode of discharge of responsibility and the substance of that which is involved in the actual discharge of such responsibility. The appeal here is also to the tests laid down in the Omar Sons and Hussain Mithu Cases, i.e., that of ascertaining "the predominant nature of the services" rendered. Therefore, this Court finds it plausible that a person may indeed be exercising supervisory power short of engaging in managerial or administrative activity and, thereby, not falling under the mischief of the exdusionary provisions of section 233(1)(Ja)(2) of the Act of 2006. That seems to be in this Court's opinion the rationale behind the High Court Division's Judgment in Mujibur Rahman vs Chairman, L, Court reported in 31 DLR, 301, wherein interpreting section 2(v) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Order) Act, 1965 (which is similar to section 233(1)(Ja) it was held that "a person does not cease to be a worker only because he is a employed in a supervisory capacity. It has to be established that the exercises function mainly of a managerial and administrative nature".</u>

53. In light of the above, reversing to the Job Description Chart in Annexure-'X2' and as asserted by the learned Advocates both for the Company i.e., Mr Ashraful Hadi and indeed for the Petitioners, i.e., Mr Siddiq it is evident, that the Petitioners are therein shown not to have any power to appoint and dismiss other employees and/or make policy decisions on behalf of the Company. That being the case, and given this Court's subscription to the judicially sanctioned objective standards as above enumerated, it is found that the Petitioner before us in these Writ Petitions not being authorized to function in managerial or administrative capacities do indeed qualify to be termed 'workers' by operation of section 233(1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006.

54. It has been brought to this Court's attention that the state of affairs that has so operated within the Company for an unduly long period as above addressed has not only witnessed the BOT wresting full control of the management and administration of the Funds from the Company as goes against the scheme and spirit of both the statutory regimes but that the BOT has done so in a manner resorting to arbitrary selection of beneficiaries for disbursal of the benefit from the Funds. This Court's attention has been drawn to the fact that the BOT has been disbursing funds on the basis of membership of the CBA, thereby, dislodging the applicable statutory criterion of entitlement to beneficial administration of the Funds based on employment status with that of membership in the CBA. Here, Mr Siddiq has explained at length that an employee in a Company while not figuring in the CBA Member, List may yet qualify to be termed a worker within the meaning of section 233(1)(Ja). Mr Siddiq aptly high-lights that Chapter 15 of the Act of 2006 as relates to disbursement of funds in favour of workers by the BOT contains section 233(1)(Ja) as incorporates a specific definition of 'worker' exclusively for the purposes of that Chapter. On the other hand, the inclusion of names of workers in the CBA Member List as governed by section 202 of the Act of 2006 is governed wholly separately under Chapter 13 where yet a different definition of 'worker' is to be found. The obvious selective reliance, therefore, by the BOT on a Chapter 13 standard in preference to that found in section 233 (1)(Ja) is in the circumstances satisfactorily submitted to be arbitrary and manifestly perverse.

55. It is against that backdrop of an obvious arrogation of authority by the BOT clearly beyond the legislative intent and contemplation, egged on by the abdication of statutory responsibilities by the Company as well as the Government, that there arises a very aggravated situation in which the BOT is found over a prolonged period to have continued to ask itself the wrong questions in law and prevailed with impunity to exercise a jurisdiction that clearly is not within its mandate to exercise. Resultantly, the BOT has over this period continued to adversely impact upon the legitimate rights and interests of the Petitioners. Appropriately, to address and rectify such illegality this Court has not previously in similar circumstances shied away from intervening. Therefore, in Writ Petition No. 5111 of 2008 it was held, by this Court, that the voter list of a CBA election cannot be the basis and determinant of the status of a worker. Indeed, that Judgment in Writ Petition No. 5111 of 2008 has been expressly relied upon in Writ Petition No. 5024 of 2012. Furthermore, in favourably finding on the Petitioner's status as a 'worker' under section 233(1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006 in light of absence of any evidence forthcoming to establish that the Petitioner there otherwise discharged administrative, managerial or supervisory function, this court in Writ Petition No. 5011 of 2008 also pertinently referred to section 336 of the Act of 2006 as reads thus:

“৩৩৬। কতিপয় ক্ষেত্রে চাকুরীর বর্তমান শর্তাবলী সংরক্ষণ ।-এই আইন অথবা কোন বিধি, প্রবিধান বা স্কীমের কোন কিছুই এই আইন প্রবর্তন হওয়ার সময় উহার দ্বারা রহিত কোন আইনের অধীন অথবা কোন রোয়েদাদ চুক্তি নিস্পত্তি বা প্রচলিত প্রথার অধীন কোন শ্রমিকের ভোগকৃত অধিকার বা সুযোগ-সৃবিধা তিনি যতদিন উক্ত প্রবর্তনের তারিখে যে মালিকের অধীন কর্মরত ছিলেন সে মালিকের অধীন চাকুরীরত থাকিবেন ততদিন পর্যন্ত ব্যাহত বা ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত করিবেন, যদি তাহার উক্ত অধিকার এবং সুযোগ সুবিধা এই আইন, বিধি প্রবিধান বা স্কীমের অধীন প্রদত্ত অধিকার ও সুযোগ সুবিধা হইতে অধিকতর অনুকূল হয়।

56. Section 336 was found in that case to be declaratory of the fact that the Act of 2006 does not indeed take away any greater financial benefit that may have been enjoyed by a worker under the earlier legislation given of course he/she fulfils the criteria to be treated as a worker under the provisions of the law as above discussed. Their Lordships in Writ Petition No. 5111 of 2008 also found implicit in section 336 the principle that new legislation ought not to be applied detrimentally to workers and that financial benefits once given to a worker ought not to be readily taken away by subsequent law. Upon a specific query by this Court, the learned Advocates for the Respondent No. 4, Company Mr Hadi and the Petitioner Mr Siddiq inform that an Appeal was filed by the BOT in Civil Appeal being No. 72 of 2010 against the Judgment in Writ Petition No, 5111 of 2008 but was subsequently dismissed for non-prosecution by the Appellate Division on 4-1-2012.

57. This Court finds section 336 an under-pinning legislative intent to generally continue to extend benefits to workers meeting the criteria therein in preference to taking it way from them. Facts in the present instances attesting to fulfillment of the conditions to continued entitlement to benefit are found on record with regard, for example, to the Petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 whose earnings including entitlements received from the Funds under the Act of 1968 were much greater than that subsequently earned given that they were unlawfully deprived of sharing in the Company's profit as disbursed from the Funds. In that light, this Court finds merit in the submissions that section 336 may be invoked in the Petitioners favour in the facts and circumstances.

58. At this juncture it is deemed prudent to consider a yet outstanding yet related issue, Mr Mahmudul Islam, appearing for the Respondent No. 2, BOT in Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007 has argued against the maintainability of the said Writ Petition submitting that the Petitioners in that Writ Petitioner ought rather to have agitated their grievances under forums provided under labour law or even have filed a general Suit. Given the nature of the claims under Writ Petition No. 227 of 2007, Mr Islam has argued that under section 3(6) of the Act of 1968, the rights to profits for 2006 was to have accrued to the Petitioners at the end of the year and are payable no later than nine months thereafter. In that context, Mr Islam argues that the maturity of that right, however, get arrested on 11-10-2006 with the coming into force of the Act of 2006 that, he submits, changed the definition of a 'worker' with a notably exclusionary connotation attached to it. The question posed by Mr Islam is whether the concerned Petitioners are therefore, to be deemed 'workers' at the time that their right would have otherwise matured under the Act of 1968, i.e., on 31-12-2006 but in fact could not under above circumstance. The response, Mr Islam submits, has inevitably to be in the negative given that on 31-12-2006 the BOT would on that date have to determine who a 'worker' is under the new Act of 2006. Mr Islam stresses that, should the Act of 2006 instead have come into effect on 1-1-2007 the scenario could have been vastly different and possibly more favourable for the Petitioners. Under that alternate scenario, the Petitioners would indeed have had a fully matured right on 31-12-2006 under the still extant Act of 2006 and, accordingly, been claimants to a fully matured entitlement.

59. This Court is unable to take into favourable consideration Mr Mahmudul Islam's argument above given its findings both regarding the maintainability of these two Writ Petitions and concerning clothing the Petitioners with the status of 'workers'. Given further that there is the common thread of employment for a minimum of six months that binds both definitions, of 'worker' in the Acts of 1968 and 2006, Mr Imran Siddiq has satisfactorily argued for the Petitioners in Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007 to qualify as 'workers' on that criterion and, thereby, to be brought under the protective umbrella of section 336 of the Act of 2006 as above enunciated. It is noted further that this was the very legal rationale behind all of those Petitioners in Writ Petition No. 2227 of 2007 applying to this Court variously to be added as Petitioners in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009. It was expressly averred in these various applications for addition as parties that the applicants therein had fulfilled the conditions set out in section 2(f) of the Act of 1968 to be classified as 'workers'. As such, the said applicants had participated in the profits of the Company in their capacity as 'workers' in accordance with the Act of 1968, had acquired a vested right to participate in the Company's profits, which has not been taken away by an express provision of law. The assertion further was of such vested right of the said applicants under the Act of 1968 to participate in the Company's profits in fact having been expressly preserved by section 336 of the Act of 2006. This Court, in allowing these applications variously, e.g. on 10-11-2009 and 19-1-2010, notably found in the applicants having an interest in the subject matter in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009 and indeed not having any interests inimical to the original Petitioners in Writ Petition No. 7326 of 2009. With the benefit of hindsight, this Court now finds that the said Orders of this Court stood and continue to stand on a firm substantive legal footing.

60. Given the findings above, and this Court's reading of the relevant provisions of law as above enunciated and their application to the facts and circumstances, it is found that the Petitioners do indeed qualify to be termed as 'workers' within the meaning of section 233(1)(Ja) of the Act of 2006. Those of the Petitioners who had been in employment of the Company prior to 2006 are also found by reference in particular to the Job Description Chart in Annexure-'X2' each to be of a status as does not bring them under the mischief of the exclusionary provisions of section 233(1)(Ja) (1) and (2). It is also found that the Company being the primary authority within the statutory scheme to determine on the nature, mode or manner and substance of the function and authority that each of the Petitioners discharges is, there-fore, also necessarily clothed with the authority to authoritatively declare on the same in the manner as done in the preparation of the Job Description Chart in Annexure 'X-2'. Within such statutory scheme the Company is also found to discharge such function for the benefit and ready reference of the BOT that without further ado must rely on the adequacy and the veracity of the same and ensure a due disbursement of benefits from the Funds. To that end, and bearing in mind that this is a Writ in Mandamus, this Court now directs the Company to forward the Job Description Chart annexed as Annexure 'X2' in its entirety and with other supporting documents as relevant to the BOT within a period of 1 (one) week from receipt of a certified copy of this judgment and Order for due disbursement of funds to all the Petitioners concerned. The BOT shall, effect such disbursals no later than a period of 3 (three) weeks of receipt of such a list of job descriptions from the Company. It will be borne in mind by the BOT, the Company and indeed the Government acting in discharge of its function of oversight that the findings of this Court operate wholly within the statutory parameters of the Act 2006, in particular and which shall be read by these three actors as being declaratory of the law in Act of 2006 and as well as of the statutorily defined roles assigned to each of these actors operating within their specific statutory boundaries, in that sense, the direction herein made must be read as one already sanctioned in law the provisions of which law had become noteworthy in the past decade or so not by any notable degree of compliance but more by the incidences of outright violation of the same. This Court's directions should be treated as a reminder to all three actors of the necessity of due compliance of the letter of the law and not to treat the cases of the Petitioners as an exception to the statutory norms of compliance found in the Act of 2006. The Company and the BOT as ordered above will, therefore, be obliged to revive statutory compliance measures and practices that had fallen into disuse for a decade or so and, therefore, ensure the due and sustained operation of the Funds with the active support of the Government. All three rotors shall do well to bear in mind that the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006 first and foremost is a beneficial piece of legislation intended to strike and maintain a harmonious relationship between workers and the employer. To that end, it is necessary that the provisions of the Act of 2006 are given as wide an interpretation as possible in consonance with such objective.

61. In light of the above, we find merit in both the Applications and substance in the Rules Nisi issued. In the result, the Rules Nisi in both the Applications are made absolute with the specific observations and directions as above.

There are no orders as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
AFM Abdur Rahman J : The Assessee-applicant 'National Hospital Chattagram (Pvt.) Ltd' preferred the instant Income Tax Reference Application under the provision of section 160(1) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 with the following formulated question in the substantive application and also one question made in the supplementary-affidavit all of which, reads as follows:

(I) In the circumstances on the facts, whether the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified maintaining the disallowances of expenses in different heads?

(II) In the circumstances and facts, whether the taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified maintaining the vacancy allowances?

(III) In the circumstances and on the facts, whether taxes appellate tribunal was justified maintaining the estimation of medicine sales?

(IV) In the circumstances and on the facts, whether Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified maintaining the estimation of house rent?

(V) in the circumstances and on the facts, whether Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified maintaining the estimation of GP Rate of medicine sales?

(VI) In the circumstances and on the facts whether the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was justified maintaining the Order of 1st Appellate Authority and the assessment order of the DCT in absence of audit report under the requirement of sub-section 3 of section 82BB of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984?

Facts of the case:

2. It has been asserted in the Income Tax Reference Application that the Assessee-applicant payees income tax under the TIN. টিআইএনঃ ৩৪২-২০০-৩৫০৪/কো-৫, and in course of period the Assessee-applicant submitted its income tax return for the assessment year 2009-2010 under the provision of Self Assessment Scheme, as provided in section 82BB (1) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984, which was selected by the National Board of Revenue upon invoking its power available under the provision of section 83BB(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984. Accordingly, the DCT concern was directed to hold audit and thereafter if required to proceed further to treat the said return as a normal return. But the DCT concern did not hold any audit although a letter was issued upon the Assessee-applicant. Thereafter, the DCT concern issued notice under section 83(1) and 79 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 directing to attend hearing the case and upon hearing the authorized representative of the Assessee-applicant disposed off the return as a normal return, assessing the tax liability of the Assessee-applicant afresh.

3. Being aggrieved with and highly dis-satisfied by the said assessment order, the Assessee-applicant preferred appeal before the first appellate authority, being আয়কর আপীলপত্র নং-১৫/কো-৫/জেন-২/২০১০-২০১১, which having been allowed in part the Assessee-applicant. preferred further appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, being ITA No. 2807 of 2010-2011, wherein the DCT concern preferred a Cross Appeal, being ITA No. 3593 of 2010-2011.
