32. Considering the above this Court finds merit in the Application and substance in the Rule issued.

33. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The Impugned Order No. 1 dated 24-11-2009 passed by the Respondent No. 1 registering BLL (IR) Case No. 362 of 2009 and Violation Misc. Case No/181 of 2011 arising out of the aforesaid BLL Case, now pending before the First Labour Court, Dhaka, are, hereby declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect. Consequentially, BLL Case No. 362 of 2009 stands declared to have been dismissed.

34. This Judgment by its very terms findings and observations shall without prejudice govern the substantive consideration and final disposal of Writ Petition Nos. 1105 of 2012, 1107 of 2012, 1108 of 2012, 1109 of 2012, 1110 of 2012, 1111 of 2012, 1112 of 2012, 1113 of 2012, 1114 of 2012, 1115 of 2012, 1116 of 2012, 1117 of 2012, 1118 of 2012, 1119 of 2012, 1120 of 2012, 1121 of 2012, 1122 of 2012, 1123 of 2012 and 1251 of 2012 in like forms as above to the fullest.

There is no Order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Senior Advocate, instructed by Serajuddin Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record — For the Appellant. 
AW Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General, (B. Hossain, Deputy Attorney-General, with him), instructed by Zinnur Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record —For the Respondent No. 1. 
Miah Abdul Gafur, Advocate-on-Record— For the Respondent No. 2.

Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated June 19, 1991 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Appeal No. 34 of 1988).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman, J.: On April 15, 1960 the appellant was appointed as an Assistant Communication Engineer in the Civil Aviation Department. The Government of Bangladesh formed a corporate body, namely, Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh by Civil Aviation Authority Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. XXXVIII of 1985). The employees of the Civil Aviation Department, hitherto enjoying the terms and conditions of the Government servants, refused to be governed by the new Service Rules and Regulations framed under the Ordinance No. LI of 1985. Some of them went on strike with effect from February 19, 1987.

2. The Government set up an Inquiry Committee on March 1, 1987. The Committee submitted a report to the Government. On the basis of that report the appellant was compulsorily retired from service under the Public Servants Retirement Act, 1974 by an order of the President of Bangladesh dated January 2, 1988.

3. The appellant challenged that order before the Administrative Tribunal in AT Case No. 22 of 1988. The Tribunal upheld the order. The appellant filed an appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, being Appeal No. 34 of 1988.

4. On June 12, 1989 the Administrative Appellate Tribunal pronounced the judgment in open court in presence of the learned Advocates for the appellant and respondent No. 2 and allowed the appeal. It was noted in the order sheet that the judgment would be in a separate sheet.

5. On June 15, 1989 on the submission of the learned Advocate of respondent No. 1, the Government, the decision dated June 12, 1989 was recalled and the appeal was fixed for re-hearing on June 19, 1989. On June 19, 1989 the Chairman of the Administrative Tribunal was absent; the appeal was heard by two Members of the Tribunal. The Judgment of the Tribunal allowing the appeal was, however, signed by the Chairman and the two Members.

6. The appellant contends that after pronouncing the decision on June 12, 1989 the Appellate Tribunal became functus officio and had no jurisdiction to review its judgment and that the Appellate Tribunal, not being a civil Court, had no jurisdiction to recall the decision announced on June 19, 1989 on alleged consent of the learned Advocate for the appellant.

7. It is further contended that when the appeal was allowed on re-hearing the Appellate Tribunal was coram non judice because section 7 (3B) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 implies that the Chairman and two Members were required to be present in the beginning of the re-hearing of the appeal.

<u>8. The respondents have not joined issues with the appellant's contentions that the Tribunal is not a civil Court and that it has no power to review. They have, however, contended that when the order was recalled the Appellate Tribunal was in seisin of the matter and not functus officio and appellant's contention that the Tribunal as a body ought to have re-heard the appeal is not correct in view of the provision of section 7(3B) of the Act. In this regard reliance is placed on Project in Charge Vs. Abdur Rahman 31 DLR 124 and General Manager, Jamuna Oil Company Vs. Golam Rahman & another 34 DLR (AD) 166.</u>

<u>9. It is submitted that the Tribunal, as an adjudicating body, has power to alter, modify or change its judgment before it is signed and sealed. Reliance is placed on Beni Madho Prasad Singh Vs. Adit and others AIR 1953 Allahabad 416, Surendra Singh Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1954 (SC) 194 at P 197, Faulad and another Vs. State AIR 1961 Allahabad P 326, Rukan Din Vs. Hafiz-ud-Din PLD 1962 Lahore 161, Sangam Lal Vs. Rent Control and Eviction Officer, AIR 1966 Allahabad (FB) 221.</u>

<u>10. In Jai Karan Vs. Panchaiti Akhara, Chow Nayan Udasi Nanak Shahi AIR 1933 Allahabad 49 (J), after hearing the arguments the learned Chief Justice dictated an order in the open Court. But immediately thereafter a request by one of the counsels of the parties that the judgment might not be signed so that the question of limitation arising in the case might further be considered was acceded to by the Court. The transcript of the judgment was, however, signed by inadvertence. Sulaiman, CJ set aside the order and reheard the matter. This was a case where a mistake committed by a functionary of the Court itself was later set right by the Court in its inherent jurisdiction.</u>

<u>11. In AIR 1953 Allahabad p. 416 it was held that by reason of the provisions contained in r. 3 of or. 20 of the CPC, jurisdiction of the Court to reconsider and rehear a case will cease only when a judgment has been signed. After it has been signed, the judgment cannot be altered or added to except as provided by section 152 Civil PC or on review."</u>

<u>12. In Full Bench case the Allahabad High Court in AIR 1966 Allahabad p. 221 after considering AIR 1954 (SC) p. 194 and AIR 1961 Allahabad 326 held "a judgment which has been orally dictated in open Court can be completely changed before it is signed and sealed provided notice is given to all parties concerned and they are heard before the change is made."</u>

<u>13. Finding these decisions are of the civil Court and that the Administrative Tribunal is not a civil Court the respondents alternatively have urged that where an Act confers a jurisdiction it impliedly also grants the power of doing all such acts or employ such means as are essentially necessary to its execution. Reliance is placed on Mohd. Fazlur Rahman Vs. Custodian of Evacuee Property AIR 1956 (FB) Hyderabad, 91.</u>

14. Our attention is also drawn to the following observation made in Craies on Statute Law, Seventh Edition, Page-111.

"If a statute is passed for the purpose of enabling something to be done, but omits to mention in terms some detail which is of great importance (if not actually essential) to the proper and effectual performance of the work which the statute has in contemplation, the courts are at liberty to infer that the statute by implication empowers that detail to be carried out."

15. The respondents further contend that there is no provision in rules for announcing the judgment and the earlier order was not passed under its sub-rule 9 of Rule 6 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 which reads as follows:

"(9) The Tribunal shall, after the application has been heard, give its decision in writing with reasons therefor, at once or on some future day of which notice shall be given to the parties, and make an order accordingly."

<u>16. Appellant in reply contends that in any case the Appellate Tribunal passed an order on June 12, 1989 which cannot be recalled or modified in view of the following sub-rule 10 of rule 6 of the Administrative Tribunals Rules, 1982:</u>

<u>"(10) The decision or order once given or made shall not afterwards be altered or modified, save for the purpose of correcting a clerical or arithmetical mistake or any error arising from any accidental slip or omission." As the decision pronounced on June 12, 1989 was not made as per sub-rule (9) of rule 6 of the Rules it did not reach any finality. The Appellate Tribunal did not become functus officio on that date and it had the jurisdiction as an adjudicating body to recall that decision subsequently and order for rehearing.</u>

17. In James A Ballentine's Law Dictionary the entry on rehearing reads as follows:

"Strictly speaking, a rehearing is simply a new hearing and a new consideration of the case by the Court in which the suit was originally held, and upon the pleadings and depositions already in the case. See Read 6 Am. St. Rep. 877, 10 At 1. Rep. 385."

<u>18. In Stroud's Judicial Dictionary (1974) it is stated a "rehearing" is a new trial, and is not satisfied by merely reading the transcript of the first trial (R V Syme, Ex p. Page [197] WAR 1953).</u>

<u>19. The word 'rehearing' means hearing again. A rehearing is a new proceeding and it implies the hearing by the same tribunal which heard the matter before. Apart from the construction that I have given to the word 'rehearing' I like to point out that it is an accepted principle of procedure that prior notice for rehearing is to be given to the parties who were present at the time of the hearing of the matter earlier. This principle is in consonance with justice and is to be extended to the constitution of the adjudicating body when it comprises of more than one person. When the matter was heard earlier by all the members of the Tribunal rehearing ought to have been done by all of them, more so, when the decision announced earlier was reversed on rehearing. The same body of the Tribunal comprising the Chairman and two Members ought to have heard the matter. The decision cited in 31 DLR 124 and 34 DLR (AD) 166 can hardly be applied in the instant case.</u>

In view of the above, the appeal is allowed and the matter is sent back to the Appellate Administrative Tribunal for rehearing by its Chairman and two Members. No costs.

End.

Sharif Uddin Chaklader J : By this rule plaintiff calls in question the judgment and order dated 15-3-2011 passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong condoning the delay of 1230 days in filing Other Appeal No. 248 of 1998.

2. Plaintiff-petitioner instituted Other Suit No. 55 of 1987 with the following amongst other prayers:

“অত্রএব বাদী নিন্মমতে প্রার্থনা করেনঃ-

3. Plaintiff prayed for injunction on the schedule land as:

চৌহদ্দীঃ-

উত্তরে আবুল বশর চৌধুরী ও বাচন বিবি খিলা ঠিলা ও পাহাড় দক্ষিণে নাদের থান নাল ও ঠিলা পূর্বে আবুল কাসেম চৌধুরীর ঠিলা জমি এবং পশ্চিমে পূর্বে পাহাড়তলী মৌজার জমি।

4. It is the case of the plaintiff that suit land which originally belonged to Ananda Charan Datta and Ghana Charan Datta, was put into auction for arrear rents in Rent Case No. 154 of 1946 and pursuant to the decree one, Abdul Latif Chowdhury, son of Haji Mobarak Ali of village Saga char under Patia Upazilla purchased the suit land in Rent Execution Case No.131 of 1947 on 8-4-1948 and sale was confirmed on 11-5-1948 and possessing the suit land until he executed power-of-attorney on 18-4-1968 in favour of his son, Abdul Basher Chowdhury and close well-wisher, Abdul Jalil and power-of-attorney holders mutated their names and also paid rents regularly. In PS survey the suit land although recorded wrongly in the name, of Nasiruddin, Hosne Ara Begum, Khadija Begum and Captain Bakhtiar but recorded persons never possessed the suit land in BS Survey, to the knowledge of the aforesaid persons and also of the Government. Defendant Nos.5 and 6.recorded the suit land in the name of Abdul Latif. The aforesaid power-of-attorney holders by registered deed dated 6-1-1985 and 21-1-1986 transferred the suit land in favour of plaintiff No.3. which was registered in the Sub Registry office, Pahartalli; by these two deeds 20 acres of land was gifted in favour of plaintiff Nos. l and 2 who got possession. After getting the, suit land as aforesaid, plaintiffs demarcated the suit land having title and possession and paid rents regularly. Plaintiffs also cut earth from the suit land, filled the lower portion and developed the suit land and constructed home-stead. Plaintiffs possessed the null land through borgaders, wherein defendants or anybody else had no possession or title and they could not demand the suit land and by this possession, plaintiffs acquired title by adverse possession. Plaintiff possessed the suit land peacefully but at present, defendant Nos.l-4 in different ways disturbed the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs and they want to include the shares in their proposed housing society and the said persons with the government employees continuously giving threat. Plaintiffs turned down the proposal of the aforesaid persons where-upon interested persons became furious and on 14-6-1987 with some gunda elements tried to get into possession by force and thereby tried to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land. Plaintiffs husband and plaintiff's tenants and local people intervened and the gunda elements leave the suit land giving open threat that they will get the suit land from government, defendant Nos. 5 and 6, through Magistrate and Police they will come back and dispossess the plaintiff. Plaintiff with her husband went to defendant No.7, Tahsildar for inquiry but did not get any information. But the plaintiff could see some employees of defendant No.5 conspiring with the gunda elements for satisfying their lust. Defendant Nos.5 and 6 only can realize tax from the plaintiff, hence the suit.

5. Defendant No. 1 and defendant Nos. 5 and 6 contested the suit. It appears that defendant No. 1 later on did not contest the suit as such we left aside the case made out by defendant No. 1 in the written statement.

6. Defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the written statement after taking preliminary objections as to maintainability of the suit, denied the plaint case line by line. It is their specific case that suit land originally belonged to Ananda Charan Datta and Gyananda Charan Datta and Nilmani Datta. 45.96 acres of land was recorded as projabili in the RS khatian. The entire land of jote for arrear of rent was put into auction and government purchased the suit land on 18-3-1934 and for managing the auction purchased land for which defendants' instituted further suit. The said lands purchased after auction still remain in previous Jote No.140. After 14 jote created by resettlement of the suit land in Miscellaneous Case No.651 of 1945-46 the suit land was resettled. After resettlement, Brojalal Chose, Sumon Lal Chose got 15.48 acres of land from several R.S. dag numbers involved in the suit and Jote No.180 was created which was recorded in R.S. No. 836/16. Brojalal Chose sold his land of Jote Nos.180. 181. 182 to Nasir Uddin, Khadija Begurn and Harun Matin and also to other persons and thereby became title less. The aforesaid purchasers in Mutation Case No.47/52-53 and JM Case No. 114/54-55 recorded their names in Jotekhatian No.835/16 and according to their possession, the suit land has been recorded in SA khatian Nos.74 and 94. The aforesaid purchase is, Nasiruddin, Khadija Begum and Harun Matin were non-Bengali and left the country for Pakistan during war of liberation and never came back and Government as per PO No. 16 of 1972 declared the property as enemy property. The said property during BS survey was recorded in the name of Government of Bangladesh. To protect the said property from illegal trespassers or illegal strangers in 1975 Government appointed Md Nurul Huda (defendant No.3) as care taker. Government through Miscellaneous Cases Nos.6 of 1980-81, 7 of 1980-81, 8 of 1980-81, 9 of 1980-81, 2 of 1981 -82 leased out the property in favour of Md Solaiman, Faruq Ahmed and others. Brojalal Ghosh was never tenant either under Ananda Charan or Gyananda Charan and was never resettlement holder of Government. Brojalal Ghose, Benulal Ghose and their heirs, who were owners of jote No. 180, 181, 182 through Resettlement Case No. 651/45-46, sold the suit land to Nash Uddin, Khodeja Begum, Harun Malin and others by several kabalas. The case of the plaintiffs of mutation of their names in Mutation Case No. 384/78-79, 480/78-79 is totally false and no such khatian was opened in the office of Assistant Commissioner, Land and Mutation Case No. 401/78-79 was not related to the suit property; that mutation case was related to Nurul Alam, son of Ashraf Ali, of village: Bakalia, Chittagong in respect of 0.28 decimals of land and Mutation Case No.430/78-79 was in respect of Pear Mohammad of Sakir-51, Keranigonj, Police Station Kotwali, Chittagong for 0.57 decimals of land. The aforesaid mutation case and khatian of the plaintiffs are false and prepared for ulterior motive. Plaintiffs and husband of plaintiff, Abul Bashar are members of gang of forged deed and they created several forged deeds and after creating different forged deeds they wanted to grab the property illegally. Criminal cases have been instituted against Abul Bashar, husband of plaintiff and also against Md Abdul Jalil and others. Double Mouring Police Station Case No. 32(1)87 under section 467/468/109 of the Penal Code was initiated on 30-1-1987. Charge-sheet was submitted and charge was framed and the case is pending in Criminal Motion No. 381 of 1989 which is pending before the Additional District Judge, 1st court, Chittagong. On these grounds defendants prayed for dismissal of the suit.

7. In the suit, plaintiff examined one witness and he was particularly cross examined by the Government. Government did not adduce any witness nor exhibited any documents.

8. Learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong by judgment and decree dated 30-4-1995 decreed the suit on the finding that "defendant government did not take any step to prove the case by adducing any witness or exhibiting any documents'. Learned Judge thereafter took into consideration as regard possession of the plaintiff which is the crux for deciding case of permanent injunction. On consideration of exhibits 3 series, exhibits 2 series, exhibits 4 series, exhibits 7 series, exhibits 5 series and exhibits 6 series held by the aforesaid exhibits, plaintiff has been able to prove their possession of the suit property and decreed the suit.

9. Against this decision defendant-Government preferred Other Appeal No. 248 of 1998 out of time by 1230 days. The application for condonation of delay was filed. After contesting hearing the delay was condoned.

10. Having aggrieved against the said decision, present rule was obtained.

11. Mr Serajul Haque with Mr Md Bashuddin Zindigir, learned advocates appearing for the petitioner. For the non contesting defendant No.3 of the suit, Mr Fida M 'Carnal, Mr AJ Mohammad All and Mr Ahsanul Karim, learned Advocates along with bunch of lawyers appeared. Mr Md Jaber, learned Assistant Attorney-General with some government pleaders appeared for defendant No. 1, appellant, opposite party No. 1. All the lawyers appeared in this rule whit 1 is for condonation of delay, not a rule on decree but made argument one after another tirelessly which cover all categories of cases on this rule.

12. Mr. Serajul Haque, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that, delay was 1230 days but in the application for condo-nation of delay no explanation was given nor the learned Judge ever considered whether the applicant gave any reason far less sufficient or satisfactory for condonation of delay and in one sentence, only in one sentence this long delay has been condoned on taking into consideration of the findings of other suit filed by the plaintiffs affirmed up to the Appellate Division and submits that, since delay has not been properly explained the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge being devoid of any substance is liable to be set-aside. Learned Advocate in the course of argument referred to Civil Revision No.701 of 2005 arisen from the selfsame order of the learned District Judge passed in Other Appeal No.255 of 1999 arisen from the selfsame suit against the selfsame judgment of the trial court wherein learned District Judge on condoning the delay of 1569 days, admitted the appeal for hearing and this judgment was challenged in Civil Revision No.701 of 2005; the High Court Division made the rule absolute and dismissed Other Appeal No.255 of 1999. Against which, defendant government did not proceed further, Learned Advocate further submits that against the selfsame judgment two appeals cannot be filed by same defendant and since Judgment passed by the High Court Division dismissing Other Appeal No.255 of 1999 against which government did not proceed further the decision operates as resjudicata on the facts of the given case. Learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to the decisions of Province of East Pakistan vs Meajan Ali Ahmed and 15 others, 18 DLR (SC) 343, the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and Assistant Custodian, Vested property, Sirajganj vs Md Abdul Majid, 2 BLC (AD) 11 and the case of The Principal Secretary, President's Secretariat, vs Mohammad Abdul Batten, 1994 BLT (AD) 90. In the decision of 1994 BLT (AD) 90 Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court did not condone the delay of 195 days and observed that:

"(2) This petition is barred by limitation of 195 days. There is an application for con-donation of the delay. Grounds taken for condonation are that the relevant Ministry asked for legal opinion on 9-9-93 for filing a Leave petition and also to get a certified copy of the High Court Division's order, that the File was sent to the Attorney-General and then to the Additional Attorney-General for opinion, that, thereafter, it was sent to the Solicitor "who was pleased to appoint an Advocate-on-Record", that the Solicitor's Office asked the Ministry of Home Affairs for supplying necessary documents and papers, that thereafter, necessary fund was ought for etc. These are not at all good grounds for condonation of the delay; rather these show utter negligence, carelessness, inefficiency or, may be, connivance of persons/officials of the petitioner-government who handled this matter. When an Assistant Attorney-General (Mr. Mashuque Hossain Ahmed) had appeared before the High Court Division and argued on behalf of the Government he certainly knew of the result of the writ petition. As such certified copy of the impugned order could have been easily obtained in time, the writ petition was filed four years after the impugned order of dismissal of the respondent under MLR 9. No Affidavit was filed raising questions as to its maintainability and inordinate delay. As to the delay in filing this Leave petition, whether it was either deliberate or due to utter negligence on the part of the petitioner's officers, there is no good ground for its condonation."

13. In the decision of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) and Assistant Custodian, Vested property, Sirajganj vs Md Abdul Majid 2BLC (AD) /1,83 days delay was not condoned observing.

14. The question raised by Mr Chowdhury has already been answered by this Division in the case of Deputy Commissioner vs Kobad Ali, 39 DLR (AD) 205 in the following terms:

"6.There is a long practice being followed since the days of Dhaka High Court that a revisional application is to be filed within the period of ninety days, prescribed by law for an appeal, and that discretion entertain an application beyond that period in a suitable case where there is no negligence or laches on the part of the petitioner. This is a long standing practice otherwise sound and reasonable, and it does not call for any departure

7. So far as the instant case is concerned the learned Judge of the High Court Division upon assigning cogent reasons has passed the impugned order in exercise of his discretion holding that the petitioner could not give satisfactory explanation for the inordinate delay of 83 days in moving the application in question."

15. In the decision of Province of East Pakistan vs Meajan Ali Ahmed and 15 others, 18 DLR (SC) 343,115 days delay was not condoned observing.

"4. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury has had no difficulty in showing that on these facts, there had been delay which it is entirely impossible to excuse. The government were aware from the outset that on account of the floods in Bogra they were already out of time on the day when the Deputy commissioner made his reference, i.e. the 22nd October, 1962. The case arising as it did out of the acquisition of rent receiving interests, a subject which has given rise to intensive litigation, of which in the main the Board of Revenue was presumably in charge, it is not easy to see why in this particular case, affecting, as is said one of the biggest Hats in the Province and a major source of revenue for the district of Bogra, it should have been necessary to relegate the papers after the decision of the High Court to the district authorities for their opinion, which in the circumstances could hardly have possessed any value. The Government's case rested on statutes, and not on considerations of balance or of justice in regard to local conditions. Before the High Court, the Province was represented by a Government Pleader. This was a case which should certainly have been dealt with in Dacca without need of reference to Bogra at all, but even allowing for the unnecessary reference to the district authorities, and the pre-occupation of those authorities with the flood, there are delays following after the 22nd October, 1962 which cannot be explained on any ground that can be acceptable in a Court to avoid the effect of limitation in respect of right that have become vested through lapse of time. There was no need for the Board of Revenue to have taken 16 'days' before referring the matter to the Legal Remembrancer, or for the Legal Remembrancer to take another 5 days before referring the matter to the Government Pleader. Worst of all is the delay of some 45 days between obtaining copies of the judgment and decree and the filing of the petition for special leave. There is no excuse for that particular period, when the file was not passing between offices, but was conceivably in the possession of the Government Pleader, who had already given an opinion in favour of filing an appeal. Once time limited by law has expired, the party which is out of time must, particularly in a case where vested rights have been assured through lapse of time, that here it is difficult to find an explanation for any period of the delay which has been allowed to occur,totaling 113 days in all, that is, nearly twice the prescribed period of limitation. 5. We are satisfied that this is a case in which the prayer for condonation cannot be entertained. The order of condonation made at the time when leave was granted was passed ex parte and is rested moreover, on an application which gave the impression that the entire period of delay was due to the floods in Bogra. Now that the true facts are known it is clear that there is no ground for allowing condonation. There is reason to think that there are other modes in which uniformity in the application of the Ordinance of 1960 can be restored qua this particular Hat."

16. Mr Md Jaber, learned Assistant Attorney-General, appearing for the opposite party, on the other hand submits that, judgment passed by the learned District Judge being well reasonable is maintainable. Learned Assistant Attorney General further submits that in the application for condonation of delay, 1230 days was not properly explained but government filed supplementary-affidavit and also application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure explaining the delay and reasons stated therein being satisfactory, learned District Judge acted within his jurisdiction in applying his discretion by condoning the delay. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that in Title Suit No.97 of 1994 decree was passed for the plaintiff in respect of the self-same land but in Appeal from Original Decree No.131 of 1998 High Court Division found that plaintiff by applying gigantic fraud tried to grab the suit property by showing a dead man alive in auction proceeding of 1948 and set-aside the decree and sent the suit back on remand. Against this decision, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal was taken properly to the Appellate Division and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1476 of 2008 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1477 of 2008, both these civil petitions for leave to appeal were dismissed as not being pressed showing that plaintiffs of that suit and also of this suit played fraud upon the court and fraud having been detected vitiated everything. Learned Assistant Attorney-General on reference to a voluminous counter-affidavit, submits that this property cannot be a secular property as Government of Bangladesh purchased the suit property on 18-3-1943 in execution of a decree in respect of the suit land, as such, whatever title plaintiff has, extinguished after the sale has been confirmed. Learned Advocate further submits that plaintiff has no locus standi to file any suit on the subject matter. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits, that, in condoning the delay fate of appeal has not reached its finality and it is only admission by which parties now can contest the suit over the dispute as such plaintiff should not be prejudiced in admission of appeal. Learned Assistant Attorney-General on reference to voluminous counter-affidavit with some papers and "Shampurak Abedan" and also application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, submits that, if the application for condonation of delay be considered along with `Shampurak Abedan Patra" and the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, then sufficient reason can be found for condoning the delay. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that from Title Suit No.79 of 1994 it appears that suit was filed for declaration of title, confirmation of possession with some other reliefs and from that suit, present plaintiff herself strike out her name and filed the instant suit for permanent injunction. Since plaintiff strike out her name from Title Suit No.97 of 1994, she has no locus standi to file the instant suit as relief sought for in the earlier suit have total impact on the instant suit. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that it is admitted position that certain portion of the schedule property is abandoned property, as such as per provision of Article 14 of PO 16 of 1972 this suit cannot proceed. Learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that unless delay be condoned, the questions relating to the maintainability of the suit shall remain unanswered. Learned Assistant Attorney-General on submission of condonation of delay relied on the decisions of Director of Housing and Settlement vs Abdul Majid Howlader, 9 BLC (AD) 51 wherein it is held:—

"16. There has been delay of 542 days in filing the revisional application by the appellant. The High Court Division refused to condone the delay on the ground that the petitioner before the High Court Division was negligent in taking step in filing the revisional application against the decree passed in Title Appeal No. 118 of 1997 affirming the decree passed in Title Suit No. 191 of 1996. In the background of the provision of law the suit filed by the respondents and decreed by the courts below was being totally non-entertainable by the civil Court the High Court Division was required to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to correct the gross error of law committed by the courts below. In that view of the matter we are of the view that the High Court Division was not correct in refusing to condone the delay and consequent thereupon in not entertaining the revisional application. The High Court Division was quite unmindful of the fact that the reliefs granted in the suit were not legally available to the respondents and consequently allowing the gross error of law to remain in effect that would amount to allow the respondents to enjoy the fruit of the decree although under the law they are not entitled to the same and thus if the decree so passed in favour of the respondents remains winter feed the appellant and respondent No. 20 would be deprived of their legal claim in the property in suit. Since the respondents obtained a decree from a Court which was not competent to pass the same being barred by the law to entertain the suit of the kind filed by the respondents or, in other words, in view of the provision of law barring the civil Court from entertaining the kind of the suit filed by the plaintiffs and decreeing the same, the High court Division was required to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to correct the gross error of law committed by the courts below. The High Court Division in spite of filing of revisional application beyond the period prescribed by a long standing practice is quite competent in its revisional jurisdiction to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction to correct gross error of law committed by the courts below or, in other words, to put law straight in a case like the present one and in that view of the matter we are of the view High Court Division was not correct in not entertaining the revisional application upon condonation of the delay for which explanation was offered, though not accepted by the said Division on the view that the petitioner was guilty of serious negligence and lathes. Such explanation for condonation of inordinate delay of 542 days, cannot be accepted as satisfactory ". What the defendant says is that there was a suit against him, and that the suit was declared to have ended by reason of a decree passed with his consent. He never consented, and the result has been that there has been fraud committed upon the court. The court was persuaded to sign a decree to which the defendant had never consented and that upon the representation that he had consented to it. Therefore once the court is asked to go back upon its own procedure, it is not a question whether there is any section in the Civil Procedure code; to warrant the action of the court amending its proceedings. It is an inherent power of every court to correct its own proceedings where it has been misled."

33. Similarly in the case reported in 24 DLR 116, it has been held that as to case where fraud is committed upon the court as well as the parties, a court has inherent jurisdiction to interfere in exercise of its power vested in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in a case of fraud upon a party the only remedy is in a suit. Here we may also quote from an unreported decision of single Bench of this court passed in Civil Revision No. 86 of 1962 decided by Ali J, on 30-4-65 on a consideration of a number of decisions his Lordship Ali, J, arrived at the following conclusion:

"On a careful perusal of these decisions as well as a number of the other authorities referred to therein I feel that it is firmly well settled that in case of fraud on a party the only remedy is in a suit. As to the cases where fraud is committed upon the court as well as the parties, the consensus of judicial opinion appears to be that the court has inherent jurisdiction to interfere in exercise of the powers vested in it under section 151. At any rate, no authority could be cited before me laying down categorically that in such cases the court has no inherent jurisdiction to interfere."

34. Unreported decision of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No.324 of 1982 on the question of fraud practice upon the court. The case of Babor Ali Prodhan vs Kinu Mia, 31 DLR (AD) 323 this decision relied by the learned Assistant Attorney-General.

35. Lastly the case of Md Refaat Ali vs Government of Bangladesh, 21 BLD 133 on inherent powers of the court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, wherein it is held that:

"9. It is true, ordinarily the court does not exercise its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure whenever a remedy is available to the aggrieved party under any provision of the Code of Civil Procedure. But it is also well-settled that if the disputed order or decree is obtained by a party by practicing fraud upon the court or it is has been occasioned due to the fault of the Court or court officials, the court has not only the competence in exercise of its inherent power under section 151 of the code to undo the wrong done to the aggrieved party but also it is imperative in the interest of justice to do so. Fraud always vitiated all solemn transactions and a fraudulent act by its own nature is a nullity in the eye of law and it is never protected by law. In such cases, it will be highly inequitable and in just to ask the wronged party to seek his relief under other arduous and time consuming provisions of law instead of giving him a relief under section 151 of the Code as the special preserve of the court for doing justice. It deserves to be noted in this connection that procedures are just means towards advancement of the cause of justice and not certainly for obstructing it in the name of technical fall-outs. The filing of an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be allowed to stand in the way of the relief the defrauded defendant is entitled to under the law. We are satisfied in the facts of the case, that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly exercised his power under section 151 of the Code in giving the appropriate relief to the worried. We find no merit in the case which fails accordingly."

36. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned advocate submits that there are time of limitation, one is prescribed, written, that cannot be condoned but other, which on proper application for condoning the delay, can be condoned.

37. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the materials filed before us and voluminous counter-affidavit of defendant No. 3 and also government.

38. Let us proceed one by one. Article 152 of the Limitation Act prescribed period of limitation for filing the appeal to the District Judge.

Description of Suit -152. Under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, (V of 1908) to the court of a District Judge.

Period of Limitation -Thirty days.

Time from which period begins to run - The date of the decree or order appealed from.

<u>39. Section 12 of the Limitation Act gives indulgence to the litigant if the litigant did not come within the prescribed period for an appeal, exclusion of time can be allowed by applying subsections 1, 2, 3 and 4. It has been held by judicial authorities that under sub-sections 2 and 3 of section 12 of the Limitation Act an appellant is entitled to get a deduction of time requisites for obtaining a copy of the decree as well as copy of the judgment if applied for copies of the decree and judgment at different times, both these periods should be excluded in computing the period of limitation provided the applications were made when his right to appeal subsist. It may be otherwise said that litigant would get the benefit of the time on which litigant has no control. A litigant shall get the period from the date the decree is signed until it was made ready for delivery. It is being now well settled that application for copy must be made before the period of appeal expired. Therefore, if the application for copy of the decree is made when the period of limitation for appeal had already run out, the appellant is not entitled to exclude time under section 12 of the Act in obtaining copy of the decree. Time requisites, as mentioned in sub-section(2) as per judicial decisions, means that in computing the period of limitation prescribed for an appeal, the day on which the judgment or order complained of was pronounced and the time taken by the court to make available the copy applied for, have to be excluded.</u>

40. Now the question of condonation of delay i.e. after obtaining the judgment and decree and after exclusion of time as provided under section 12 if the litigant do not come within the prescribed period, then also the litigant can come before the appellate/revisional forum if the litigant could satisfy the court as to his conduct for not moving the court within prescribed period. Section 5 of the Limitation Act gives remedy which runs as :—

"Section 5. Extension of period in certain cases Any appeal or application for a revision or a review of judgment or for leave to appeal or any other application to which this may be made applicable by or under any enactment for the time being in force may be admitted after the period of limitation prescribed thereof, when the appellant or applicant satisfies the Court that he had sufficient cause for not prefer-ring the appeal of, making the application within such period."

41. This section would not automatically apply. It requires two ingredients for its application, one is satisfy the court and next is sufficient cause. Satisfy the court means that after due diligence, after obtaining the certified copy if the litigant do not come in court in time, and the explanation covering the entire period which inspire the court to condone the 'Unusual' delay, sufficient cause include Lawyer's wrong advice, mistake or oversight of the todbirkar, moving on wrong forum, disturbance in the country etc. It is to be borne in mind that sufficient cause is liberally construed to be applied by the court judiciously, not arbitrarily or capriciously that applicant act bonafide, negligent, nor inaction nor want of bonafide.

42. This law has been applied in different ways on the facts of each case some time we find six days delay has not been condoned (Bangladesh vs Abdul Wahab, 45 DLR 30) some time we find 4,000 days delay has been condoned, the condonation of delay is exclusively within the discretion of the court and this discretion is to be applied on the conduct of the litigant.

43. It is admitted position that appeal when tendered was out of time by 1230 days. Let us go through the applications, one for con-donation of delay, next, 'Shampurak abedanpatra' whether this type of application is allowable in court we do not understand and third, on the same date an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the Government. In front of shampurak abedanpatra' there is no reason for filing of the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the same date, if it is on different dates then the case may be otherwise. Whatever the case may be, let us read the application for delay i.e. first application filed on 17-9-1998 wherein it is stated that 'decree was passed on 30-4-1995 and decree was drawn up on 7-5-1995. That's all. No other narration excepting the period of delay. The person who sworned affidavit has not mentioned the post he hold in the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong. In what authority he act on behalf of the government has not been disclosed. We do not understand Jela Proshashok' office can be used as residence of the person. In the affidavit it has been written as:

হলফনামা

আমি বাদশা মিয়া পিতা মৃত আবুল কাশেম মোহাম্মদ জামাল, সাকিন-পাথর ঘাটা থানা-কোতয়ালী জিলা-চট্রগ্রাম বর্তমানে জেলা প্রশাসকের কায্যালয় চট্রগ্রাম........।

44. From the affidavit we do not find in what capacity this gentleman sworned the affidavit.

45. Identity of this man is very difficult and doubtful. A supplementary-affidavit in the nature of 'Shampurak Abedan Patra' was filed on 25-11-2010 i.e. long after 12 years of the first -original application for condonation of delay. In this 'Shampurak Abedin Patra' for condonation of delay, paragraphs Nos. 3, 4, 5 and 6 relates to the merits of the government case. Paragraphs Nos. 6 and 7 relates to explanation as regard condonation of delay. We may quote paragraphs 6 and 7:

৬। উপরে বর্ণিত বিবরণ থেকে দেখা যায় যে অত্র আপীল দপ্তরের কোন গাফিলতি ছিল না । মাননীয় উচ্চ আদালতে একাধিক নজির আছে যে আইনজীবী বা আইনজীবি ক্লার্কের কারণে মামলায় কোন ক্ষতি হইলে তৎজন্য মামলার পক্ষগণ দায়ী হইতে পারে না।

৭। আলোচ্য ক্ষেত্রে আপীলকারীপক্ষের আপীল দায়েরের ক্ষেত্রে অনিচ্ছাকৃত ভাবে ১২৩০ দিন বিলম্ব ঘটিয়াছে। অপরদিকে নালিশী মূল মোদ্দমা ও রায় ডিক্রি non-entertainable suit ও এখতিয়ার বহির্ভূত রায় ডিক্রি হওয়ায় বিজ্ঞ আপীল আদালতের অন্তনির্হিত ক্ষমতা প্রয়োগপূবর্ক ন্যায় স্বার্থে বিলম্ব মওকুফ করে আপীলটি গ্রহন করা আবশ্যক । এই বিষয়ে মহামান্য সুপ্রিম কোর্টের আপীলাত বিভাগের 9 BLC (AD) 51 এ প্রকাশিত Housing and Settlement vs Abdul Majid Howlader মামলার রায় প্রতিষ্ঠার যোগ্য । উক্ত রায়ের প্রকাশিত কপি পৃথক ফিরিস্তি সহ বিজ্ঞ আদালতে দাখিল করা হইল।

46. Paragraphs Nos. 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 described locus standi of the plaintiff. On a reading of the explanation we do not find the requisites as regard obtaining certified copy, as there is no mention as to on which date certified copy of the impugned judge was applied, how the delay accrued in the original application. We find entire application directed toward conduct of the government pleader. We do not find what action has been taken by the government against its pleader. This affidavit was sworn by Abu Monsur Hossain Chowdhury as:

শপথনাম

আমি আবু মনসুর হোসেন চৌধুরী বয়স-৫২ বৎসর পিতা হাজী আহম্মদ হোসেন চৌধুরী সাকিন আর এস শাখা জেলা প্রশাসক অফিস ঢাকঘর-কোতয়ালী থানা কোতয়ালী জিলা-চট্রগ্রাম বর্তমান জেলা প্রশাসকের কার্য্যালয় চট্রগ্রাম.........।

47. Without disclosing what nature of work he did.

48. On the same date, application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed. In the cause title it has been described as "the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set-aside the decree being barred by law". We do not understand how this application can be said to be treated to be an application for condonation of delay. This is for separate reason. The appeal has not yet been admitted but government pleader filed this application for setting aside the decree and that too, on the same date of filing of Shampurak Abedanpatra. In this application all through it has been stated from first to last page about the conduct of the plaintiff as plaintiff played 'gigantic fraud' and she has no locus standi to file the suit as the schedule attracts abandoned property. This application also filed by the same person, Abu Monsur Hossain Chowdhury with the same status i.e. resides in the office of the 'Zilla Proshashok'. From all these application it is clearly shown that the plaintiff played fraud upon the court in obtaining decree and government pleader practiced gigantic fraud upon the court but there is no explanation for condoning the delay. Moreso the person who made affidavit his status has not been disclosed. This is one side of the appellant.

49. Let us now go to the other part. It has been held by different decisions that long delay can be condoned on the conduct of the litigant. Now we see the conduct of the litigant i.e. government. From the order sheets of the appeal it appears that this appeal was tendered on 17-9-1998 and at that time District Judge was Mr Md Jahirul Islam and from Order No.l dated 19-10-1999 it appears that application was filed along with memorandum of appeal. Thereafter, we find that his lordship Mr Justice Siddiqur Rahman Miah was District Judge, who is now going to be retired but government and its machineries keep the matter hanging. Application for condonation of delay is hanging for long 13 years of filing of the application. Suddenly this matter was taken up by the learned judge who condoned the delay of 1230 days in a sentence. It is settled principle of law that if the delay be condoned on the date of filing of application or at an early date then the applicant need no explanation of the delay from the date of filing and its disposal but when the application was not disposed of at an early date and the condonation matter kept in hanging for unlimited period then the applicant/ government is to explain why the matter of condnation of delay was not disposed earlier. It appears long 13 years after filing of the appeal and application for condonation of delay, the application has been disposed of shows the character of the government lawyer. It appears that earlier on two occasions plaintiff came before this court, in Civil Revision No. 701 of 2005 and CO No. 86 of 2011 for disposal of the application for condonation of delay expeditiously but government, when a decree has been passed legally or illegally, keep mum and suddenly rise from slumber in 2011 and was successful in obtaining one sentence favourable order from appellate court and delay was condoned.

50. Now the other point. We find defendant No. 3 as well as government made sub-missions on merit of the case but this rule relates only for condonation of the delay, Government as well as defendant No. 3 argued that certain portion of the case property is abandoned property as such as per Article 14 of PO No. 16 of 1972 no one can take this property. Yes if the entire property be abandoned then one cannot take the abandoned property. Article 14 of PO 16 of 1972 runs as follows:

"14. (1) Any property vested in the Government under this Order shall be exempt from all legal process, including seizure, distress, ejectment attachment or sale by any officer of a court or any other authority, and no injunction or other order of whatever kind in respect of such property shall be granted or made by any Court or any other authority, and the government shall not be divested or dispossessed of such property by operation of any law for the time being force.

Government lawyer as well as Assistant Attorney-General as well as defendant No. 3 lawyers referred to the decision passed by this court while dispose of First Appeal No. 131 of 1998, let us quote the certain portion of the judgment:

"Furthermore some portion of the suit property was declared abandoned property and accordingly the plaintiffs prayed for declaration that the suit property is not an abandoned property. In such a position the trial court ought to have separated the abandoned property from the schedule of the plaint. It is settled principle that no suit can be heard by the civil court when the same is admittedly declared as abandoned property."

51. It is the stand of the government that the entire land was purchased by government in 1943. If the entire land was purchased by the government, then how did this property become abandoned property. Government lastly took the stand that a portion of the land is abandoned property. Government cannot have two stands in respect of a property. It is either purchased or abandoned but not two at a time, it is settled that if it is the stand of the government that a position of land is abandoned property then before declaring the property as abandoned property, Government must go for partition of the property, separate the portion then declare it as abandoned. Reference may be made to the case of Rahima Akther vs Asim Kumar Bose, 40 DLR (AD) 23 where it is held In the case of Zillul Huq vs Maloti Bala Dey, 50 DLR 367 it is held "Now the question that calls for our immediate consideration is whether the co-owner of an undivided property can maintain possession in the entire disputed property to the exclusion of other co-owners and whether the Government stepping into the shoes of the absentee co-owners can oust the co-owner in possession of the entire ejmali property by exercising executive power. The answer to this question is an emphatic no. The settled law is that a co-owner's right in undivided joint property extends over every inch of the joint property and his/her possession over the entire property cannot be termed as unlawful by any means. In such a case, the co-owner in possession of the entire ejmali property and their only remedy lies in a suit for partition for carving out their shares in the property in question by way of partition metes and bounds. In the instant case, the Government, stepping into the shoes of r and Bimala Kanta, who becam aliens in due course of law, cannot better right than Birendra and Bimala as such, possession of disputed property without bringing a suit for partition to separate the enemy partition of the property in dispute."

52. Now other question. On a reading of the judgment it appears that learned judge was busy in finding locus standi and gigantic fraud by the plaintiff. That can be done after delay has been condoned not before that. Not a single word was 'expend' as to the explanation as been given, is satisfactory or it can he accepted. Just in one sentence 'for the reasons stated above delay has been condoned' without discussing the merit of the application. This type of judgment cannot be kept on record. This Judgment shows that the learned Judge lacking total legal knowledge to deal with this type of matter.

53. Lastly, most vital aspect which totally oust the Government out of court. Government against the self same judgment, filed Other Appeal No.255 of 1999 before the District Judge with prayer for condonation of delay for 1596 days. We do not understand against the self same judgment government filed two appeals, one is out of time by 1230 days other is out of time by 1596 days. Appellate Court condone the delay but in Civil Revision No.701 of 2005 (judgment dated 15-4-2009) this court set-aside the judgment of the appellate court and dismissed the appeal. Government did not proceed further. Since one appeal is dismissed from the self same judgment at the instance of the self same party other appeal by the self same party cannot proceed. This also shows conduct of the government lawyer which is very unfortunate.

54. We are not oblivious of the fact that Appellate Division condoned the delay of more than 4000 days but this decision is not application of the given case as, we may summaries, as:—

i) Appeal with application for condonation of delay was tendered and filed on17-9-1998.

(ii) Shampurak Abedan and application under section 151 of the Code were filed on 12-11-2010.

(iii) Matter was disposed on 15-3-2010. Other appeal No. 255 of 1999 was filed against the selfsame judgment for condoning delay of 1596 days (whereas in this appeal 1230 days delay has occurred); appeal was allowed. (v) Civil Revision No. 701 of 2005 was taken and Rule was made absolute dismissing the appeal preferred by the government. (vi) Government did not proceed further stamping the fate of this appeal.

<u>55. Court is not protecting the property of government and if Government lawyer failed to protect the property court has no duty to come in aid of Government. Let us take in this way. Every lawyer has a chamber and can take pace of the proceedings of his case. Criminal/ Civil/ Writ and other through a clerk. Government is the biggest/largest litigant who has GP, PP lot of AGPS and APPS with a handful of hands to look after the proceeding. Delay may be one/ two months or 3 months for different official performances but when it goes a long way that it itself speak negligence and lack of bona fide which cannot be condoned. With these observations we find substance in this Rule.</u>

56. In the result, this Rule is made absolute. No costs.

57. The impugned judgment and order dated 15-3-2011 passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong in Other Appeal No.248 of 1998 is set-aside.

Send down the lower courts at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 4.7.85 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 84 of 1983).
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, C.J.: In this appeal by special leave the only question is whether the High Court Division is well founded in law in refusing pre-emption in full on a finding that the land of the Pre-emptor, who is a contiguous land-holder, is not wholly contiguous to the land transferred. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is dated 4 July 1985 in Civil Revision No. 84 of 1983.

2. Appellant-Pre-emptor is the owner of Plot No.2575 of Mouza Alipur. Some portion of Plots Nos. 2574 and 2573 were transferred by their owner under a kabala dated 3 June 1976, whereupon the appellant filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the Munsif, Faridpur, claiming pre-emption of both the plots taking the ground that these two plots are contiguous to his own land. His claim was resisted by the respondent-transferee taking the ground that only a part of Plot No. 2574 is contiguous to the appellant's land that Plot No. 2573 is not at all contiguous, and as such he is not entitled to pre-empt both the plots. The trial Court allowed the pre-emption in respect of both the plots finding them to be contiguous to the pre-emptor's land. This finding was confirmed in appeal by the Subordinate Judge. But in revision, as stated above, a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division reversed the finding in respect of Plot No. 2573 and modified the decision of the courts below and allowed pre-emption only in respect of Plot No. 2574 which he found to be contiguous to the pre-emptor's land in Plot No. 2575. The pre-emptor came before us for leave to appeal and leave was granted to consider whether both the Plots, 2574 and 2573, being allegedly contiguous to each other and forming a compact block, should have been allowed on pre-emption on the ground of "contiguity."

<u>3. The learned Single Judge did not find Plot No. 2573 to be contiguous to appellant's land, Plot No. 2575, and refused pre-emption to this extent relying upon an observation of this Court in Ahmed Hossain Vs. Basharat Ali, 32 DLR (AD) 54. In that case lands in several plots comprising five different holdings, but touching each other only marginally and not forming a compact block of land, were sought to be pre-empted by a person claiming that his land was contiguous to these five lands, which were transferred under a single Kabala. In that case five different lands transferred "were close to each other in a zig zag way" and the pre-emptor's land was not directly contiguous to any of these lands transferred except one of these lands, namely, a tank. This tank was also separated from the pre-emptor's land by a public path. The courts below including the High Court Division ignored the public path which belonged to the Government and over which no other person put forward any competing claim for pre-emption. In these circumstances, the Courts below held the tank to be contiguous to the pre-emptor's land and allowed pre-emption of all the lands transferred. But on appeal, this Court took the view that the word "contiguous" was not "neighbouring", but it meant actually "touching" and that the tank being separated by a public path it could not be held to be contiguous to the pre-emptor's land. This was the main reason for this Court's interference with the finding of the courts below and pre-emption was refused on the ground that "contiguity" was snapped by the public path. In that connection this Court made a query as to whether these five different lands, which were transferred under a kabala could be held to be contiguous to each other so as to form a single compact block, and found the answer in the negative. Indication was, however, given in that judgment that had those five plots been closely connected together holding a compact block of land and had there been no public path between the pre-emptor's land and the compact block including the tank, the principle of "contiguity" might have been applicable.</u>

<u>4. A similar question came up before this Court in a subsequent case, Hazi Tozammbar Ali vs. Abdus Sailor, 34 DLR (AD) 217. Three of the Judges of this Court were common to the decisions in both the cases, one in 32 DLR (AD) 54 and the other in 34 DLR (AD) 217. In the latter, the lands transferred consisted of seven plots, all recorded under a single khatian and the pre-emptor's land was contiguous to two of those seven plots, but nevertheless, he was held to be owning land "contiguous to the land transferred", because though the pre-emptor's land was contiguous to two of the seven plots transferred, but all those seven plots were not only contiguous to each other but they together constituted one single block of land; as such the entire block was treated as contiguous to the land of the pre-emptor. In that connection the policy behind allowing pre-emption to a contiguous land-holder was explained and it was observed that one of the purposes for allowing pre-emption to a contiguous land-holder was apparently to help enlarge small uneconomical agricultural holdings by consolidation or amalgamation.</u>

5. In the instant case, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division relied only upon the previous case, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 54. The later one in 34 DLR (AD) 217 was not probably placed before him. Facts of the two cases are quite distinguishable. In the previous case there was no contiguity at all between the land of the pre-emptor and the land transferred; secondly, the several lands transferred lay here and there and did not constitute a single block to be treated as one land. Now, if the principle laid down in the 34 DLR case is applicable to the present case, pre-emption as a whole, that is, in respect of both the plots transferred, should be allowed. But on close examination we find that this principle is not applicable here.

<u>6. Admittedly, the appellant's land, Plot No. 2575, is contiguous to Plot No. 2574, but it is not contiguous to Plot No. 2573. However, if both these plots are closely contiguous to each other and form a compact block of land, then only this principle may be applied. Evidence recorded in the case, however, does not appear to support the claim as to contiguity forming one compact block. But the all-important question is whether both these two plots were transferred as a whole under the kabala dated 3 July 1976? The answer is clearly in the negative. Only some parts of these two plots were transferred. The areas thus transferred measure only 20 decimals out of 70 decimals of land, which is the total area of both the plots, 2574 and 2573. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division allowed pre-emption of this portion transferred measuring 20 decimals, that is, 2/7, from Plot No. 2574. Whereas this area lies in both the plots. This modification as to the area pre-empted. We find, has been made in a rough and ready manner. For, admittedly this 20 decimals of land was transferred from both Plot Nos. 2574 and 2573. A pre-emptor is entitled to pre-empt only the area of land actually transferred. Therefore the appellant's claim to pre-emption cannot exceed 20 decimal, which he has been already allowed from one plot. As to the other plot, neither is there any evidence what area was transferred from each of the two plots, nor is there any evidence whether the two areas transferred from these two plots themselves remain contiguous after the transfer. Anyway, the transferree has not raised any objection to the pre-emption of 20 decimal from only one plot—No. 2574. In the circumstances, pre-emption as a whole, which is of both the plots, we find, has been rightly refused.</u>

The appeal is dismissed with costs.

End.

Tajuddin (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Farah Mahbub: Since common question of law and facts are involved in both the writ petitions as such, those have been heard together and are being disposed of by this single judgment.

2. In these Rules Nisi issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 6-3-2013 (Annexure-D) passed by the learned Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 1st Court, Jessore in Artha Rin Suit No. 35 of 2011 as well as the judgment and decree dated 6-3-201 (Annexure-D) passed by the learned Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 1st Court, Jessore in Artha Rin Suit No. 36 of 2011 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and hence, are of no legal effect.

3. In view of the statements so have been made in both the writ petitions Mr Sifar Mustafa, the learned Advocate appearing for the respective petitioners of both the writ petitions drawing attention to the impugned judgment and decree dated 6-3-20013 (Annexure-D) submits that the same has been decreed under section 13(3) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (in short, the Ain, 2003). In this regard, drawing attention to the said provision of law he goes to submit that in order to invoke section 13(3) the Adalat has to be satisfied that the defendants concerned have admitted the claim of the plaintiff bank and that to that effect the bank has to make an application. In this regard, referring to paragraph Nos. 5, 7, 11, 12 and 13 of the written statements so have been filed by the respective defendants including the petitioner he goes to argue that this petitioners, the defendant No. 2 has categorically denied the claim of the plaintiff bank, as is apparent therefrom; rather making an application on 24-1-2013 (Annexure-C) this petitioner brought attention to the Adalat about the disputes so have been agitated therein and made a prayer to fix up another date for peremptory hearing upon taking evidence on the assertion so made by the petitioner. But the Adalat without giving any observation and findings whatsoever on the application dated 24-1-2013 and also in the absence of any application of the respondent bank has decreed the suit invoking the provision as contained in section 13(3) of the Ain, 2003. Accordingly, he submits that both the impugned judgment and decree should be knocked down for having been passed without jurisdiction. In support he has referred the case of Md Afran Uddin Akand vs Artha Rin Adalat and others reported in 15 BLT 343.

4. Conversely, Mr Kazi Akhtar Hossain, the learned Advocate by filling affidavit in opposition on behalf of respondent-bank submits drawing attention to the statement so made in paragraph 13 of the written statements so filed by the defendants submits that there the petitioner has admitted the claim of the bank stating, inter-alia, "অত্র বিবাদী ইচ্ছাকৃতভাবে লোন পরিশোধ করিতে গড়িমসি করেন নাই। I" In view of the stated admissions of the defendant petitioner the Adalat has rightly exercised power under section 13(3) of the Ain in decreeing the suit. In support, he has referred the case Md Kamal Uddin Akand vs Artha Rin Adalat and other reported in VI ADC (2009) 383. He further submits that for challenging the judgment and decree this petitioner has alternative forum as provided under section 41 of the Ain, 2003. Having not invoked the same these Rules must fail on the count of maintainability

5. In order to appreciate the respective arguments of the contending parties let us first have a look at section 13 of the Ain, 2003, which runs as under-

“১৩।মামলার বির্চায্য বিষয় গঠন ও নিষ্পত্তি। ১। বিবাদী কর্তৃক লিখিত জবাব দাখিল হওয়ার পরবর্তীতে ধার্য্য একটি নির্ধারিত তারিখে আদালত উভয় পক্ষকে যদি উপস্থিত থাকে শুনানী করিয়া এবং আরজি ও লিখিত বর্ণর্না পর্যালোচনা করিয়া মামলার বিচার্য বিষয় যদি থাকে গঠন করিবে এবং যদি বিচার্য বিষয় না থাকে আদালত অবিলম্বে রায় বা আদেশ প্রদান করিবে।

২। উপ-ধারা (১) এ নির্ধারিত তারিখে কোন বা উভয় পক্ষ যদি অনুপস্থিত থাকে তা হইলে আদালত আরজি ও লিথিত বর্ণনা পর্যালোচনা করিয়া মামলার বির্চায বিষয়, যদি থাকে গঠন করিবে এবং যদি বিচার্য বিষয় না থাকে আদালত অবিলম্বে রায় বা আদেশ প্রদান করিবে।”

৩। মামলার যে কোন পর্যায়ে লিখিত বর্ণনায় কিংবা অন্য কোনভাবে বিবাদী কর্তৃক বাদীর আর্জিও বক্তব্য স্বীকৃত হইয়া থাকিলে এবং উত্তরূপ স্বীকৃতির ভিত্তিতে যেরুপ রায় বা আদেশ পাইতে বাদী অধিকারী সেরূপ রায়  বা আদেশ প্রার্থনা করিয়া বাদী আদালতের নিকটে দরখাস্ত করিলে আদালত বাদী ও বিবাদীর মধ্যে বিদ্যমান অপরাপর বিষয় নিষ্পত্তির জন্য অপেক্ষা না করিয়া উপযুক্ত রায় বা আদেশ প্রদান করিবে।

৪। মামলার শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য প্রথম তারিখে অথবা মামলার যেকোন পর্যায়ে যদি আদালতের নিকট প্রতীয়মান হয় যে পক্ষদ্বয়ের মধ্যে ঘটনা অথবা আইনগত বিষয়ে কোন বিবাদ নাই, তাহা হইলে আদালত অবিলম্বে রায় বা আদেশ প্রদান করিয়া মামলা চুড়ান্ত নিষ্পত্তি করিবে।

6. "Upon reading section 13 it is clear that after filing of the written statement the court, on a subsequent date, upon hearing both the parties if they are present and on perusal of the plaint and written statement will frame issue, if there be any and if there is no issue to be framed then the court may dispose of the suit by delivering judgment or order. That means the court will have to peruse the plaint and written statement filed by both the parties on a subsequent date and come to a conclusion as to whether issues are to be framed or judgment and order is to he delivered. Again, in section 13(3) it has been categorically stated that on perusal of the written statement if it appears to the court that the defendant admitted the claim of the plaintiff the court can pass judgment or order on the basis of such admission. This may be done even before deciding any other issues, if framed. Again section 13(4) on the other hand, categorically says that when the court will be of the opinion at any stage of the suit that there is no dispute between the parties as regards the facts and circumstances or the law then the court can dispose of the suit finally. So on perusal of the aforesaid provisions of law it appears that the court before passing any judgment or order or finally disposing of the suit shall have to take into consideration the facts stated in the plaint and written statement of the parties and to determine that whether the defendants admit the claim of the plaintiff and also to determine whether there is any dispute between the parties as regards the facts as stated in the pleadings" as has been observed in Md Arfanuddin Akan vs Artha Rin Adalat reported in 15 BLT 343.

<u>7. In view of the above, it is apparent that in order to pass judgment and decree under the said provision the Adalat has to be satisfied that there is an admission by the defendant concern over the claim so made by the plaintiff bank and to that effect the Bank is required to make an application. Moreso, the legislature having used the word এবং after the words “বাদীর আরজির বক্তব্য স্বীকৃত হইয়া থাকিলে” and “উক্তরুপ স্বীকৃতির ভিত্তিতে যেরুপ রায় বা আদেশ পাইতে বাদী অধিকারী” made those two requirements conjunctive. In the instant case, the defendants including the petitioner in their written statements, so filed in both the suits, have categorically disputed the claim of the plaintiff bank, as is apparent in particular from paragraph Nos. 5 and 7 of the written statements. However, on examining the entire order sheets, as have been annexed as Annexure-C-1, it does not reflect that on the alleged admission of the defendant-petitioner the bank has made an application to the Adalat with a prayer to pass judgment and decree under section 13(3) of the Ain. Rather, the Adalat has decreed the suit invoking the said provision of law and based its findings on the assertion –</u>

<u>“...........বিবাদী কর্তৃক লোন পরিশোধে ইচ্ছাকৃত ক্রটি ছিলনা মর্মে উল্লেখ থাকায় লোনের বিষয়টি বিবাদী কর্তৃক স্বীকৃত হইয়াছে বলিয়া বিবেচিত হয়।..........’</u>

8. This statement was not the only pleadings of the defendants, rather in their written statements they have categorically disputed the claim of the plaintiff bank and to that effect the petitioner made a prayer before the Adalat by filing an application on 24-1-2013 to fix up another date for peremptory hearing of the suit upon recording evidence on that score. But the Adalat has rejected the same and ultimately, decreed the suit under section 13(3) of the Ain without taking any evidence whatsoever.

9. Be that as it may, we have no manner of doubt to find that the impugned judgment and decree dated 6-3-2013 passed in connection with Artha Rin Suit Nos.35 and 36 both of 2011 have been passed without jurisdiction. The said view of ours also finds support in the case reported in 15 BLT 343 at paragraph 13 which are quoted hereinbelow—

"Considering the decisions referred above and discussions made herein above we are of the view that if the Adalat passes any order which is wholly without jurisdiction not is excess of jurisdiction, when despite of the fact that the law provided forum for appeal, the petitioner cannot be debarred from availing the jurisdiction under Article 102 of die Constitution. Because the question of jurisdiction of the Court goes to the very root of the matter brought before it and when the court does not have any jurisdiction to see, everything done subsequent thereto shall fall through and the Court which has got no jurisdiction to pass such order over the matter shall not go into flue merit of the matter as decided in the case of the case of Managing Director, Rupali Bank Ltd vs Tafazal Hossain and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260."

10. In that view of the matter the decision so has been referred by the respondent Bank cannot be made applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

11. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute.

12. The impugned judgment and decree dated 6-3-2013 (Annexure-D) passed by the learned Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 1st Court, Jessore in Artha Rin Suit Nos. 35 and 36 both of 2011 are hereby declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and hence, are of no legal effect.

13. The Adalat is hereby directed' to frame issues upon considering the pleadings of both the contending parties and to hear and dispose of both the suit expeditiously in accordance with law.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.
