full_judgment:
Md Badruzzaman J: The five writ petitions heard together. Since all the writ petitions involve similar facts and identical question of law, they are taken together for disposal by this single judgment.

2. In Writ Petition No. 1385 of 2009 Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the post of the petitioner and upper division assistants of Bangladesh post office should not be treated/determined as the post of second class gazetted officer with the pay scale of Taka 5,100-10,360 of the nation-al pay scale, 2005 with the designation of administrative officer.

3. In both Writ Petitions No. 8706 of 2009 and 8707 of 2009 Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why direction should not be given to grant same pay scale and gazetted status and to extend the facilities in respect of pay scale and status as granted to the Upper Division Assistants to the Secretariat of Bangladesh [vide circulars dated 13-9-1995 and 28-4-1997 of Ministry of Establishment and Circular dated 1-6-1999 of Ministry of Finance as contained in Annexures-B, B(1) and B(2)] to the petitioner and other Head Assistants of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education.

4. In Writ Petition No. 7272 of 2009 Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to grant same pay scale, 2nd Class Gazetted status and to extend the facilities as granted to the Upper Division Assistants of the Secretariat of Bangladesh [vide circulars dated 13-9-1995 and 28-4-1997 of Ministry of Establishment and Circular dated 1-6-1999 of Ministry of Finance as contained in Annexure- B, B(1) and B(2)] to the petitioner and other Head Assistants of Public Health Engineering.

5. In Writ Petition No. 4544 of 2010 Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to extend the facilities in respect of pay scale and status as granted to Upper Division Assistant of Bangladesh Secretariat [vide office order dated 10-8-1981 of Ministry of Finance and Circulars dated 13-9-1995 and 28-4-1997 of Ministry of Establishment and Circular dated 1-6-1999 of Ministry of Finance as contained in Annexures- C, D, D(1) and D(2)] to the petitioner and other Upper Division Assistants and Upper Division Assistant-Cum-Accountants under the Directorate of Primary Education.

6. These rules were earlier heard by another Division Bench of this Court analogously and by judgment and order dated 10-1-2011 those were made absolute. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order the respondent Government filed Civil Petition for leave to appeal being Nos. 320 of 2012, 1939 and 1932-33 of 2011 and 837 of 2012 before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The Appellate Division, after hearing the Leave Petitions analogously, by an order dated 10-1-2013 set aside the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division and sent back these writ petitions on remand before this Bench to dispose of the matter afresh on merit.

7. Facts, relevant for the purpose of the disposal of the rules, in short, are as follows:

The petitioner in Writ Petition No. 1385 of 2009 was appointed as Upper Division Clerk in the office of the Post Master General, Eastern Circle (now Central Circle), Dhaka by appointment letter dated 10-11-1979 (Annexure-A) and she joined the service in time. Her service has been confirmed and made permanent by order dated 7-1-1987 (Annexure-B) with effect from 6-10-1985. In the meantime, by a circular dated 23-5-1984 (Annexure-C) the post of Upper Division Clerk has been re-designated as Upper Division Assistant.

8. In Writ Petition No. 8706 of 2009 the petitioner obtained BA degree and appointed as typist by office order dated 4-4-1981 in the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education and his service was confirmed by office order dated 30-7-1983. Eventually he was promoted to the post of Upper Division Assistant on 10-4-2006.

9. In Writ Petition No. 8707 of 2009 the petitioner after obtaining B.A. degree was appointed as Lower Division Assistant by office order dated 6-11-1974. He joined the service on 14-11-1974 in the office of District Inspector of Schools, Dhaka. On transfer he joined in the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education on 13-5-1976. Then he was promoted to the post of Upper Division Assistant on 27-6-2000 and lastly to the post of Head Assistant on 25-3-2008.

10. In Writ Petition No. 7272 of 2009 the petitioner was appointed as Clerk-cum-Typist by appointment letter dated 25-8-1977 (Annexure-A) in the office of Superintending Engineer, Public Health Engineering, Chittagong Circle. He was promoted to the post of Upper Division Assistant on 30-11-2002 and then to the post of Head Assistant on 15-2-2009.

11. In Writ Petition No. 4544 of 2010 the petitioner was appointed as Upper Division Assistant-cum-Accountant under the Directorate of Primary Education by appointment letter dated 25-5-1983 (Annexure-A) and he joined in the service on 1-6-1983. Then by order dated 13-11-1983 his service was made permanent with effect from 1-6-1983.

12. All the petitioners are serving in different positions in different department/ministries of the government. The petitioners and other Head Assistants and Upper Division Assistants of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education, Directorate of Primary Education, Bangladesh Post Office and Public Health Engineering and similar staffs working in Bangladesh Secretariat and in the High Court Division had been discharging the same functions and accordingly had been enjoying the same status and privileges. But the Government by notification dated 13-9-1995 changed the designation of Upper Division Assistant of Bangladesh Secretariat to Administrative Officer. Then the Government by another notification dated 28-4-1997 upgraded the post of Administrative Officer as Class II Gazetted post and their pay scale was enhanced to Taka 1725-3725. In the notification it was stated that the scope of work and responsibility of the holders of the post would remain same as was before. Lastly, by notification dated 01-6-1999 the pay scale of Class-II Gazetted Officers was further enhanced to Taka 3400-6625 while the status and privileges of the petitioners and other Head Assistants and Upper Division Assistants of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, Directorate of Primary Education, Bangladesh Post Office and Public Health Engineering remained unchanged, although they have also been serving under the same government. In the present premises the petitioners served notices demanding justice upon the respondents through their engaged advocates to upgrade their gazetted status and pay scale as have been given to the Upper Division Assistants of Bangladesh Secretariat but the respondents did not take any action in response thereto.

13. Having no other equally efficacious alternative remedy for their redress, the petitioners filed their respective writ petitions for invoking our jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the Rules Nisi as aforesaid.

14. The respondent-government contested the rules by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying the claim of the petitioners stating, inter-alia, that the writ petitions are not maintainable inasmuch as the petitioners being government servants, the only forum available to them is the Administrative Tribunal constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution; people working in different organizations of the Republic may have the same designation but their promotion, salary, scale of pay etc. may not necessarily have to be the same and those are guided by their recruitment rules and the service condition of the employees working in the Secretariat are not applicable to the petitioners and that the post of personal officer is the feeder post of Assistant Secretary which is applicable only to employees working in the Secretariat and thus the same benefits cannot be extended to the petitioners.

15. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners in all the writ petitions submits that though the respondents granted higher scale of pay, other facilities and Gazetted status to the employees of equivalent ranks posted in Bangladesh Secretariat, but they are not granting the same to the petitioners which is discriminatory, arbitrary and infringement of the petitioners' fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution. He further submits that several writ petitions including Writ Petition No. 7478 of 2003 and Writ Petition No. 2256 of 2002 involving identical questions of facts and law have already been settled by making the rules absolute and the judgment and order passed in Writ Petition No. 2256 of 2002 has been affirmed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 218 of 2004, reported in 59 DLR (AD) 54 and the principle enunciated therein being also applicable to the present Writ Petitions, the rules may be made absolute with the same direction.

16. To refute the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners, Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney-General seriously raised the question of maintainability of the writ petitions. He contended that all the petitioners are admittedly public servants. The issue raised essentially is one of terms and conditions of service therefore their writ petitions are plainly barred under Article 117 of the Constitution. He further submits that the petitioners as government servants serving in different departments, under different ministries of the Government and their recruitment rules and service conditions are also different. Settled principle is that, he stressed, there is no flat application of the equality clause to every class of servants serving under a Government. Equality Rule is only applicable among the equals. This does not mean that the petitioners are remediless. They can well seek their remedy, if, available, before the Administrative Tribunal.

17. Mr Motahar Hossain, learned Deputy Attorney-General at the time of hearing of the rules also made submissions reiterating the same contention as have been made by learned Attorney-General. He, in addition, cited series of decisions of our apex Court, namely, Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111; Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19; Government vs Azizur Rahman reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27; Bangladesh vs Mohammad Faruque reported in 51 DLR (AD) 112; Delwar Hossain Mia vs Bangladesh reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120; Government of Bangladesh vs Md Abdul Halim Mia reported in 9 MLR (AD) 105 = 9 BLC (AD) 134; Molla Md Anwarul Huq vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 8 ADC (2011) 782; Khalilur Rahman vs Md Kamrul Hasan reported in 11 MLR (AD) 5 = 10 BLC (AD) /93 and Bangladesh vs Mosharraf Hossain reported in 32 BLD (AD) 67.

18. We have considered the submissions of the learned Counsels for on the contending parties, perused the writ petitions, affidavits-in-opposition and the Annexures appended thereto.

19. In these cases the petitioners have come up before this Division for invoking our jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution for enforcement of their fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 29, 31 of the Constitution which, in their words, have been infringed and violated in the way that respondents did not grant higher scale of pay, other facilities and Gazetted status to their which have already been granted to the employees of equivalent posts in the Bangladesh Secretariat and thus they have been discriminated. On the contrary, the government forcefully raised the question of maintainability of the writ petitions on the ground that the petitioners having been serving in the service of the Republic, their redress, if any, lies before the Administrative Tribunal. Since the fitness of things requires deciding maintainability first let us examine how far the writ petitions stand maintainability-test.

20. Article 117 of the Constitution clearly stipulates that notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, the Administrative Tribunal will exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic pursuant to which the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 was enacted and the Administrative Tribunals were set up to adjudicate the disputes of persons in the Service of the Republic. Article 117(2) of the Constitution states categorically that 'where any administrative tribunal is established under this article, no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal'.

21. In the case of Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111, the constitutionality of section 3(3) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 together with the judgment of the Administrative Tribunal was challenged. In that case redress of the persons in the service of the Republic in respect of their infringement of fundamental rights has been settled by delivering a comprehensive judgment which is the leading judgment in the field. In para 48 of this reported case, the apex Court, in outlining the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal as well as High Court Division, observed that "within its jurisdiction the tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice and for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising out of sub-clause (a), but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1937 SC 386 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India AIR 1987 SC 357 ( para 2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke the fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)".

22. The above principle settled in Mujibur Rahman's case adopted by our apex Court in many subsequent judgments and the said ratio is still governing the field.

23. In the case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27, the vires of some rules, regulations and various notifications were challenged as unconstitutional. Concurring with the principles settled in Mujibur Rahman's case Appellate Division held the writ petition to be maintainable. In para 80 of this judgment the Appellate Division held:

"In making his submission that while deciding the case of Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR AD 111, this Division did not take into consideration Article 44 of the Constitution. Mr Amirul Islam did not notice that Article 44(1) of the Constitution was in all fairness brought to the notice of this Court by the government-respondents themselves in that case (vide paragraph 47 of the Report) and the jurisdiction of an Administrative Tribunal to strike down an order for infringement of fundamental rights or any other law (but not the jurisdiction to strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality) was conceded (vide paragraph 48 of the report). The right to move the High Court Division under Article 102(1) for enforcement of the fundamental rights is a fundamental right itself and is guaranteed by Article 44(1) and that has been recognized by the separate concurring judgment in paragraph 77 of the report. But the right of judicial review under Article 102(2) is neither a fundamental right nor a guaranteed one. This power was never conferred upon the tribunals under Article 117 of the Constitution (Paragraph 77of the Report)."

24. Appellate Division in paragraph 81 of Shafiuddin Ahmed's case held that 'the supplemental, as opposed to substitutional, role of the tribunals constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution was already conceded and permitted to the tribunals in Mujibur Rahman case and no power of judicial review under Article 102(2) was conceded to the tribunals in that case. The writ petitioners' relief could not have been obtained by a supplemental role performed by the tribunals. They have rightly invoked the jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102(1) of the Constitution. The writ petitions were fully maintainable'.

25. Question of maintainability of the writ petition was again raised in the case of Delwar Hossain vs Bangladesh reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120. The writ petitioners of the case, who were appointed in the BCS (Police) cadre, challenged notification dated 3-2-1998 by which government regularized the respondent No. 4-63 of the writ petition in the post of ASP with retrospective effect from 20-3-1991. They alleged that the impugned order was contrary to the provisions of the BCS (Police) Composition and Cadre Rules 1980, the BCS Seniority Rules, 1981 and the principle laid down in Md Abdul Mannan vs Hasan Mahmud Khandaker, reported in 16 BLD (AD) 147 = 1 BLC (AD) 44. They also alleged that the impugned order was violative of the fundamental right guaranteed to the writ petitioners under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution. High Court Division discharged the rule holding that the writ petition was not maintainable as barred under Article 117(2) of the Constitution. Concurring with the ratio decidendi of Mujibur Rahman's case the Appellate Division affirmed the judgment of High Court Division and held as follows:

"Inviting our attention to Article 44 (1) of the Constitution that guarantees the right to move the High Court Division in accordance with clause (1) of Article 102 for the enforcement of the fundamental rights Mr. Abdur Rab Chaudhury, learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that the High Court Division was wrong in its 'view that the writ petition was not maintainable.

The question is no longer res Integra. It has been answered by this Court in Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 111 in the following terms: 'within its jurisdiction the tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising of sub-clause (a), but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1987 (SC) 385 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India, AIR 1987 (SC) 357 (para 2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102 (1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)'. We find no reason to revise our earlier view. The gravamen of the writ petitioners' grievance is that by the impugned order of promotion their seniority has been affected. Seniority and promotion of civil servants being terms and conditions of service the Administrative Tribunal is possessed of the exclusive jurisdiction to hear the dispute in such matters. The case is thus fully covered by our decision in the cited case. No substantial question of law has been made out for grant of leave."

26. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Abdul Halim Miah reported in 9 MLR (AD) 105 = 9 BLC (AD) 134 the writ petitioners, civil servants, without challenging vires of law, had challenged certain decisions taken at the meeting of the Standing Committee and the placement in the gradation list and publication in the official gazette have been challenged by way of an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. The impugned decisions alleged to have infringed the petitioners' fundamental right guaranteed under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. High Court Division made the rules absolute, being found maintainable. Appellate Division expressing the same view arrived at Mujibur Rahman's case allowed the appeal by setting aside the judgment of the High Court Division. In paragraph 34 of that judgment our apex Court held:

"The right of judicial review under Article 102(2) of the Constitution is neither a fundamental right nor a guaranteed right. Similarly, the judicial review of an administrative action is neither an all weather remedy nor a remedy for all wrongs but is only available only when there is no other equally efficacious remedy. The writ petitioners have challenged the impugned decisions alleged to have been infringed their fundamental right guaranteed under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, but in view of the provisions of Article 117(2) of the Constitution the Parliament has set up the Administrative Tribunal by enacting Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 for exercise of the functions enumerated in Article 117(1) i.e. by setting up of the Administrative Tribunal to exercise the jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the republic etc. Article 117(2) provides that no Court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal. Section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act 1980 specifically provides how the jurisdiction under Article 117(1) is conferred upon any other Court. In the case of 44 DLR (AD) 111 it has further been cautioned that an aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, alleged contravention of some fundamental right which may ultimately turn out to be frivolous or vexatious or not even wrongly attracted in the case and asked to be a ground so that great value of the right given under Article 102 (1) is not frittered away or misused on the pretext of alternative remedy.....".

27. In the case of Khalilur Rahman vs Md Kamrul Hasan reported in 18 BLT (AD) 486 = 11 MLR (AD) 5 relying on the ratio decidendi of Mujibur Rahman's case, Appellate Division also held:

"As has already been mentioned that in the case of Mujibur Rahman it has clearly been stated in the background of what circumstance in spite of the bar of Article 117(2) of the Constitution a writ petition can be filed under Article 102 of the Constitution and can be entertained by the High Court Division even the contention raised and adjudicated sought relates to term and condition of the service of a person in the service of the Republic. Therein it has been held that except on the limited ground i.e when the vires of the law is challenged or a relief by way of striking down of a particular law on the grounds of its Constitutionality sought, writ petition by the High Court Division can be entertained or in other words a person in the service of the Republic can file a writ petition on limited grounds as regard the matters, even though the same relates to the condition of service. So law is now settled that except on the limited scope a writ petition involving question of determination of the question of the matters relating to term and condition of service of a person in the service of the Republic is not entertainable by the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution'.

28. In the case of Molla Md Anwarul Huq vs Government of Bangladesh, VIII ADC (2011) 782, the High Court Division held the writ petition to be maintainable as it found that the guidelines under challenge, having been published in Official Gazette, had the force of law and Appellate Division upheld the judgment of the High Court Division.

29. In a recent case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Mosharraf Hossain reported in 32 BLD (AD) 67 the writ petitioner, who was a Bench Reader of the Appellate Division, had challenged the vires of the 'বাংলাদেশ সুপ্রীম কোর্ট (আপীল বিভাগ) এর কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীদের নিয়োগ বিধিমালা, ২০০০' as being unconstitutional as discriminatory and sought for a direction upon the government to grant him the status of First Class Gazetted Officer with a pay scale of Taka 9000-405 x 16-15480 under the National Pay Scale, 2005. The Appellate Division after accepting the principles laid down in Mujibur Rahman's case, Shafiuddin's case and Shamsul Haque's case found the writ petition maintainable as the vires of constitutionality of 'বিধিমালা ২০০০' was challenged.

30. In the case of Bangladesh vs Azizur Rahman reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19 the writ petition, which was filed by Assistant Engineers of Bangladesh Engineering Services in different cadres, held maintainable by the apex Court as the vires of constitutionality of 'The Bangladesh Ad-hoc Appointees (Counting and Determination of Seniority) Rules 1990' was challenged together with the petitioners' grievance as to their, seniority. In the said case, as the vires of law was challenged, the apex Court in answering the question of maintainability held that it is found from the facts of the writ petitions that the question of fundamental right invoked therein has been so mixed up with the facts and statutory rules that the question of fundamental right cannot be extricated for exclusive consideration in a petition for enforcement of fundamental right. Therefore, the High Court Division rightly held the writ petitions to be maintainable under Article 102 (2)'.

31. It appears that our apex Court consistently expressed its disapproval in invoking writ jurisdiction in respect of terms and conditions of people in the service of the Republic unless vires of law on the ground of its constitutionality is challenged. The apex Court by reference to Article 117 of the Constitution made it simply clear that where Administrative Tribunal is established under this article no Court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic in that the Administrative Tribunal is conferred with jurisdiction to look into the matter. The Appellate Division has gone as far as to say that even if within its jurisdiction the tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice and for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising out of sub-clause (a) of Article 117 (1) of the Constitution.

32. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Shamsul Huq reported in 59 DLR (AD) 54, relied upon by the learned Advocate for the petitioners, the writ petition, which was filed by the Personal Officer of the Supreme Court, challenging vires of two notifications on the ground of their constitutionality, was held to be maintainable on the ground that the impugned notifications had the force of law saying that 'the principle as laid down in 50 DLR (AD) 27, in the facts and circumstances, are applicable in the present appeal as the writ petitioners challenged the order as contained in Annexures D(1) and D(2), which were issued under section 5 of the Services (Re-Organisation and Conditions) Act, 1975 and have the effect of law. Accordingly, the writ petition is maintainable'.

33. It appears that the instant writ petitioners did not challenge vires of any law on the ground of its constitutionality, as such the ratio of the decision reported in 59 DLR (AD) 54 is not applicable in these cases.

34. In Writ Petition No. 7478 of 2003 (judgment of which is relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioners) the writ petitioner, an Upper Division Assistant of High Court Division sought for direction to grant Gazetted status as had been granted to Upper Division Assistants in the Secretariat on the ground of discrimination. In that writ petition though question of maintainability was raised but the learned Assistant Attorney-General could not produce any authority of our apex Court on the point of maintainability. The High Court Division also without any reference to the decisions of our apex Court, as discussed above, held that "we have heard the learned Advocate of both the sides and perused the petition. On the question of forum, it is very true that the petitioner is in the service of the Republic of Bangladesh. He is posted in the office of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. As such, any grievance with regard to the terms and conditions of his service, the Administrative Tribunal is the proper forum. But in this case, his fundamental right to be treated equally with other similarly placed employees of the Republic and his entitlement to equal protection of law under Article 27 of the Constitution is involved. The learned Assistant Attorney-General could not explain as to why the petitioner and other Upper Division Assistants posted in the office of the High Court Division were treated differently from their counter-parts posted in the Secretariat on and from 1-7-1977 by the above notification dated 10-8-1981. This is a glaring instance of discrimination to the prejudice of the petitioner and similarly placed other employees in the country including those in the office of the High Court Division. This is also a violation of fundamental right of the petitioner and similarly placed others, guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution". This judgment seems to us as a judgment per incuriam and thus not binding upon us in view of the ratio settled by the apex Court in Mujibur Rahman's case and subsequent cases.

<u>35. In these cases the writ petitioners did not challenge the vires of any law on the ground of its constitutionality but only canvassed before us one issue that they have been subjected to discrimination in that the respondents did not grant them higher scale of pay, other facilities and gazetted status as have been granted to their counter-parts posted in the Secretariat vide Circulars dated 13-9-1995, 28-4-1997 and 1-6-1999 and thus their fundamental rights have been infringed. The grievance of the petitioners clearly relates to their terms and conditions of service and accordingly their redress, if any, is well within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal established under Article 117(1) of the Constitution. In view of the principles laid down in the judgment of Mujibur Rahman's case, subsequent judgments and the judgment relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioners reported in 59 DLR (AD) 54, as discussed above, the petitioners should have agitated their grievance before the Administrative Tribunal for their redress but they instead, have come before this division for invoking our power of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution and, as such, we are led to hold that the writ petitions are not maintainable. For what we have stated above we are not inclined to go into the merit of their cases. Resultantly, these rules are liable to be discharged as not being maintainable.</u>

<u>In the result, the rules are discharged, however, without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

Salina Akter Chowdhury, Advocate ------ For the petitioner. 
Md Zakir Hossain, Advocate ------ For respondent No. 5.
parties:
Probir Kumar Paul ------ Petitioner

full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: By filing an application under Article 102 of the Constitution, the writ petitioner Mr. Probir Kumar Paul, who is a Government servant under the Ministry of Health, sought to question the legality and propriety of the Memo No. স্বাঃ অধিঃ/প্রশা-৩/হিসাব রক্ষক বদলী/৫১০/০৯ dated 29-6-2014 issued under the signature of the Director (Administration) of the Directorate of Health, Mohakhali, Dhaka (respondent No. 3) on behalf of the Director General, Directorate of Health, Mohakhali, Dhaka (respondent No. 2) transferring the petitioner from Civil Surgeon Office, Cox's Bazar to Upazilla Health and Family Welfare Office of Cox's Bazar, Sadar Upazilla (annexure-F).

2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that the petitioner while serving in the Republic as an Accountant under the Ministry of Health was transferred to Civil Surgeon's Office of Cox's Bazar on 15-6-2014 by an office order under Memo No. স্মাঃঅধিঃ/প্রশা-৩/হিসাব রক্ষক বদলী/৫১০/০৯ and, then, joined there on 23.06.2014 and, thereafter, the Civil Surgeon's Office of Cox's Bazar (respondent No. 4) on 24-6-2014 forwarded the petitioner's joining letter to respondent No. 2. On 19-6-2014 when one Md Ishaq Numan filed the Writ Petition No. 6088 of 2014 challenging the petitioner's transfer order, a Division Bench of the High Court Division stayed the said order for a period of 3 (three) months. On 29-6-2014 Respondent No. 3 transferred the petitioner by issuing office order vide Memo No.  স্মাঃঅধিঃ/প্রশা-৩/হিসাব রক্ষক বদলী/৫১০/০৯ dated 29-6-2014 from Civil Surgeon's Office, Cox's Bazar to Upazilla Health and Family Welfare Office of Cox's Bazar Sadar Upazilla. Being aggrieved with the aforesaid transfer order, the petitioner approached this Court and obtained this Rule.

3. No factual statement made in the writ petition was controverted by the respondents by way of filing any affidavit. Respondent No. 5 Md Osman Gani entered his appearance by adding himself as a party in this case. However, he also did not file any affidavit-in-opposition.

4. Mrs Salina Akter Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, refers to annexures A and B and submits that it is evident from these papers that within a very short span of time the respondents transferred the petitioner twice simply to harass him and, thus, she terms the action of the respondents in transferring the petitioner to be arbitrary and malafide. She next refers to the Notification dated 11-6-1982 issued by the Ministry of Establishment under the Memo No. ইভি/এসএ ১-১/৮২-২/২৩৪(১০০)(বদলীযোগ্য পদে ৩ বৎসরের অধিককাল কর্মরত বেসামরিক কর্মকর্তাদের বদলী সংক্রান্ত বিজ্ঞপ্তি) and submits that as per the above law of the land, the petitioner is entitled to remain in the present position for at least three years and, thereafter, the respondent will be in a position to transfer the petitioner, but in the case of the petitioner the provisions of the above law were not followed. By referring to the subsequent transfer order, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the petitioner was demoted by the said letter, as the petitioner is currently holding the post of Accountant and by the subsequent transfer letter the petitioner was asked to perform the duty of the Coordinator (সমন্বয়কারী) in the accounts department.

5. With regard to invoking of Article 102 of the Constitution, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the Administrative Tribunal is not a proper forum as the said Tribunal is not empowered to pass any kind of interim order staying operation of the impugned order and, therefore, the said forum is not an equally efficacious forum. In support of her submission on this point, she refers to the case of Qumrul Hasan vs Bangladesh 49 DLR (AD) 44 and in particular she relies upon the observation made in paragraph 5 of the said case.

6. By making the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioner prays for making the Rule absolute.

7. Per contra, Mr Md Khurshedul Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney General, submits that the Government is at liberty to transfer its employees and officers at any time and the latter are duty bound to comply with the Government's order without raising any question. He argues that the presumption of the orders, actions and decisions of the Government functionaries is that the same are taken in public interest and, thus, bonafide. He professes that in order to rebut the aforesaid presumption an aggrieved person must make out a clear case of malafide with reference to categorical allegation against specific person/s. By reading out the statements made in the writ petition, he submits that nowhere within the four-corners of the petition, any specific allegation of personal grudge or revenge has been made against any of the respondents.

8. He then vehemently opposes the submission of the learned Advocate of the petitioner on the issue of the maintainability of this writ petition and submits that the Constitution in unambiguous terms and expression has prohibited that no Court shall deal with the Government servants service matter. By placing the facts of the case of Qumrul Hasan vs Bangladesh 49 DLR (AD) 44, he submits that the facts of the said case are completely different from those of the present case and the ratio emanated from the said case is applicable only in those cases which are factually similar. By referring to the cases of AKM Enayetullah vs Bangladesh 18 BLC 679 and SM Shah Jamal vs Bangladesh 19 BLC 768, the learned DAG submits that the law is by now well-settled that Administrative Tribunal is the proper forum for the Government servants to seek remedy against any action, decision or order of the Government. In concluding his submissions, the learned DAG humbly opines that the Rule is not only liable to be discharged, but also the petitioner deserves to be penalised by imposing exemplary costs upon him.

9. Mr Md Zakir Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No. 5, narrates to this Court the practical difficulties that are being faced by his client and submits that due to passing of two interim orders in two writ petitions, including the present one, respondent No. 5 has not been able to join his workplace as an Accountant. He next submits that respondent No. 5 is happy and ready to join anywhere he is transferred but due to operation of the interim order, at present, he is not being able to perform his functions. To deal with the issue of maintainability, he forcefully submits that the transfer is a common and usual official order of the Government and, therefore, a Government servant cannot be aggrieved by a transfer order. He posits that 'transfer' clearly comes within the purview of the terms and conditions of the service and, as per the provision of Article 117 of the Constitution, the petitioner is required to approach the Administrative Tribunal and seek remedy therein.

10. By making the above submissions, the learned Advocate for respondent No. 5 prays for discharging the Rule.

11. The apparent only issue to be adjudicated upon by this Court as to whether the office order, by which the petitioner has been transferred for the second time within a span of only one month, was passed by the concerned State-functionary in accordance with the law. Prior to adjudicating upon the aforesaid issue we need to see whether the Administrative Tribunal is empowered to examine the legality of the said transfer order and, further, if it is capable of passing interim order in course of trial of the cases pending before it. That is why, the issue of maintainability, as has been raised in the present writ petition by the respondents on the ground of availability of efficacious forum, is required to be dealt with at first, before embarking upon the factual aspect of this case.

12. In order to properly address the maintainability issue, it would be profitable to look at the provision of Article 117 of the Constitution which runs as follows:

117.(1) Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of-

(a) the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic, including the matters provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishments;

(b).............

(c).............

(2) Where any administrative tribunal is established under this article, no court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal;

Provided that Parliament may by law provide for appeals from, or the review of decisions of any such tribunal.

13. From a plain reading of the above Constitutional provision, it is apparent that while Article 117(1) contains an ousting Clause which starts with "notwithstanding anything contained hereinbefore" declaring that whatever the provisions are engraved in the Constitution, including power of judicial review, the Parliament is empowered to establish Administrative Tribunals for adjudication of the Government servants' grievances linked and associated with their service. Thereafter Article 117(2) heralds that all the Government servants are required to file applications before the Administrative Tribunal if they want to seek remedy against any order, action or decision with regard to the terms and conditions of their service. The Constitution framers by employing the above words "notwithstanding anything contained hereinbefore" have emphasized the provision that the dispute relating to or arising out of the Government servants' service-related matters shall not be dealt with by any Court other than the Administrative Tribunal. Furthermore, by engraving the words "relating to and arising out of" in our Constitution, the Constitution framers have sought to mean that all types of service-related issues of the Government servants, during their service-time and even after the retirement, shall be handled by the Administrative Tribunal. The said emphasis has further been augmented by incorporating the provision under Article 102(5) of the Constitution which is reproduced below:

102(5) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires, "person" includes a statutory public authority and any court or tribunal, other than a court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force or a tribunal to which article 117 applies.

14. It appears from a plain reading of this provision of the Constitution that the two tribunals, namely Military Tribunal, (Tribunal which conducts trials for the person who are in defence services) and Administrative Tribunal, (the Tribunal for the Government servants constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution) have been excluded from the ambit of "person".

15. Thus, from a concurrent reading of Articles 102(5) and 117 of the Constitution, the intent of the Constitution framers with regard to the forum for trial of the service-related matters of the Government servants may clearly be found. In other words, while Article 117 categorically imposes prohibition upon the Courts other than Administrative Tribunal to entertain any case about the Government Servants' service-related matters, Article 102(5) states that no order or judgment passed by the Military Tribunal or Administrative Tribunal shall be amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. However, as per the decision propounded in the case of Shaheda Khatun vs Administrative Appellate Tribunal 3 BLC (AD) 155, after submitting a Government servant her/himself into the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal, s/he is competent to raise the question as to whether the Administrative Tribunal was constituted properly (coram-non-judice) in adjudication upon the case, or whether the Administrative Tribunal had exceeded its jurisdiction in conducting the trial (without jurisdiction) or whether the learned Judge/Member of the Administrative Tribunal performed his duty being biased (malafide), can be looked into by the High Court Division by exercising its power under Article 102 of the Constitution, if an aggrieved party opts to avail himself/herself of the writ jurisdiction instead of preferring an appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The rationale behind this is that although the Administrative Appellate Tribunal is also capable of turning down an order or judgment of the Administrative Tribunal on any of the above three grounds, because of the nature of appointment of the Learned Chairman and Members of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, they may not be as bold as a High Court Judge is in declaring any order against the office of the President, Prime Minister and other Ministers and, that is why, they may not always be in a position to deliver the expected impartial judgments and order. The above ratio of Shaheda Khatun's case has originated from the ratios of the cases of Khandoker Mostaq Ahmed vs Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 223, Jamil Huq vs Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 125, Kh. Ehtashamuddin Ahmed vs Bangladesh 33 DLR (AD) 154, Abdur Rouf vs Abdul Hamid Khan 17 DLR (SC) 515, Nur Mohammad vs M Ahmed 39 DLR (AD) 1, Miah Mohammad Latif vs Province of West Pakistan PLD 1970 (SC) 180 = 22 DLR (SC) 98, Federation of Pakistan vs Syeed Ahmed PLD 1974 (SC) 151, Ali Jan vs Bangladesh 37 DLR (AD) 161, Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh 33 DLR (AD) 201 and many other unreported cases. Those ratios have been propounded by our Apex Court in course of dealing with the judgments and orders predominately passed by the Military Tribunals and Land Tribunals, in other words, the Tribunals other than Administrative Tribunals. Thus, the aforesaid ratios are actually applicable for challenging the judgment and order of the Military Tribunal and other Tribunals in the writ jurisdiction, as the judgment or order passed by those Tribunals being not appealable, the aggrieved person remains without any remedy, even the aggrieved person finds that the Military Tribunal was not formed as per the provision of the relevant law of the land (coram-non-judice) or the Military Tribunal did not have the jurisdiction to try the case (without jurisdiction) or the judges of the Military Tribunal were vindictive towards the accused or otherwise influenced (malafide).

16. In our humble analysis of the ratio laid down in the cited case of Shaheda Khatun vs Administrative Appellate Tribunal 3 BLC (AD) 155, we see that our Apex Court has vested a concurrent jurisdiction in the High Court Division empowering it to review the order and judgment passed by the Administrative Tribunals on the above three grounds. That is how the Government servant's position is well protected and guarded in comparison with the position of the persons in the defence service inasmuch as there is no Appellate Tribunal for them and, for this reason, our Apex Court has made the law for them that if the judgment of the Military Tribunal can be attacked on any of the above three grounds, the High Court Division may entertain a writ petition ignoring the provision of Articles 45 and 102(5) of our Constitution. In other words, since the Administrative Appellate Tribunal is well competent to look into the matters of 'coram-non-judice', 'without jurisdiction' and 'malafide' in course of hearing the appeal against the order or judgment of the Administrative Tribunal, evidently the Government servants' position is invincible in contrast to the vulnerable position of the persons serving in the defence services for whom there is no Appellate Tribunal. More so, in the Administrative Tribunal, if an applicant takes the above three issues as the ground for attacking an impugned order, the Administrative Tribunal is well competent to deal with the two issues among the said three issues, namely 'without jurisdiction' and 'malafide' inasmuch as the Administrative Tribunal, as a trial forum, is in a better position to take oral evidence of the petitioner and the person/s against whom the allegation of malafies is brought and, similarly the issue of 'without jurisdiction' also may be taken up for consideration by the Administrative Tribunal or other Court/Tribunal or quasi-judicial body, if the concerned State-functionaries exceed their power or usurp the functions of other bodies or functionaries. However, if the other issue, namely 'coram-non-judice', is placed before the Administrative Tribunal or any other Tribunal/ Court of first instance taking it as a ground for attacking the impugned order, it should be seen by the Tribunal/Court of first instance to be misconceived, for, the question of 'coram-non-judice' arises only where an adjudicating forum is required to be formed or constituted as per the provisions of relevant law, but the trial commenced or took place without constituting the said Court/Tribunal properly.

17. It follows that after filing a case in the Administrative tribunal, while the issue of 'coram-non-judice' is something that can be presented before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal or the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction for their examination, the issue of 'malafide' or 'without jurisdiction' can be more conveniently and comprehensively examined by the Administrative Tribunal itself as a forum of first instance, on top of examining the other legal and factual issues involved in a particular case.

18. In a catena of cases, the Apex Court of this land has been maintaining the position for decades holding that the proper forum for dealing with the issues/subjects connected with the Government servants' service-matter is Administrative Tribunal, for, the same is the mandate of the Constitution. Particularly, entertainment of the writ petitions by the High Court Divisions regarding the transfer issues have been seriously deprecated by the Apex Court in a number of cases. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs SM Farid Uddin 54 DLR (AD) 95 wherein two writ petitions were filed challenging the transfer orders, the Apex Court lambasted the High Court Division having expressed their views in the following terms:

"The order passed by the High Court Division in both the writ petitions are on the very face illegal and we cannot think how a Division Bench could pass such an order." (Para 5)

19. From the impugned letter as well as from the Annexure-B to this writ petition, it is evident that the petitioner was transferred twice in a short span of time i.e. within one month. Since the Government Servants are required to be placed or deputed as and when the concerned Ministry or Department or Division or Directorate or Corporation or Institution needs an employee or officer in a particular post and area and, as per law, the Government servants are obliged to abide by the said transfer order. Thus, there is hardly any scope for the Government servants to challenge any transfer order taking recourse to the Notification dated 11-6-1982 issued by the Ministry of Establishment under the Memo No. ইভি/এসএ ১-১/৮২-২/২৩৪(১০০)(বদলীযোগ্য পদে ৩ বৎসরের অধিককাল কর্মরত বেসামরিক কর্মকর্তাদের বদলী সংক্রান্ত বিজ্ঞপ্তি), which is merely a guideline for the convenience of the concerned State-functionaries responsible for transferring the Government Servants. However, there may be cases where an employee or officer may be victim of personal grudge of higher authority and consequently they may be transferred from one place to another place as a means of punishment. In the above background, if it is found that the order was passed malafide, as per the latest decision of this Court propounded in the cases of AKM Enayetullah vs Bangladesh 18 BLC 679 and SM Shah Jamal vs Bangladesh 19 BLC 768, the Administrative Tribunal, being the forum of first instance, will be in a better position to deal with the allegations of malafide inasmuch as it is likely that taking evidence, both oral and documentary, from the aggrieved-applicant and the opposite party, may be required to effectively adjudicate upon the allegation of malafides.

20. In the case at hand, thus, the Administrative Tribunal can comprehensively examine the allegation of malafides for transferring the petitioner twice within a month in tandem with adjudicating upon the legal issue as to whether the petitioner is entitled to work for three years in the work-station where he was transferred initially.

21. The adjudication of the above issue, that the Administrative Tribunal is well competent and more than efficacious forum to examine the legality of the transfer order, leads us to undertake the examination of the next issue of whether the Administrative Tribunal is empowered to pass an interim order pending trial of the petitioner's case.

22. Here in this case, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has argued that since the Administrative Tribunal is not competent to issue an interim order staying operation of the impugned transfer order, approaching the Administrative Tribunal would have been a futile attempt by the petitioner and in an endeavour to substantiate her arguments, she has relied upon the case of Qumrul Hasan vs Bangladesh 49 DLR (AD) 44, particularly, the paragraph 5 thereto. Apparently from a reading of only the cited paragraph it may seem that there has been a deviation by our Apex Court from the settled principle laid down in the series of cases for last decades. However, from a minute reading of the entire case, it appears to us that in the cited-case the petitioner having submitted himself to the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal challenged the order of his transfer from the Bangladesh Embassy at Stockholm to the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry and, then, prayed for an order of stay of the said transfer order. The Administrative Tribunal rejected the prayer for stay which was upheld by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and, lastly, by the Apex Court. Thus, it appears that in the said case the petitioner at first submitted himself to the jurisdiction of Administrative Tribunal and, thereafter, made an application for staying the impugned order of transfer. So, the ratio laid down in the said case is not applicable in the case at hand in the light of the fact that in this case the petitioner has directly jumped to the jurisdiction of this Court without first surrendering himself to the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal.

23. From a minute reading of the case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 44, it appears that the Apex Court has discussed the provision of Article 117(1) of the Constitution at Paragraph 4 of the said cited-case and did not record any observation with regard to the import of Article 117(2) or make suggestion for the Government servants as to their appropriate course of action with regard to obtaining an interim order. However, in our view, if a wording engraved in Article 117(2) is read, together with the provisions of Article 102(5) of the Constitution, it becomes crystal clear that for the Government servants approaching other Court regarding service-related matters is completely prohibited. When Article 117(2) of our Constitution in unambiguous wordings says that "no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal", section 7(1) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 or the Rules made thereunder cannot restrict the functions of the Administrative Tribunals.

24. The rationale behind taking the above view is that while on the one hand 'transfer', being a term and condition for the Government servant, clearly appears to be a 'matter falling within the jurisdiction' of the Administrative Tribunal, on the other, if a Government servant after approaching the Tribunal does not get a remedy to stop the abuse of power of his higher authority, the said harassed-Government servant, who is Constitutionally prohibited to take shelter to other Courts, remains without any protection and, thus, vulnerable, which cannot be said to have been intended by the Constitution framers nor had the Legislature, in incorporating section 7(1) in the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980, contemplated that the Government servants would be barred from praying for an interim order from the Administrative Tribunal.

25. However, it is our view that Section 7(1) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 is silent about the Administrative Tribunal's Power to grant any interim relief e.g. injunction, direction, stay etc, but in no way can it be said that the said Section prohibits entertaining an interim prayer.

26. While most of the quasi-judicial bodies, such as Review Panel under the delegated Legislation named Public Procurement Rules, 2008, Review Committee under the Customs Act, 1969 etc, have been vested with the power to pass necessary interim order, non-incorporation of the power of passing interim order in the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980, which is set up under the mandate of article 117 of the Constitution, thus, may be seen to be an omission on the part of the Legislature.

27. Moreover, in laying down the ratio that 'the Administrative Tribunal has no power to grant interim relief' in the cited case of Kamrul Hasan vs Bangladesh 49 DLR (AD) 44, the Apex Court referred to the decisions of the landmark case of Mujibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 111 and Kazi Nazrul Islam vs Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation 45 DLR (AD) 106, but nowhere in the Mujibur Rahman's case, the Administrative Tribunal's competency to pass an interim order was discussed. In Kazi Nazrul Islam's case as well, the issue of passing an interim order was not examined, as the case involves adjudication of the issue as to whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal had the power to send the case back on remand to the Administrative Tribunal. It is our humble understanding that on making the reference to those two cases in the Kamrul Hasan's case that in both the cases a remarkable observation was made saying that the Administrative Tribunal is not a Court proper, for, the appointment of its judges and staffs are controlled by the Government and, further, the provisions of CPC have limited application.

28. However, the milestone decision of Mujibur Rahman's case, which was referred to in Kamrul Hasan's case, the Apex Court has laid down the principle that the Administrative Tribunal is the sole forum to try the Government servants' service-connected matter. The other noticeable ratio laid down in the Mujibur Rahman's case is that in adjudication upon the cases, the Administrative Tribunal is not only competent to examine the violation of any law, but it can also look into the allegation of infringement of the fundamental rights. Therefore, it is our view that when a Tribunal is empowered to examine the infringement of fundamental rights in addition to possessing the power of examining the violation of any law, Rules, Regulations, Orders, Circulars, Guidelines etc, it would sound unusual and inconsistent that the said Administrative Tribunal lacks the power to pass an interim order, particularly when there is no bar for the Administrative Tribunal to do so.

29. In view of the unambiguous provision of Article 117(2) of the Constitution that "no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal" and there being no prohibitory provision in the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 and, further, while most of the Tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies created by simple Statute or Rules have been equipped with the power of passing the interim orders, non-Conferment of the same power in the Administrative Tribunal, which has been created pursuant to the Supreme Law, being appeared to us to be a mere omission on the part of the Legislature resulting in the frustration of the Constitutional scheme, we hold that the Administrative Tribunals are competent to pass an interim order if the same is required for a fair and effective disposal of a case. The Administrative Tribunal, however, must be mindful that they should pass an interim order only in a fit and proper case.

30. It follows that the instant Rule is destined to be discharged on the ground of maintainability of writ petition and, thus, there is no necessity to embark upon the examination of the facts of the case.

<u>31. Before parting with the judgment, we like to record that in course of hearing of service-related matters of the Government servants, on the query from the Court, on many occasions it was informed by the Law Officers employed in different Writ Bench’s that the Government is in the process of amendment of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 in order to insert a provision empowering the Administrative Tribunal to pass necessary interim order in section 7(1) of the said Act, but till date the same has not been done. Enactment of any law being an exclusive function of the Parliament, this Court does not fancy passing any direction upon the Legislature to amend the law. However, the Supreme Court being the competent authority to interpret the Constitution and other laws, whenever there surfaces any vacuum or loopholes in any law, it becomes the duty of the Supreme Court to convey the matter to the Government by making appropriate observation. Accordingly, we feel it pertinent to observe that because of non-incorporation of a provision in section 7(1) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 enabling the Administrative Tribunal in a clearer expression [for example, section 7(G) - issuing any interim order of direction, injunction, stay and statusquo and any other interim order, only in an appropriate and fit case, as may be necessary for ends of justice and for effective and speedy disposal of the cases and subsequently vacating the said interim order/s.], the High Court Division is receiving thousands of transfer-related cases every year. In the backdrop of the provision of Article 117(2) of the Constitution, while there is no scope for other Courts or Tribunals to deal with the transfer matters of the Government servants, it is highly desirable that the Legislature should consider whether to incorporate the provision in section 7(1) of the Administrative Tribunals. Act, otherwise there will be a Constitutional derailment on the part of the Legislature, as has been observed in the celebrated Masdar Hossain Case, 52 DLR(AD) 82. It is noted that now-a-days the Government servants working in Union Parishad, in different offices. of Upazilla, Districts, Divisions, Directorates and Secretariats are very often complaining against their respective controlling authorities as to their transfer, promotion, accommodation, arrears and other service-related issues and given the above prevailing scenario, if the Administrative Tribunals are not equipped with the power of passing of interim orders, the scheme of our Constitution for setting up Administrative Tribunals would be frustrated. Therefore, time has come for the Bangladesh Law Commission to undertake the issue and work on it.</u>

32. Office is directed to send a copy to the Bangladesh Law Commission for their perusal so that they may actively consider the observation made in the penultimate paragraph of this judgment.

33. With the aforesaid findings and observations, the present Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

End.

Sikder Mahmudur Razi, Advocate ------ For Respondent No. 5.
