Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Bangladesh Secretariat and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
AKM Shahidul Huq J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents Nos. 1-3 to show cause as to why the in action and latches in issuing appointment letters to the petitioner Nos. 1, 2, 4 and 7 for the Post of Bench Assistant and petitioner Nos. 3 and 5 for the post of MLSS and the petitioner No. 6 in the post of Process Server in the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban and failure to accept their joining letters should not be declared to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondent Nos. 1, 2, & 3 should not be directed to appoint the petitioner Nos. 1, 2, 4 and 7 in the post of Bench Assistant and the petitioner No. 3 and 5 in the post of MLSS and the petitioner No. 6 in the post of Process Server in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban Parbattaya Zila as per vide Annexure-C, C-1, E and F to the writ petition and as to why respondent No. 1 and 2 should not be directed to issue fresh Sanction Letter for appointment of the petitioner in the said posts in continuation to the Memo No. 10.132.011.00.00.044.2011-341 dated 6-6-2012 as provided in Clause (gha) to the said Memo Vide annexure-G and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short fact for disposal of the instant Rule is that the petitioners are citizens of Bangladesh and the respondent No. 1 is the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and the respondent No. 2 is the Deputy Secretary (opinion), Law and Justice Department, Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and the respondent No. 3 is the District and Sessions Judge, Bandarban Parbattya Zila, Bandarban and the appointing authority under the SRO No. 46-Ain 2008 and respondent No. 4 is the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban Parbattya Zila, Bandarban and the Chairman of the Selection Committee under SRO No. 46-Ain/2008 and the respondent No. 5 is the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and the respondent No. 6 is the Deputy Commissioner, Bandarban and the addresses given in the cause-title are correct for the purpose of service of notices.

3. The respondent No. 4 issued a Memo No. CJM/B-Ban/2011-95 dated 19-2-2011 for appointment of officers and employees in the vacant posts in the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban in accordance with the জুডিশিয়াল-ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেসী ও মেট্রোপলিটন ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেসীর আদালত সমূহ (সহায়ক কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা, ২০০৮ and with reference to the Memo No. 10.132.011.00.00.044.2011-154 dated 12-4-2011 and the Memo No. 19.132.011.00.00.044.2011-229 dated 23-5-2011 issued from the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh for different posts including Bench Assistant, Typist Copies, Process Server and MLSS and an advertisement was published in the Daily Purbokone on 25th July, 2011.

4. In accordance with the said advertisement the petitioners have applied for their respective posts to Mr La Mong, Chairman, Selection Committee and then Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban now posted as the Additional District and Sessions Judge, Chittagong complying with all the requisites as required in the said advertisement.

5. The said Selection Committee was formed by the respondent No. 3 under office order No. 2 dated 10-7-2011 as the appointing authority under Rule 2(Aa) of the said Rules of 2008.

6. The petitioners have appeared in the written examination, viva voce and practical examinations on different dates fixed by the Selection Committee and being successful in all the three examinations have been selected by the Selection Committee along with forty four others who have also been selected for other posts. The petitioner Nos. 1, 2, 4 and 7 have been selected for the post of Bench Assistant and the petitioner No. 6 for the post of Process Server and the petitioner Nos. 3 and 5 have been selection for the post of MLSS. The names of the petitioner Nos. 3, 5 and 6 was recommended and forwarded by the section Committee on 17-12-2011 under Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2011-162 dated 27-12-2011 and the names of the petitioner Nos. 1, 2, 4 and 7 were also recommended and forwarded to the respondent No. 3, the appointing authority by Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2011-162 dated 1-11-2011 for appointment along with others. The respondent No. 3 made orders to issue their appointment letters on 1-1-2012 and 2-11-2011 respectively.

7. After the final selection, the Selection Committee has advised the petitioners to wait for some time on the ground of filing of a Writ Petition being No. 7257 of 2011 by some of the employees who have been occupying the said posts in the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate on deputation from the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Bandarban prior to the advertisement and after establishment of the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban praying their appointment and thus a waiting list was published by the Selection Committee for the petitioners when forty four officers/ employees in other posts who have appeared in the examinations along with the petitioners and came out successfully have been given issuing appointment letters for the petitioners on the ground of stay order in the writ petition.

8. The said deputed employees voluntarily made an application to the Chief Judicial Magistrate for their release for the purpose of joining to their substantive posts stating that they are not willing to pursue the Writ Petition No. 7257 of 2011 which they filed praying for their appointment in the vacant posts in the court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Chittagong and the respondent No. 4 released them and informed the matter to the Solicitor by Memo No. CJM/Band/2012-305 dated 15-11-2012.

9. On 30-4-2013 the said deputed employees through their Learned Advocate prayed for discharge of the Rule issued in the Writ Petition No. 7257 of 2011 on the ground of non-prosecution and a Division Bench of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, comprising of their Lordships Ms. Justice Farah Mahbub and Mr Justice AKM Zahirul Hoque has been pleased to discharge the Rule for non-prosecution by their order dated 30-4-2013. Though the stay order expired on 13-12-2012 and no further extension was given but the Bench has also been pleased to vacate the order of stay granted earlier by the said order.

10. Upon expiry of the stay order the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban and the Chairman of the Selection Committee by his Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2013-7(ka) dated 6-1-2013 forwarded the list of the petitioners again to the respondent No. 3 namely, the appointing authority and the District and Sessions Judge, Bandarban for their appointment in vacant posts enclosing their names against the respective posts stating that they have been finally selected after written, viva voce and practical examinations in accordance with the Memo No. 10.132.011.00.00.044.2011-154 dated 12-4-2011 and Memo No. 10.132.011.00.00.044.2011-229 dated 23-5-2011 issued by the respondent No.1 but they were kept in the waiting list due to the stay order in the Writ Petition No. 7257 of 2011 and that the writ petitioners came on deputation from the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Bandarban have gone back to their original posts in the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Bandarban voluntarily. In the said Memo the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban has further stated that the other 44 officers/employees who were selected at the same time have already been posted in accordance with the recommendations made under Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2011-137 dated 1-11-2011 and the Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2011-162 dated 27-12-2012. The posts for which the petitioners have been finally selected and kept waiting remained vacant and they are urgently required for smooth functioning of the Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban.

11. On receipt of the said recommendation from the respondent No. 4 the respondent No. 3 namely, the appointing authority and the District and Sessions Judge, Bandarban has published a Notice by his Order No. 37 dated 27-5-2013 under Memo No. Judge/Band/2013-144 dated 27-5-2013 containing Roll numbers of the petitioners and mentioning their posts asking them to appear before him on or before 30-5-2013 with Admit Cards, original Certificates of Academic Qualifications, original nationality Certificates together with all other relevant documents.

12. In compliance with the said Notice the petitioner have appeared before the respondent No. 3 and produced and deposited the original copies of Certificates. The respondent No. 3 has asked the petitioners to join on 6-6-2013 and collect the appointment letters on 6-6-2013 from his office. On 6-6-2013 the petitioners submitted their joining letters to the staff of the respondent No. 3. They were kept waiting for the whole day in the office of the respondent No. 3 on the hope that the respondent No. 3 will arrive shortly in his office but at the end of the day it was made known to them that the respondent No. 3 is on leave and he has solicited opinion and direction from the respondent Nos. 1 and 2.

13. Mr Md Abdus Salam Mamun, with Mr Shajada Akhter Bakul, learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners while Ms. Shuchira Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1.

14. Mr Abdus Salam Mamun learned Advocate submits that the respondents are under legal obligation to accept joining reports of the petitioners and issue them the appointment letters for the post for which they have been selected and recommended for appointment.

15. Learned Advocate further submits that the petitioners have got selection and recommendation for the purpose of appointment in their respective posts by a competent selection committee constituted by the respondent No. 3 in accordance with the provisions of Rule 2 (Chaa) and 4(4) of the জুডিশিয়াল-ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেসী ও মেট্রোপলিটন ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেসীর আদালত সমূহ (সহায়ক কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা, ২০০৮ issued under the SRO 46-Ain/2008  dated 3rd March, 2008 and came out successfully in competitive written, viva voce and practical examinations. They have been called by the respondent No. 3 for appointment and delaying their appointment is illegal and malafide. He further submits that after final selection the petitioners have been kept in the waiting list because order of stay issued in the Writ Petition No. 7257 of 2001 while other 44 co-examinees have been appointed in their respective posts from the same selection and recommendation.

16. He also submits that respondent No. 3 by his order No. 37 and Memo No. Judge/ Band/2013-144 dated 27-5-2013 asked the petitioners to appear before him on 30-5-2013 with their admit Cards, Original Copies of the certificates of academic qualifications, Nationality Certificate and other relevant papers for appointment and the petitioners appeared before him, produced and deposited the Certificates and the respondent No. 3 took their interview and found the petitioners perfectly qualified and delaying their appointment by issuing appointment letters is illegal and malafide.

17. Learned Advocate next submits that petitioner's names are appearing from the list forwarded by the respondent No. 4 under Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2011-137 dated 1-11-2011 and the Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2011-162 dated 27-12-2011 and the appointing authority and the then District and Sessions Judge, Bandarban has passed Orders to issue appointment letters for finally selected candidates on 2-11-2011 and 1-1-2012 which included the names of the petitioner.

18. Learned Advocate also submits that the petitioner have been finally selected by the selection committee and forwarded to the respondent No. 3 on 1-11-2011 and 27-12-2011 along with other candidates but they were kept waiting only because of the stay order which has expired on 13-12-2012 and thereafter the respondent No. 4 again forwarded their names to the respondent No. 4 on 6-1-2013 in continuation of earlier Memos and with recommendation for appointment and inaction on the part of the respondent No. 3 in issuing the appointment letters to the petitioners is arbitrary, malafide, without any lawful authority and as such illegal and void.

19. Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner lastly submits that the respondent No. 1 and 2 are under obligation to extend sanction letter for the posts of the petitioners and latches and in action on their part is illegal, arbitrary, malafide and without lawful authority.

20. Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in course of submissions referred the case of Md Sirajul Islam vs Bangladesh reported in 27 BLD (HCD) 355 (2007) = 60 DLR 79, 15 MLR (AD) 425 (2010), 22 BLD (AD) 199 (2002) = 7 BLC (AD) 144, 22 BLD 387, 23 BLD 7 (2003) = 8 BLC 1, 52 DLR 7, 52 DLR 308. The rule is being contested by Respondent No. 1 by filing affidavit-in-opposition.

21. Ms Shuchira Hossain, learned Assistant Attorney-General in reply to the submissions as advanced by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that respondent No. 3 has solicited opinion and direction from the respondents No. 1 and 2 Vide Memo No. জেজ/বন্দ-৩০১৩-১৪৬ dated 30-5-2013.

22. The learned Assistant Attorney-General further submits that selection committee as a whole did not send any recommendation letter regarding appointment of the petitioners to the appointing authority respondent No. 3. Only Mr La Mong, the then Chief Judicial Magistrate and Chairman of the selection committee, during pendency of the Rule and stay order granted by the Hon'ble High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7257 of 2011 sent solely a recommendation letter for the appointment of the petitioners Vide Memo No. সিজেএম/বাবান/২০১৩ ৭(ক) dated 6-1-2013.

23. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioners as well as the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 1, considered the statement as made in the application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and also considered the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent No. 1 against the writ petition also considered the submissions as well as the citations as referred by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in support of his contention. On perusal of the impugned Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/2011-137 dated 1-11-2011 and Memo No. CJM/Ba-Ban/ 2011-162 dated 27-12-2011 and the Memo No. CJM/BaBan/2013-7(Ka) dated 6-1-2013 issued by Chairman/11, Selection Committee and Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban to the appointing authority, the District Judge, Bandarban Parbattya Zilla, Bandarban vide Annexure-C, C-1 and E to the writ petition and also Order No. 37 dated 27-5-2013 issued under Memo No. Judge Band/2013-144 dated 27-5-2013 issued by learned District Judge and Sessions Judge, Bandarban Parbattya Zila, Vide Annexure-F to the writ petition.

24. In the case of Md Sirajul Islam vs Bangladesh reported in 27 BLD (HCD) 355 (2007) = 60 DLR 79 which runs as follows:

"It is held that "Since the petitioners are all found qualified in the written and viva voce tests and finally selected for appointment to their posts vide advertisement, the petitioners obviously have "Legitimate Expectation" that they will be soon appointed by the respondents and the respondents acted illegally in not doing so apparently for no visible reason."

"When the earlier recruitment process vide advertisement was not completed or cancelled and the petitioners were left hanging about the result of the same the petitioners have legitimate expectation to know the result and final outcome of the recruitment process where they participated pursuance of the advertisement."

25. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Shahinur Bari reported in 15 MLR (AD) 424 (2010), High Court Division which runs as follows:

"The High Court Division held that the legitimate expectation transformed into lawful right of the petitioners"

26. The Appellate Division affirmed the decision of the High Court Division and dismissed the Leave Petition.

27. In the case of Chairman Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury reported in 22 BLD (AD) 199 = 7 BLC (AD) 144, which runs as follows:-

It is held that "an expectation could be based on an express promise or representation or by established past action of settled conduct. The representation must be clear and unmbiguous. It could be a representation to the individual or generally to a class of persons."

"Every such legitimate expectation does not by itself fructify into a right and therefore it does amount to as right in the conventional sense".

28. The High Court Division in arriving its decision in the instant case relying the decisions reported in 1 WLR 1482, 2AC 629 and number of reported decisions of All England Reports.

29. In the case of Bangladesh Soya-Protein Project Ltd. vs Secretary, Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief reported in 22 BLD 378 = 6 BLC 681 which runs as follows:

Government is always under an obligation to act fairly and reasonably even where the other party has got no legal right in the conventional sense. This is so even in the case of a contract where the Government is one of the contracting parties.

30. In the case of Asab Khan vs The Court of Settlement reported in 23 BLD (HCD) 7 (2003) = 8 BLC 1 which runs as follows:-

"Legitimate expectation is a concept of administrative law which means that an administrative authority cannot abuse discretion by disregarding undertaking or statement of its intent. Where an action of the administrative authority adversely affects legal right of an individual, duty to act fairly and reasonably is implicit."

31. In the case of North South Property Development Ltd. vs Ministry of Land reported in 52 DLR 7 which runs as follows:—

"A case of legitimate expectation would arise when a body by representation or by past practice aroused expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill."

32. In the case of Rabia Basri vs Bangladesh Biman reported in 52 DLR 308 which runs as follows:—

"The petitioner's expectations of being absorbed in the service after satisfactory completion of five years’ service cannot but be said to their legitimate expectation and in all fairness they should be absorbed in their service."

33. In the case of MP Sugar Mills Vs State of LIP reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 621 which runs as follows:-

"Doctrine of promissory estoppels has been variously called 'promissory estoppels,' requisite "quasi estoppel' and 'new estoppels'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppels/it is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppels. The true principle of promissory estoppels seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct, made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealing which have taken place between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not."

"This observation of Lord Denning clearly suggests that the parties need not be in any kind of legal relationship before the transaction from which the promissory estoppels takes it origin. The doctrine would seem to apply even where there is no pre-existing legal relationship between the parties, but the promise effect a legal relationship which will arise in further."

"The true promise of promissory estoppels, therefore, seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowledge or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it." If it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppels need not be inhabited by the same limitation as estoppels in the street same of the term. It is equitable principle evolved by the Courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason in logic or principle of promissory estoppel should also not be available as a cause of action if necessary to satisfy the equity.

34. In the case of Commissioner of Customs Vs Monohar Ali reported in 8 BLC (AD) 2003 which runs as follows:-

'The importers having acted on the promise made by the appellants under section 25A of the Act to accept the price determined by the Government appointed inspectors the appellants cannot go back on that promise as it was meant to be binding on them."

35. In the case of Nurunnessa vs Babar Ali Bepari reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 86 = 33 DLR (AD) 124 which runs as follows:

"Promissory estoppels—Government making promise—Promises acting on the promise—No, lack of power of the Government to make the promise-Government bound by the promise."

36. In the case of Central London Property Trust Ltd. vs High Trees House Ltd. (1) Denning J considered the effect of an arrangement made by the parties and concluded.

"Where parties enter into an agreement which is intended to create legal relation between them and in pursuance of such arrangement one party makes a promise to the other which he knows will be acted on and which is in fact acted on by the promise the Court will treat the promise as binding on the promisor to the extent that it will not allow him to act inconsistently with it even though the promise may not supported by consideration in the strict sense."

37. In another case of Secretary Ministry of Industries Nationalized Industries Division vs Saleh Ahmed and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Saleh Ahmed reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 91 where our Apex Court held that "the Government took the decision on agreement to release the mill in question lack of power on the part of the Government to do so is not the plea, rather a belated plea was taken that the decision has been revised by the Government although no such case was made out. Hence applying the aforesaid principle the least that can be said is that the respondents cannot be allowed to act inconsistently and the decision to release the mill remains binding on them. The High Court by the writ has enforced this decision "to complete the formalities for transfer of the mill to the petitioner."

<u>38. On due consideration of the aforesaid we find substance in the Rule. The respondents are under legal obligation to issue the appointment letters for the posts they have got selection and recommendation for the purpose of ; appointment in their respective post by competent selection committee constituted by the respondent No. 3 in accordance with the provisions of Rule 2 (chaa) and 4(4) of the জুডিশিয়াল-ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেসী ও মেট্রোপলিটন ম্যাজিষ্ট্রেসীর আদালতসমূহ (সহায়ক কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারী) নিয়োগ বিধিমালা, ২০০৮ issued under the SRO No. 46-Ain/2008 dated 31d March, 2008 and came out successfully in competitive written, viva voce and practical examinations. They have been called by the respondent No. 3 for appointment and delaying their appointment is illegal and malafide and we also declared fairly to accept the joining letters to have been done without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and respondent No. 1, 2 & 3 are hereby directed to appoint the petitioners No. 1, 2, 4 and 7 in the post of Bench Assistant and the petitioner Nos. 3 and 5 in the post of MLSS and the petitioner No. 6 in the post of Process Server in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bandarban, Parbattaya Zila, as per vide Annexure-C, C-1, E and F to the writ petition and also respondent No. 1 and 2 are hereby directed to issue fresh sanction letter for appointment of the petitioners in the said posts in continuation to the Memo No. 10.132.011.00.00.0044.2011-341 dated 6-6-2012 as provided in clause (gha) to the Memo vide Annexure -G to the writ petition.</u>

39. Accordingly, the Rule is hereby made absolute.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute, without any order as to costs. The impugned Memo Vide Annexure-G to the writ petition is hereby declared to have been done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

End.

full_judgment:
Zafar Ahmed J: In this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure Rule was issued on 23-6-2011 upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned order No. 80 dated 19-8-2010 passed by the learned District Judge, Bogra in Money Execution Case No. 10 of 2000 now pending in the Court of District Judge, Bogra should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule this Court passed an ad-interim order staying all further proceeding of Money Execution Case subject to payment of a sum of Taka 2,00,000 to the decree-holder opposite-party within 6 (six) months. It appears that pursuant to the said order the petitioner on 18-12-2011 paid Taka 1,00,000 on 17-1-2012 Taka 50,000, on 8-2-2012 Taka 50,000 and on 8-5-2012 Taka 50,000 total Taka 2,50,000 in LA/C No. বগ 524, through Sonali Bank, Bogra Branch to the opposite party.

3. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that the opposite party namely Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, Regional Office, Bogra (in short the 'BHBFC') as applicant on 30-4-1998 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1998 in the Court of District Judge, Bogra under Article 27 of the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 (President's Order No. 7 of 1973, hereinafter referred to as the 'Order, 1973') against the borrower-present petitioner (hereinafter referred to as the 'borrower') praying for amongst others an order for sale of the schedule mentioned property for realization of outstanding dues of Taka 4,91,142.94 as on 31-1-1998 and for an order to pay interest at the rate of 17.5% with penal interest as per terms and conditions of the mortgage deed till realization of the money.

4. It has been stated in the application of the Miscellaneous Case that on an application of the borrower to construct a building on the scheduled land, the BHBFC opened loan case No. BaGa 524 and after completion of the required formalities granted a loan of Taka 1,85,000 in favour of the borrower. Thereafter, as per application of the borrower the BHBFC granted additional loan of Taka 27,000. By accepting the terms and conditions of the loan the borrower on 28-2-1983 and 27-12-1983 respectively executed and registered mortgaged deed in favour of the BHBFC and the latter vide cheques issued on different dates paid Taka 1,85,000 and Taka 27,000 total Taka 2,12,000 to the borrower, the last cheque being issued on 7-10-1983. With the money given by the BHBFC, the borrower completed the construction of the house.

5. It has further been stated in the said application that as per terms and conditions of the loan the borrower was liable to pay interest at the rate of 13% on both the principal and the additional loan. For the principal loan the payable monthly installment was Taka 1,795.59 and for the additional loan the monthly installment was Taka 239.44. The borrower obtained the rebate facility and reduction of interest rate given by the Government and the monthly payable installment was rescheduled at Taka 3,250.93 which the borrower was liable to pay from 1-7-1994. In spite of repeated reminders by the BHBFC, the borrower failed to pay the principal amount in 43 instalments and the interest in 40 instalments which stood as on 31-1-1998 with penal interest at Taka 1,32,497.15 and the total amount payable as on 31-1-1998 was Taka 4,91,142.94.

6. The borrower i.e. the present petitioner did not contest the Miscellaneous Case. The BHBFC examined Md Abdur Rahman as a sole witness and produced sanction letters (exhibit 1, 1(ka)) and mortgage deed (exhibit 2).

7. The Miscellaneous case was heard and disposed of ex-parte and the learned District Judge, Bogra vide order dated 26-11-1998 allowed the same and granted the BHBFC permission to attach the scheduled property and sell the same through auction for realization of Taka 4,91,142.94 and further to realize interest at the rate of 17.5% till realization of the same.

8. On 24-8-2000 the BHBFC filed Money Execution Case No. 10 of 2000 before the District Judge, Bogra. The borrower entered appearance in the said Execution Case on 14-10-2004.

9. Pending disposal of the Execution case, the borrower on 22-11-2007 filed an application in the Miscellaneous case under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure (in short 'CPC') and Article 27(7)(d) of the Order, 1973 for amendment of the operating part of the ex-parte order dated 16-11-1998 passed in the Miscellaneous case thus: মাননীয় আদালতের ২৬-১১-৯৮ তারিখের আদেশের শেষাংশে প্রার্থকের দাবীকৃত সমুদয় টাকা আদায় কালতক এরপর ১৭১/২%  সুদ পাইবে, তাহা সংশোধিত হইয়া মর্গেজ দলিলের শর্ত ও কর্পোরেশনের নিয়ম অনুসারে প্রার্থক সুদ পাইবে”। The said application was allowed vide order dated 3-3-2008 passed in the Miscellaneous Case. Thereafter, the BHBFC on 30-7-2009 filed an application in the Execution Case for amendment of the application of the said Execution Case for deleting the words 17.5% interest rate' as mentioned in paragraph Nos. 7 and 10 of the said application and inserting the words to realize interest as per terms and conditions of the mortgage deed and rules of the Corporation' in its place. The Court below vide order dated 19-1-2010 allowed the application of the BHBFC.

10. It appears from the order dated 19-1-2010 passed in the Money Execution Case that a dispute arose as to actual amount of outstanding money due to the BHBFC by the borrower. The relevant portion of the said order dated 19-1-2010 runs thus:

"It appears from the record that there is a dispute about the amount of the claim of decree holder. Two separate statements of account as regards claim of the decree holder HBFC but the amount mentioned in the calculation sheet of that decree holder and that of judgment are quite different. In order to ascertain the actual claim as per prevalent rules of HBFC both side are directed to sit together to arrive at a consensus amount of claim of decree holder. To 17-2-10 for filing a consensus amount by both sides."

11. However, the consensus amount was not filed in the Court.

12. The Court below vide order dated 25-4-2010 directed the BHBFC to submit the actual claim and the BHBFC submitted the same in the Court on 26-5-2010. On 19-8-2010 the statements of account submitted by the BHBFC was taken up for hearing. The borrower prayed for an adjournment of the hearing which was rejected and the statement of account submitted by the BHBFC claiming Taka 4,42,871.16 as outstanding dues was accepted by the Court. Challenging this order the borrower moved the instant revisional application, obtained a Rule and order of stay.

13. The Rule has been contested by the BHBFC by filing counter-affidavit.

14. During the course of hearing both the borrower-petitioner and the BHBFC-opposite party filed several sets of affidavits annexing various types of documents in support of their respective claims. The contesting parties also filed up to date statements of accounts refuting the accounts submitted by the other side.

15. The learned advocate for the borrower-petitioner vehemently argues that the borrower has repaid the full dues and in fact he has paid more and as such the BHBFC may be directed to return the excess money to the borrower. On the other hand, by filing the counter affidavit dated 8-1-2015 the BHBFC claimed that till November 2014 the borrower has paid Taka 6,92,743.91 which includes Taka 2,50,000 paid after issuance of the Rule and the outstanding amount remains at Taka 3,42,015.99.

16. As per order of this Court the records of the Money Execution Case No. 10 of 2000 have been transmitted to this Court. We also directed the learned Advocate of the BHBFC to produce the relevant file of the loan case and accordingly, learned Advocate produced the same before us.

17. We have perused the revisional application, several sets of affidavits filed by both the parties and documents annexed thereto. We have also perused the records of the Money Execution Case and the loan case.

18. Upon perusal of the above mentioned records a more fundamental question arose other than the issue centered around the dispute in respect of statements of accounts which is whether the ex-parte order dated 26-11-1998 passed in the Miscellaneous Case and the Money Execution Case arising thereof are maintainable.

19. In the Money Execution Case the borrower on 4-6-2009 filed an application under Order XXI, rules 2 and 69 and section 151 of CPC and Article 27(7)(d) of the Order, 1973 (Annexure-F) for staying the auction proceedings to be held on 15-6-2009. In the said application it has been categorically stated that the borrower did not withdraw the additional loan amount of Taka 27,000. It was alleged in the said application that the BHBFC had committed fraud upon the Court.

20. The BHBFC on 30-7-2009 filed a written objection (Annexure-G) denying the allegations of fraud. However, in the said written objection it admitted that it had granted an additional loan amount of Taka 27,000 to the borrower, but the latter only received the cheque of Taka 14,000 and did not receive the cheque of Taka 13,000. The borrower repaid Taka 14,000 with interest in the financial year 1986-87. It was further stated in the written objection that although in the application of the Miscellaneous Case the BHBFC mentioned about the additional loan but it did not claim the said amount, it only claimed the principal loan amount of Taka 1,85,000 and interest accrued thereon.

21. In the application of the Miscellaneous Case (Annexure-A) it has been stated inter alia:

“প্রার্থনা বিভিন্ন তারিখে বিভিন্ন চেক মূলে ১,৮৫,০০০ টাকা এবং ২৭,০০০ টাকা একুনে ২,১২,০০০ টাকা উক্ত ঋণ গ্রহীতাকে প্রদান করেন ৷ প্রার্থক সর্বশেষ ইং ৭-১০-৮৩ তারিখে চেক প্রদান করে এবং প্রতিপক্ষ কর্তৃক বাংলাদেশ সরকারের অর্থ মন্ত্রণালয় প্রদত্ত রেয়াত সুবিধা গ্রহণের পরও সরকার কর্তৃক সুদের হার হ্রাস করার ফলে ৩,২৫০.৯৩ টাকা কিস্তি পুনঃ নির্ধারিত হয়।যাহা ১-৭-৯৪ তারিখ হইতে পরিশোধ যোগ্য বটে।

বন্ধকী দলিলের শর্ত মোতাবেক প্রতিপক্ষ ঋণ গ্রহীতা ঋণের শেষ কিস্তির টাকা যে মাসে গ্রহণ করিবে তাহার পরবর্তী ৩য় মাসের প্রথম দিন হইতে মাসিক কিস্তি পরিশোধ করিতে শুরু করিবে৷ কিন্তু প্রতিপক্ষ প্রার্থক কর্পোরেশনের তলব তাগাদা সত্বেও ৪র্থ মাসের আসল টাকায় মাসিক কিস্তি এবং ৪০ মাসের কিস্তির টাকা পরিশোধে ব্যর্থ হয়।ঐরূপভাবে প্রতিপক্ষ ৪৩ মাসের আসল এবং ৪০ মাসের সুদেৱ কিস্তির টাকা পরিশোধে ব্যর্থ হইলে ৩১-১-৯৮ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত দণ্ড সুদ সহ কেয়ার পরিমাণ ১,৩২,৪৯৭.১৫ টাকা।

উক্ত প্রকারে প্রতিপক্ষ প্রার্থক কর্পোরেশনের মাসিক কিস্তির টাকা ও সুদের টাকা পরিশোধে ব্যর্থ হইঁয়াও মঞ্জুরীপত্র এবং বন্ধকী দলিলের শর্ত ভঙ্গ করিয়াছে। প্রার্থক কর্পোরেশন প্রতিপক্ষ এর নিকট হইতে ৩১-১-৯৮ তারিখ পর্যন্ত সমস্ত পাওনা একযোগে ৪,৯১,১৪২.৯৭ টাকা আদায়ের হকদার হইতেছে৷”

22. Our attention has been drawn to a letter lying with the loan case file which is dated 30-4-1992 issued by the Regional Manager, Bogra of the BHBFC. By this letter the borrower was informed about various matters relating to payment of instalments, rates of interest, rebate facility etc. In the said letter it was mentioned that the borrower has taken a loan of Taka 2,12,000 from the BHBFC. The relevant portion of the said letter is quoted below:

উপরোক্ত ঋণ কেসের মাধ্যমে আপনি অত্র কর্পোরেশন হতে মোট = ২,১২,০০০ টাকা ঋণ গ্রহন করেছেন৷ কর্পোরেশনের বকেয়া/ সম্পূর্ণ ব্যাংক-৪/গৃনিঋক-১০/৮৭ (অংশ)/৮৩ নং পত্রে বাংলাদেশ সরকারের অর্থমন্ত্রণালয় কতিপয় রেয়াত সুবিধা প্রদান করেছ���ন যা-নিম্নে উদৃত করা হলঃ

23. It clearly appears from the above quoted extracts that the BHBFC claimed that the borrower received the additional loan amount of Taka 27,000. In the application of the Miscellaneous Case the BHBFC did not provide any details or break down of accounts. The application simply states that the borrower failed to repay the loan in 43 monthly instalments and the interest in 40 instalments. Therefore, without any details of accounts and in the absence of any statement that the money claimed excludes the additional loan amount of Taka 27,000, it appears that the total claimed amount includes the additional loan amount of Taka 27,000 and the interest accrued thereon.

24. There is another aspect of the case which requires judicial scrutiny. It appears from the application of the Miscellaneous Case the BHBFC claimed that the total outstanding as on 31-1-1998 stood at Taka 4,91,142.94 which includes penal interest. The prayer portion of the application as contained in paragraph No. 10(ka) states: “আরজী বর্ণিত ৩১-১-৯৮ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত ৪,৯১,১৪২.৯৪ টাকা আদায়ের নিমিত্তে নিম্ন তপশীল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তি দেওয়ানী কার্যবিধি আইনের বিধান অনুযায়ী আদালত যোগে নিলাম বিক্রয়ের আদেষ দিতে মর্জি হয়৷”The learned District Judge vide order dated 26-11-1998 allowed the Miscellaneous Case and the prayer 10(ka). So, admittedly the BHBFC claimed penal interest which was allowed by the Court below.

25. Now, the question is whether the BHBFC is permitted under the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973, Order, 1973 (President's Order No. 7 of 1973) and Regulations made thereunder to claim penal interest.

26. PO 7 of 1973 is silent about the nature and rates of interest. Clause (10) of Article 21 of the Order, 1973 states. "The rate of interest chargeable on loans made by the Corporation shall be determined by the Government from time to time." Under clause 2(c) of Article 37 of the Order, 1973 the conditions subject to which the Corporation may grant loan will be regulated by the Regulation made under the Order. Under regulation 11 of the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Loan Regulations, 1977 (in short the BHBFC 'Regulations, 1977') the BHBFC is permitted to charge simple interest on all loan remaining outstanding due to it. Regulations 1977 has been repealed by the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Regulations, 1996 (in short 'the Regulations, 1996') which was published in Bangladesh Gazette on 25-9-1997. Regulation 11 of Regulations, 1996 contains identical provisions to that of Regulation 11 of the repealed Regulations, 1977 i.e. simple interest shall be charged on all loans. For ready reference regulation 11 of Regulations, 1996 is quoted below:

"Simple interest shall be charged on all loans remaining outstanding due the House Building Finance Corporation established under the House Building Finance Corporation (Act VIII of 1952) and transferred to & vested in the Corporation with effect on and from the 1st April, 1971."

27. So, under both the repealed Regulations, 1977 and Regulations, 1996 the BHBFC is permitted to charge simple interest on all loans, not the penal interest.

28. The most shocking aspect of the case, as it appears from the letter dated 16-11-1994 issued by the Regional Manager, Bogra to the borrower which has been lying with the loan case file, is that the BHBFC used to charge penal interest as matter of custom which has been abolished from 1-10-1993. For ready reference paragraph 5 of the said letter is quoted below:

“১-১০-১৯৯৩ তারিখ হতে দণ্ড সুদ এর প্রথা রহিত করা হয়েছে। তবে, সরকারী নির্দেশ অনুযায়ী ১২টির অধিক কিস্তি থেলাপী হলে বকেয়া আসনের উপর ২% অতিরিক্ত সুদ চার্জ করা হবে৷ এ চার্জকৃত সুদ পরবর্তী জমা হতে প্রচলিত নিয়মে সমন্বয় করা হয়ে ৷ ভবিষ্যতে সরকার/কর্পোরেশন এর পরিচালনা বোর্ড কর্তৃক অতিরিক্ত সুদের হার পরিবর্তন করা হলে অথবা দণ্ড সুদ প্রথা পুনপ্রবর্তীত হলে পরির্বীত হারে সুদ পরিশোধ করতে আপনি/আপনারা বাধ্য থাকবেন।”

29. The BHBFC, in the first place, was not permitted under the law to charge penal interest. Nevertheless, the custom of charging penal interest has been abolished from 1-10-1993. The case was filed on 30-4-1998 by the Regional Office, Bogra. In the application it has been categorically stated that the outstanding dues include penal interest in spite of the fact that the BHBFC had knowledge that law does not permit it to charge penal interest on loans and the custom of charging the same has been abolished from 1-10-1993.

30. Facts narrated above are summarised thus: firstly, the BHBFC claimed in the application of the Miscellaneous Case that it gave the borrower additional loan amount of Taka 27,000 and accordingly ex-parte order dated 26-11-1998 was passed. Subsequently, in the Execution Case the BHBFC admitted that the borrower in fact availed additional loan of Taka 14,000 which he repaid with interest long before filing the case and he did not avail the additional loan of Taka 13,000. In spite of this admission by the BHBFC, it did not take any step to amend the application of the Miscellaneous Case and the ex-parte order, and secondly, the BHBFC had knowledge that it is not permitted under the relevant Regulations to charge penal interest on loans and the custom of charging penal interest has been abolished since 1-10-1993. Nevertheless, in the application of the Miscellaneous Case it claimed penal interest on loans which was allowed vide the ex-parte order. In view of this admitted position we have no hesitation to hold that the case of the BHBFC is based upon falsehood and fraud. The BHBFC committed fraud upon both the borrower and the Court.

31. In SP Chengalvaraya Naidu vs Jagannath (1994) 1 SCC 1 it has been observed, "The Courts of law are meant for imparting justice between the parties. ...We have no hesitation to say that a person, whose case is based on false-hood, has no right to approach the Court. He can be summarily thrown out at any stage of the litigation. ... A fraud is an act of deliberate deception with the design of securing something by taking advantage of another. It is a deception in order to gain by another's loss. It is a cheating intended to get an advantage. A litigant, who approaches the Court is bound to produce all the documents executed by him, which are relevant to the litigation. If he withholds a vital document in order to gain advantage on the other side then he would be guilty of playing fraud on the Courts as well as on the opposite party."

32. In the famous case of Lazarus Estates Ltd. vs Beasley (1956) 1 QB 702 Lord Denning said,

"No judgment of a Court, no order of a Minister can be allowed to stand if it has been obtained by fraud.

Fraud unravels everything."

<u>33. Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation is a statutory body created by PO 7 of 1973. But unfortunately in the instant case it behaved in an unscrupulous manner like a high street shark loan company. It reminds us of the character 'Shylock' as depicted by William Shakespeare in the drama The Merchant of Venice' written in the late 16th century.</u>

<u>34. We are mindful of the fact that in the instant civil revision filed under section 115(1) of CPC, the borrower has challenged the legality of the order dated 19-8-2010 passed in the Money Execution Case. Neither the Execution proceedings nor the ex-parte order dated 26-11-1998 passed in the Miscellaneous Case, from which the Execution Case arose, has been challenged. But, upon scrutiny of facts, circumstances and laws discussed above, in particular when we have found a definite case of fraud on part of the BHBFC, if we confine ourselves to the impugned order, the same would occasion failure of justice. We have to decide now, what should be the appropriate order that we should pass.</u>

<u>35. It is now well settled principle of law that in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the High Court Division has wide power to do justice in a case and in appropriate case where the order under revision is set aside this Court can pass any consequential order necessitated by the facts of the case.</u>

36. In Jatindra Nath Nandi vs Krishnadhan Nandi, 56 CWN 858 it was held,

"In any event, this Court is perfectly competent to see that proper orders are made when the matter comes up in revision before this Court. The mere fact that the plaintiffs did not move should not stand in the way of this Court making an order in accordance with law, as all the necessary parties are represented before us."

37. In the case of Md Shajahan Khan vs Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Munshiganj 11 BLT (AD) 60 it was held by our apex Court that,

It is well settled that once the conditions in section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure are satisfied and the High Court's jurisdiction to interfere is established, the proceedings as a whole from start to finish can be scrutinized and any order necessary for doing justice may be passed. There is no limit to the area in which the revisional power is to be exercised by the High Court Division in the facts and circumstances of each case."

38. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case and in view of the above mentioned decided cases, we are of the opinion that in order to secure the ends of justice the appropriate order that we should pass is to set aside the ex-parte order dated 26-11-1998 passed in the Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1998 and the entire proceedings of the Money Execution Case No. 10 of 2010 arising out of the said Miscellaneous Case. However, the BHBFC is at liberty to amend the application of the Miscellaneous Case, if after settling the accounts of the borrower-petitioner, any outstanding arrear remains due to it. In settling the accounts the BHBFC must adhere to the observations made in this judgment and follow the relevant circulars time to time by it and comply with the provisions of the BHBFC Regulations, 1996 in particular, clauses (iv), (v), (vii) and (viii) of regulation 10. Be it mentioned here that clause (vii) of regulation 10 has been amended and replaced by a new clause (vii) in 1999 which has been published in the Gazette on 25.07.1999. For ready reference the relevant clauses of regulation 10 of Regulations, 1996 mentioned above are reproduced below:

10 (iv) The total amount of loan with interest & charges shall be recoverable within such period as shall be stipulated in the mortgage deed or agreement of hypothecation or pledge, as the case may be, or as may be subsequently extended & rescheduled by the Corporation under intimation to the borrower:

10 (v) The nature and rates of interest & the mode of repayment, adjustment thereof will be determined by the Corporation from time to time:

10 (vii) If the borrower does not pay or is not willing to pay IDCP in the manner prescribed in Regulation 10 (vi) above, it may be added to the principal & be repayable by the borrower concerned at monthly instalments along with the monthly instalments fixed initially and in that event the amount of monthly instalments shall be revised and refixed by the Corporation: (this is the original text prior to amendment)

10 (vii) If the borrower does not pay or is not willing to pay IDCP in the manner prescribed in Regulation 10(vi) above, it shall be added to the normal interest and be repayable by the concerned borrower at monthly instalments together with the monthly instalments of loan fixed initially and in that event the amount of monthly instalments of loan shall be revised or refixed by the Corporation: (the amended text)

10 (viii) In case of regular repayment of dues by monthly instalments the principal & interest will be adjusted as per re-payment schedule fixed by the Corporation. In the event of default, the sum of or sums of money repaid or recovered against the loan account concerned, will be adjusted firstly with the defaulted interest including additional interest (if any) and the residue (if any), will be adjusted with the principal. In case of advance payments the amount paid in advance will be adjusted with the principal subject to being readjusted with subsequent defaulted instalments and the balance (if any) with the principal.

39. The term 'IDCP' referred to in clause (vii) of regulation 10 above means "the interest during construction period i.e. the interest chargeable/charged on each amount of the principal advanced to the borrower concerned from the date of delivery of the first cheque to the date of delivery of the last cheque and such other period as may be determined by the BHBFC from time to time, (clause (c) of regulation 1A(1) of Regulations, 1996).

Principal': means and includes the total amount given by the Corporation to a borrower as loan, plus the amount chargeable as insurance premium/Risk Guarantee Fund subscription, legal charge, IDCP (if any) and other statutory costs (if any), (clause (a) of regulation 1A(1) of Regulations, 1996).

'Normal interest': means and includes the interest which is not compound and chargeable/charged on the principal as the rate/rates fixed or refixed by the Corporation from time to time, (clause (b) of regulation 1A(1) of Regulations, 1996).

40. The amended application, if any, must comply with the provisions of clause 2 of Article 27 of the PO 7 of 1973 which provides that the application shall state the nature and extent of the liability of the borrower and his surety to the BHBFC, the grounds on which it is made and such other particulars as may be prescribed.

41. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The ex-parte order dated 26-11-1998 passed in the Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1998 by the learned District Judge, Bogra and the entire proceedings of the Money Execution Case No. 10 of 2010 arising out of the said Miscellaneous Case now pending in the Court of District Judge, Bogra are set aside. Since the Money Execution case is set aside the BHBFC-opposite party is directed to return Taka 2,50,000 (two lacs fifty thousand) to the borrower-petitioner which has been paid to it by the latter after issuance of the instant Rule within a period of 1 (one) month from the date of receipt of this judgment. The BHBFC is at liberty to amend the application of the Miscellaneous Case within a period of 1(one) month from the date of receipt of this judgment, if after settling the accounts of the borrower, any outstanding arrear remains due to it. On the other hand, if it transpires that the borrower has paid excess money to the BHBFC, the same would be returned to him within this period.

42. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case the BHBFC-opposite party is directed to pay a cost of Taka 1,00,000 (one lakh) to the borrower-petitioner within a period of 1 (one) month from the date of receipt of this judgment.

Send down the judgment and order along with the LCR of Money Execution Case No. 10 of 2010 at once. The learned Advocate for the BHBFC opposite party is permitted to take back the original file of the loan case.

End.
